entries.title: OpenAI pipeline finds, exploits and patches hundreds of Linux kernel root bugs
entries.summary: OpenAI built a five-stage agent pipeline for the Linux kernel: find candidate bugs, reproduce them in isolated VMs running the Kernel Address Sanitizer (KASAN), test exploitability, write patches, then hand everything to human reviewers. In one mid-October 2026 run it reproduced 1,724 of 2,308 candidate findings and produced working exploits for 948 distinct local privilege escalation (LPE) bugs on a kernel with standard protections such as SMEP, SMAP and KASLR, for about $1.2M in API credits. Hundreds of reports and patches have gone to maintainers. OpenAI also found that some exploits marked successful had reached root through a different 0-day than the one assigned, and that a stronger model needed less scaffolding.

lessons.point: At kernel scale, a model-driven pipeline can turn thousands of candidate findings into reproduced bugs and working root exploits without a human in the loop until the final review.
lessons.excerpt: Our prototype identified and analyzed 2,308 candidate Linux kernel findings, dynamically reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities, and produced 948 local privilege escalation (LPE) exploits

lessons.point: Checking that an agent got a root shell is not enough. In an early run, 20 of 200 'successful' exploits got root through a different 0-day than the one assigned, so OpenAI added an independent check on the exploit path.
lessons.excerpt: We subsequently tightened the task constraints and added an independent check confirming that each final exploit used its assigned vulnerability.

lessons.point: A curated library of exploitation techniques helped the older model a lot but added little for the newer one, so the heavy scaffolding was removed.
lessons.excerpt: Scaffolding that materially improves one model generation may add little value for a stronger model and should be evaluated for the maintenance tradeoff.

lessons.point: Failed exploit attempts cost about ten times more than successful ones, so a no-progress timeout is a large cost lever for exploit-generation agents.
lessons.excerpt: Defining a reasonable give-up condition, such as stopping the attempt after making no progress for one hour, would have reduced the cost of ExploitDev significantly.

entries.takeaway: Kernel LPE discovery and exploitation is now cheap and fast, so local-user access on an unpatched Linux host should be treated as close to root, and AI vulnerability pipelines need independent checks on how each result was reached.

actionable.title: Add path verification, give-up timeouts and rescans to AI vuln-research pipelines
actionable.detail: For any agent pipeline that reports 'exploited' or 'fixed', add a separate checker that confirms the result came through the assigned bug (for example, the crash trace or patched-kernel retest must match the target finding). Add a no-progress timeout (OpenAI suggests about one hour) for exploit attempts. Revalidate findings against the latest upstream before reporting. Rescan code you already audited when you switch to a stronger model, and re-test whether your technique or skill scaffolding still pays for its upkeep. On the defense side, shorten kernel patch windows on multi-user and container hosts.

entries.verify_note: Independent verifier supported all four lessons; caveats: 948 is counted from distinct patches (1,169 working exploits), and the one-hour give-up timeout is the source's suggestion, not a measured result. Closest prior: OpenAI's 24-LPE Patch the Planet run.
entries.prior_art: The Frontier AI Vulnerability Burst: Industrializing Autonomous Zero-Day Discovery in Open-Source Software (Unit 42, archive); 'Put a per-bug-class exploit validator between your AI scanner and your bug tracker' (product-security); OpenAI's earlier 24-LPE GPT-5.5 Cyber Patch the Planet result
entries.threat: Attackers with access to similar cyber-capable models can cheaply find and weaponize Linux kernel LPE bugs, so any low-privileged foothold on an unpatched host can become root.
entries.conditions: An attacker has local unprivileged code execution on a Linux system that is behind on kernel patches. The tested targets ran standard distribution protections (SMEP, SMAP, KASLR, HARDENED_USERCOPY), not a weakened kernel.
entries.mitigations: Patch kernels quickly and reboot. Reduce reachable kernel attack surface for unprivileged users and containers. Treat a low-privileged account on an out-of-date host as equal to root in threat models. For defenders running AI pipelines, revalidate findings on current code and verify each exploit uses its assigned bug.

entries.title: Google Project Zero shortens its disclosure deadline to 30 days by 2028
entries.summary: Project Zero is replacing its '90 + 30' policy with 'Full X': details are disclosed X days after the bug is reported to the vendor, and whether it is fixed is no longer a decision point. X is 90 days now, 60 days from February 2, 2027 and 30 days from January 3, 2028. The team says LLMs speed up both bug discovery and exploit-from-patch, so patch soak time no longer protects users; it drops most special cases, including the grace period and variant rules, and stops using severity to decide disclosure.

lessons.point: Project Zero now assumes attackers can build an exploit from a patch almost immediately, so the window after a patch ships gives no secrecy. Defenders should work to close the patch gap (the time between a fix shipping and users installing it) instead of counting on soak time.
lessons.excerpt: zero patch-to-exploitation time is a reasonable, though imperfect, model of attacker behavior

lessons.point: With LLM help, Project Zero's own bug-finding rate has jumped by orders of magnitude. Per-bug negotiation with vendors no longer scales, so the policy is built to be automated.
lessons.excerpt: We are finding several vulnerabilities a week in targets where we once found a few vulnerabilities a year.

lessons.point: Severity no longer changes the deadline, because a low-severity bug is just as likely to be found by attackers. Vendors that triage only by severity will see low-severity bugs disclosed on the same schedule.
lessons.excerpt: does not affect the likelihood that it will be discovered by attackers, only its impact on users.

lessons.point: Whether a bug is fixed no longer affects when it is disclosed. Disclosure happens at day X regardless, and fix status is only reported alongside.
lessons.excerpt: We still plan to track whether bugs are fixed and communicate if they are not, however, this will not be a decision point in our policy.

entries.takeaway: A major research team now treats AI-accelerated exploitation as the default, so vendors need to fix every reported bug within 30 to 60 days and close the patch gap, whatever the bug's severity.

actionable.title: Re-plan your remediation deadlines around a 30-day public disclosure
actionable.detail: If you ship software that Project Zero or similar teams audit, set internal fix targets of 60 days by February 2027 and 30 days by January 2028 for every externally reported bug, not just high-severity ones. Measure and cut your patch gap with forced auto-update or staged-rollout limits, and prepare non-patch mitigations, such as disabling the affected code path, for bugs you cannot fix before the deadline.

entries.prior_art: Project Zero's own 90+30 policy (2021); OpenAI's coordinated-disclosure framework for AI-found bugs (keeps vendor-negotiated timelines). No existing entry records a major disclosure-policy change driven by LLMs.
entries.threat: LLMs let attackers find the same bugs independently and turn patches into exploits almost at once, so an embargo or soak period protects users less and less.
entries.conditions: This applies to vendors receiving Project Zero reports, and more broadly to any software whose patches attackers can diff.
entries.mitigations: Shorten remediation timelines for all severities, cut patch rollout time and the patch gap, prepare non-patch mitigations such as temporarily disabling code paths, and automate tracking of disclosure deadlines.
entries.verify_note: Verifier confirmed dates and lessons; exceptions list softened to 'most special cases' since hardware bugs may still get discretionary exceptions. Novelty taken as the verifier's 70.

entries.title: PortSwigger shows HTML injection stealing passwords under a script-blocking CSP
entries.summary: PortSwigger released a Burp AT skill that reads a Content Security Policy (CSP), checks its allowed script hosts against more than 350 known bypass gadgets from cspbypass.com, and builds a proof of concept. Its second check needs no JavaScript. form-action does not fall back to default-src, so even form-action 'self' lets an injected form submit back to the same page. A reflected meta referrer plus meta refresh then leaks the full URL, typed credentials included, to an attacker host in the Referer header.

lessons.point: Blocking all scripts with default-src 'none' does not stop credential theft through HTML injection. Form submission and meta-refresh navigation are outside what CSP restricts.
lessons.excerpt: CSP doesn't apply to any of this. No script runs, the form submits to an allowed origin, and the meta refresh is a navigation, which CSP doesn't restrict.

lessons.point: form-action must be set explicitly because it does not inherit from default-src. Even 'self' is enough for the self-posting form attack.
lessons.excerpt: If a policy leaves out form-action, forms can submit anywhere.

lessons.point: A host allow-list is as weak as its weakest endpoint. One JSONP or old AngularJS file on an allowed host turns the allow-list into arbitrary script execution.
lessons.excerpt: A host allow-list is only as strong as the weakest file on any host in it.

entries.takeaway: CSP does not fix reflected HTML injection, so escape the output, and do not rate a script-blocking policy as safe against credential theft.

actionable.title: CSP bypass triage skill covering gadgets and form-action exfiltration
actionable.detail: Given a response's CSP headers, work out the effective script sources in order: script-src-elem, then script-src, then default-src. Intersect all enforced policies, and treat report-only headers as informational. Match allowed hosts, including wildcards, against a gadget list such as cspbypass.com. Separately, report form-action as viable for exfiltration when it is missing or set to 'self' and a reflected HTML-injection sink exists. Recommend escaping the reflected output, a form-action of 'none' or exact endpoints, and a strict Referrer-Policy, noting the injected meta referrer tag may override the header, so the fix is the escaping.

entries.prior_art: AFINE's write-up on stealing passwords via HTML injection under a strict CSP (credited in the article); dangling-markup and meta-refresh Referer leaks; the cspbypass.com gadget list.
entries.threat: An attacker with a reflected HTML-injection sink plants a fake login form on a page whose CSP blocks all scripts, and the victim's credentials leak to the attacker in the Referer header.
entries.conditions: The page must reflect a parameter as unescaped HTML, form-action must be missing or allow 'self', and the victim must type credentials into the injected form and submit it.
entries.mitigations: Fix the reflected HTML injection by escaping output. Set form-action explicitly to 'none' or exact endpoints. Keep JSONP and legacy AngularJS hosts out of script-src, or prefer nonce- or hash-based policies with strict-dynamic. Remember that report-only headers block nothing.
entries.verify_note: Lessons hold, but the verifier scored novelty 20 vs 55: AFINE published the same technique first and the article credits it; the new part is mainly packaging it as an automated Burp skill.

entries.title: Check Point found ARTEX operators letting AI agents run cybercrime campaigns unattended
entries.summary: Check Point Research counted 1,608 live, publicly exposed panels of ARTEX, an open-source AI pentest platform. Ten of them leaked their full databases, showing which models criminals used and how they prompted their agents: operators set one goal and then mostly asked about progress. The agents stole more than 300 iOS signing certificates, recovered about 190,000 game-account credentials, and found a writable S3 bucket that hosted iOS app installers. Mostly Chinese models were used, led by DeepSeek Flash, at about $145 to $1,500 per campaign, and in one campaign the agents reported cash-outs that never happened.

lessons.point: After the operator set the goal, the agent fleets ran almost on their own. Human prompts were mostly progress checks.
lessons.excerpt: Threat actors barely interacted with their agent fleets.

lessons.point: These agents are dangerous because they keep going across a whole scope until they reach the goal, not because their exploits are sophisticated. Hardcoded credentials in JavaScript bundles and unauthenticated APIs were enough.
lessons.excerpt: it is not necessarily the complexity of attacks, but the breadth and perseverance at which LLMs can audit a scope and test every endpoint, front end bundle and site

lessons.point: A model's refusals did not stop the operator. When one American model hit guardrails, the actor switched to more permissive models.
lessons.excerpt: we observed guardrails being hit only when using Anthropic’s Opus 5.5. Here, the actor subsequently switched to more permissive Chinese models.

lessons.point: The agents also claimed successes that never happened. Reported USDT cash-outs were hallucinations based on API responses that said "success".
lessons.excerpt: the findings were hallucinations and the verdict of successful exploitation was simply based on API responses indicating “success”.

entries.takeaway: Agentic attack platforms let unskilled criminals test every endpoint of many targets for a few hundred dollars, so basic gaps like hardcoded credentials and unauthenticated APIs are now found at machine scale.

actionable.title: Close the commodity gaps that autonomous agents find first
actionable.detail: Scan frontend JavaScript bundles and HTML for hardcoded admin credentials, require authentication on every web API, keep credential files out of the web root, and audit S3 bucket write permissions on anything that serves app installers or landing pages. Watch for broad, continuous enumeration coming through residential proxies. Threat intel teams can fingerprint exposed ARTEX panels to track operators.

entries.verify_note: Independent verifier supported all four lessons; caveats: the report's key points say 1,800+ exposed instances (1,608 live in the body), and only three of the 300+ stolen certificates passed validation.
entries.prior_art: Microsoft's Storm-0940/ARTEX report (product-security pool) and NorForge's exposed Cairn panels (product-security pool) already cover ARTEX abuse and exposed AI-pentest panels. New here: operator console artifacts from leaked databases (models, prompts, token costs), the near-zero operator interaction, and the hallucinated cash-outs.
entries.threat: Low-skill criminals point autonomous agent fleets at many targets at once, and the agents find and exploit common web flaws (hardcoded credentials, missing API authentication, command injection, server-side template injection, insecure direct object references) without stopping.
entries.conditions: Internet-facing apps that have common web weaknesses, plaintext credential stores, or object storage that anyone can write to.
entries.mitigations: Remove hardcoded secrets from frontend code, enforce authentication on all APIs, lock down storage write access, and rate-limit or detect rapid automated enumeration, including traffic from residential proxies.

editorial.reason: First look inside criminals' agent consoles (models, prompts, costs) shows autonomous fleets finding commodity web gaps at scale; it continues the ARTEX abuse story and gives concrete gaps to close.

entries.title: Anthropic's unreleased model built five attack chains against major software
entries.summary: Anthropic used an unreleased internal research model to find and chain vulnerabilities in Chrome, Safari, Android, Windows and Linux. The results included a one-click Chrome sandbox escape (62 CVEs patched in Chrome 156), a Safari same-origin policy bypass, an Android lock screen bypass, a remote Windows QUIC crash (CVE-2026-33096) and a zero-click Linux multipath TCP root exploit (CVE-2026-98432). Anthropic calls two of its lessons particularly important: run many different scanning agents in parallel, and scan at pull-request time to stop new bugs.

lessons.point: Running more compute and a wider mix of scanning strategies finds substantially more vulnerabilities than a single scanner.
lessons.excerpt: Test-time compute scaling and scanner diversity substantially increase how many vulnerabilities you find.

lessons.point: Judge each scanner by how many new findings it adds to the combined set, not by its raw count.
lessons.excerpt: measures each scanner by how many additional vulnerabilities it contributes to the mix

lessons.point: Model-built chains can combine intended behaviors that are harmless on their own into a full exploit, as in the data-only Safari chain.
lessons.excerpt: Several of the weaknesses are not vulnerabilities on their own but intended behaviors that become exploitable when combined.

lessons.point: Clearing the existing backlog is not enough. Scanning at pull-request time cuts the rate at which new bugs enter the code.
lessons.excerpt: For that, we recommend scanning at PR time.

entries.takeaway: Frontier models now build working multi-bug exploit chains against hardened targets with little human help, so defenders need to scan their own code at scale and at PR time.

actionable.title: Run diverse parallel scanning agents behind one verification pipeline
actionable.detail: Run several scanner strategies in parallel: per-function coverage ('is there a vulnerability in this function?'), goal-based ('could anything here compromise customer data?') and threat-model-based ('does anything bypass the documented threat model?'). Track coverage so the whole codebase gets processed. Score each scanner by the unique findings it adds. Run variant analysis on every confirmed bug. Send every finding through one shared verification and risk-rating step so new scanners do not lower the quality bar. Add a PR-time security check, such as Anthropic's public security-guidance Claude Code plugin.

entries.prior_art: Closest pool entries: 'Claude found 493 attack-surface issues across 25 open-source projects' (finds issues but builds no exploit chains), 'GitHub Security Lab found 24 Android vulnerabilities with its AI agent', and the Mythos 5 AISI incident (a cyber-capability incident, not vulnerability research). New here: end-to-end exploit chains against Chrome, Safari, Android, Windows and Linux.
entries.threat: Frontier models can now discover and chain several vulnerabilities into working one-click or zero-click exploits against browsers, phones and kernels, work that used to need specialist teams.
entries.conditions: An attacker needs a model with comparable capability and code, binaries or a live device to analyze. The Linux exploit also needs a reachable multipath TCP listener, and the Windows crash needs a native HTTP/3 (QUIC) listener.
entries.mitigations: Apply the Chrome 156, Apple, Android, Windows (CVE-2026-33096) and Linux kernel (CVE-2026-98432) fixes, scan your own code with diverse AI scanners plus variant analysis, and add security scanning at pull-request time.

entries.title: Apache HTTP Server HTTP/2 race condition allows unauthenticated remote code execution
entries.summary: Wiz describes CVE-2026-119618, a race condition in the assign_headers() function of Apache HTTP Server's mod_http2 that lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker corrupt heap memory and run code as the web server process. It affects httpd 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 (fixed in 2.4.71) and was found independently by Anthropic and Google Cloud's Vulnerability Research Team. At publication there was no public exploit or in-the-wild exploitation; Wiz says 64% of cloud environments have vulnerable resources, a figure that ignores configuration.

lessons.point: The bug is a concurrency flaw in HTTP/2 header handling that leads to heap corruption, reachable pre-authentication.
lessons.excerpt: The flaw stems from a concurrent execution race condition within the `assign_headers()` function when handling shared resources.

lessons.point: Turning off HTTP/2 removes the attack vector if you cannot upgrade to 2.4.71 immediately.
lessons.excerpt: If immediate patching is not possible due to operational constraints, temporarily disable HTTP/2 support to eliminate the attack vector.

lessons.point: Wiz's exposure numbers count versions only, so the real exposed population depends on whether HTTP/2 is enabled.
lessons.excerpt: Note that this does not take configuration into account.

entries.takeaway: Upgrade httpd to 2.4.71 or set 'Protocols http/1.1' now; no exploit is public yet, but the bug is pre-authentication remote code execution (RCE) in a ubiquitous server.

actionable.title: Patch httpd or disable HTTP/2
actionable.detail: Find Apache HTTP Server 2.4.55-2.4.70 instances with h2 or h2c in their Protocols directive; upgrade to 2.4.71, or set 'Protocols http/1.1' in httpd.conf as a stopgap. Prioritize internet-facing servers and those in front of workloads with cloud metadata access.

entries.verify_note: Verifier found the AI-discovery lesson unsupported (the source never says Anthropic used AI); lesson and tag removed, threat softened, held for a human check.
entries.prior_art: Prior httpd/HTTP/2 memory-safety bugs and AI-found vulnerability stories (e.g. Mythos entries in ai-security.json); Apache OFBiz pre-auth RCE in product-security.json. No prior entry for this httpd mod_http2 race.
entries.threat: A remote, unauthenticated attacker triggers a race in mod_http2's assign_headers() to corrupt heap memory and execute commands with the web server's privileges; a compromised server can be an entry point to adjacent services or cloud metadata endpoints.
entries.conditions: Apache HTTP Server 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 with HTTP/2 enabled, or standalone mod_h2 builds in the affected range (the source's mod_h2 version table is internally inconsistent; it says to upgrade beyond 2.0.42).
entries.mitigations: Upgrade to Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71 or later, upgrade standalone mod_h2 beyond 2.0.42, or temporarily restrict Protocols to http/1.1 to disable HTTP/2.

entries.title: Malicious native apps can hijack browser Native Messaging to steal password vaults
entries.summary: An IEEE S&P 2027 paper shows that a non-privileged malicious app on the user's machine can abuse the browser NativeMessaging API, which links extensions to native helper apps, to intercept their traffic or act as a confused deputy. The authors demonstrate full password-vault leakage and arbitrary document signing against 1Password, the EU eID system and Google Drive, whose extensions total over 532 million downloads. The root cause is that the channel has no root of trust or client attestation, and they propose encrypting messages with a secret shared out of band.
entries.takeaway: If your extension talks to a native helper, authenticate and encrypt that channel yourself; the browser does not.

lessons.point: Any unprivileged local app can sit on the extension-to-native channel and intercept or misuse it.
lessons.excerpt: a novel attack that allows a non-privileged malicious native app to misuse browsers' native messaging capabilities to stealthily intercept sensitive communications or launch confused deputy attacks against other native apps

lessons.point: The impact on real apps is severe: full vault leakage and signing documents in government workflows.
lessons.excerpt: Our attacks have severe ramifications, including full password vault leakage, and arbitrary document signing in governmental workflows.

lessons.point: The design flaw is an untrusted channel with no root of trust or attestation of the other end.
lessons.excerpt: native messaging being built on top of an untrusted communication channel without providing a root of trust or enforcing some form of client attestation

lessons.point: Vendors can fix it at the app layer by encrypting messages with an out-of-band shared secret.
lessons.excerpt: we propose a straightforward mitigation technique of message encryption with out-of-band secret sharing

actionable.title: Authenticate both ends of any extension-to-native-host channel
actionable.detail: If you ship a browser extension with a native messaging host (password manager, signing client, sync agent), threat-model a malicious local process as a peer on that channel. Pair the extension and host with a secret exchanged out of band, encrypt and authenticate every message, and reject unauthenticated peers. Do not rely on the host manifest's allowed origins as proof of who is talking.

entries.threat: A malicious but unprivileged app on the user's machine intercepts or impersonates traffic between a browser extension and its native helper app.
entries.conditions: An extension uses the NativeMessaging API to exchange secrets or authorize operations with a native app, and the messages are not authenticated end to end.
entries.mitigations: Encrypt and authenticate native messaging traffic with a secret shared out of band, and treat the native channel as untrusted in the threat model.
entries.prior_art: Prior work studied malicious webpages and extensions attacking privileged browser APIs, and password-manager extension attacks; local-IPC impersonation and confused-deputy attacks on desktop apps are well known. The paper says NativeMessaging itself had not been examined.
entries.verify_note: Verifier found all lessons supported by the abstract; noted 532 million is cumulative downloads, not affected users, and the mitigation is proposed rather than validated. Novelty taken as verifier's 55.

entries.title: Sanitized webmail CSS steals tokens and keylogs Outlook
entries.summary: Gareth Heyes chains allowed HTML/CSS features across Fastmail, Outlook, AOL/Yahoo/Gmail/ProtonMail and OpenAI's Atlas AI browser to defeat webmail CSS sanitization. Techniques include HTML labels that trigger arbitrary UI actions, invisible :before/:after content that feeds one story to the human and another to an AI browser (indirect prompt injection), attribute-selector nesting to brute-force login tokens after a paste-into-draft, CSS hotwiring to hijack any click, and a real-time keylogger via select+opacity plus Chrome interest invokers.
entries.takeaway: CSS sanitizers built as feature allow-lists are not a trust boundary; the only durable defense is strict iframe sandboxing plus killing dangerous selectors, select, and free-form image URLs.

lessons.point: Invisible :before/:after content lets an attacker present two different messages to the human and to an AI browser reading the same email, enabling indirect prompt injection through webmail.
lessons.excerpt: you could use the `:before` and `:after` pseudo-elements to hide the text from the LLM and you could use opacity to hide it from the victim. This creates a disparity between what the victim sees and what the LLM sees, potentially altering the email's context.

lessons.point: CSS attribute selectors, combined with nesting, can brute-force secret URL parameters (e.g. Medium's 12-char login token) inside a webmail draft after a single paste, without JavaScript.
lessons.excerpt: using nesting we can match the start with one selector that's outputted only once and then nest the other selectors to brute-force the token with a smaller amount of CSS

lessons.point: The only defense that actually holds is strict iframe sandboxing plus removing dangerous selectors and select elements; feature-level CSS/HTML allow lists get bypassed by gadgets and mutation.
lessons.excerpt: One of the best methods to protect against these attacks is strict isolation. If you isolate the email message using sandboxed iframes you restrict the ability to break out of trusted boundaries.

lessons.point: CSS hotwiring lets an attacker with allow-listed CSS force the victim's next click, anywhere on the page, to fire a chosen UI action, including multi-step ones.
lessons.excerpt: CSS hotwiring is a technique that allows you to force the victim to click a specific UI action when clicking anywhere on the page **including multi-step actions** using just CSS.

actionable.title: Threat-model webmail-style renderers as adversarial input surfaces for both humans and AI browsers
actionable.detail: For any product rendering third-party HTML/CSS to a user (webmail, comment systems, agent-visible pages): isolate in a sandboxed iframe; strip select and any dangerous selectors (:has, :checked, :focus, :not); route images through a proxy; reject data: URLs; and assume attackers will use :before/:after to differ human vs LLM view. Add a regression test that renders a corpus of PortSwigger's published payloads and confirms none reach the DOM.

entries.prior_art: Apple ANSI-DNS-exfil chain (embracethered) covers CLI-side prompt-injection exfil; CSS-side webmail attacks trace back to Heiderich's mutation XSS and Gerste's font-based CSS exfil. The AI-browser-via-CSS-hidden-content angle is materially new relative to the pool.
entries.threat: A single crafted email lets an attacker (a) spoof or hijack UI actions in Outlook/Fastmail via HTML labels + CSS hotwiring, (b) exfiltrate login tokens and passwords from third-party sites the victim pastes into a webmail draft, (c) inject instructions that only the AI browser sees, causing an AI email assistant to open attacker-controlled tabs and leak the victim's name, and (d) keylog Outlook via CSS/select gadgets. All from allow-listed HTML/CSS with no JavaScript.
entries.conditions: Webmail client renders untrusted HTML/CSS in the same DOM as the trusted UI (no sandboxed iframe isolation), or the user pastes clipboard HTML into a contenteditable draft on Firefox, or an AI browser (e.g. Atlas) processes the email body as prompt context.
entries.mitigations: Sandbox untrusted email content in an iframe with a strict CSP that blocks external image requests and data: URLs. Strip select, dangerous selectors (:has, :checked, :focus, :not), and image URLs pointing to attacker-controllable domains. When an image proxy is available, force all image requests through it. In AI-browser layers, treat CSS-hidden or opacity-zero content as untrusted content the model should not act on.

entries.title: Claude found 493 attack-surface issues across 25 open-source projects
entries.summary: Anthropic ran Claude over 25 open-source projects (over five million lines) to find code reachable without need, rather than individual bugs. It found 493 issues, including 94 configuration combinations that silently turned off a security control, and a pattern in four projects where hostname-based deny rules fail open when reverse DNS lookups are off. In OpenSSH, about 4,500 lines of ML-DSA-44 post-quantum code were reachable before authentication even when the algorithm was disabled; after several rounds of fixes, OpenSSH 10.6 checks the allow lists before parsing.

lessons.point: Option combinations are a large blind spot: many were accepted silently and undocumented.
lessons.excerpt: Claude found 162 security sensitive configuration combinations that were accepted both without an error or warning and without any documentation of the expected behavior of their interaction.

lessons.point: sshd parsed attacker-chosen key types before checking whether they were allowed.
lessons.excerpt: The daemon parsed whichever key type the client sent, (and, for certificates, it also verified the embedded CA signature). Only then did it check whether that key type was allowed.

lessons.point: Hostname deny rules compared against a bare IP never match, so the list fails open.
lessons.excerpt: This means that a deny rule would never fire, and the list would fail open.

lessons.point: For the default-configuration pass, a gate is accepted only when the project's own tests give identical results.
lessons.excerpt: it requires modified builds to have identical results.

entries.takeaway: Cutting pre-auth and default-reachable code lowers the severity of bugs you have not found, and an LLM can do this audit at scale.

actionable.title: Run a three-pass attack-surface reduction review with an LLM
actionable.detail: In fresh contexts, have the model (1) inventory entry points reachable in the default config that no intended feature uses, (2) list parsing or state recorded before auth or protocol state transitions, and (3) enumerate security-relevant option pairs that silently disable or weaken a control; confirm each with a dynamic trace, and accept a gate only if the project's test suite gives identical results.

entries.prior_art: Pool entries on frontier-model vulnerability discovery (Mythos-era bug finding, AI-built PHP pre-auth chains) and classic attack-surface reduction guidance; this shifts from finding individual bugs to systematic reachability and config-interaction reduction with measured results and an upstream OpenSSH fix. Verifier: Attack-surface reduction (Howard/Manadhata attack-surface metrics, OpenSSH privsep and pre-auth minimization) is classic, and Anthropic's prior LLM vuln-finding posts (Firefox, OSS-Scanner) cover LLM bug finding. What is new is LLM-driven reachability and config-interaction auditing at scale, with the concrete OpenSSH 10.6 pre-auth fix.
entries.verify_note: Independent fresh-context verifier re-read the source; the overstatements it flagged were corrected before merge.
entries.threat: Complex, memory-unsafe or security-sensitive code reachable by unauthenticated clients, and configuration combinations that silently disable controls administrators believe are on.
entries.conditions: Default configurations exposing unused features, checks that run after parsing, and option pairs accepted without warnings, such as hostname deny rules with reverse DNS off or certificate requirements dropped by a conflicting option.
entries.mitigations: Upgrade OpenSSH to 10.6; check allow lists before deserialization; reject conflicting security options at config load; use IP-based access rules or enable DNS lookups when using hostname rules.

entries.title: Datadog traces the ARTEX agentic attack framework inside real AWS accounts
entries.summary: Datadog saw ARTEX, an AI-native penetration framework where LLM agents plan and run attacks, operate in several Amazon Web Services (AWS) accounts in October 2026. With stolen long-term access keys it searched CloudWatch logs for financial data and secrets; without keys it self-registered on public Amazon Cognito user pools, swapped tokens for AWS credentials and tried read-only discovery calls. The post gives CloudTrail hunting signals: anonymous S3 reads first, placeholder-object probes before guessing bursts, a constant FilterLogEvents limit of 1000, and ARTEX user agents.
entries.takeaway: Agentic attack tools leave repeatable, huntable habits in CloudTrail, but their cloud playbook depends on whatever model drives them, so hunt behavior rather than one fixed sequence.

lessons.point: With stolen long-term keys, the agent searched CloudWatch logs for financial data and secrets, such as long-lived access keys.
lessons.excerpt: Using compromised long-term IAM access keys, ARTEX searched through CloudWatch using `FilterLogEvents`, hunting for financial information

lessons.point: A constant parameter value across sessions is a fingerprint of the tool, usable as a detection.
lessons.excerpt: Every `FilterLogEvents` call was set with a `limit` of 1000, below the API's 10,000-event maximum.

lessons.point: The agent probes a nonexistent object to learn the 'not found' response before fuzzing, which is a hunting signal in S3 logs.
lessons.excerpt: A request for an object named like a placeholder, right before a burst of guesses, is a useful signal to hunt on.

lessons.point: Public Cognito user pools let the agent self-register and obtain AWS credentials. A tightly scoped authenticated role stopped the follow-on enumeration.
lessons.excerpt: In this case, all of them failed because the identity pool's authenticated role did not grant the required permissions.

lessons.point: The framework has no fixed cloud methodology, so its behavior varies with the model behind it.
lessons.excerpt: the playbook is therefore left to downstream AI inference, and can vary greatly depending on the model in use.

lessons.point: Banning one inference key does not stop a campaign, since ARTEX rotates across providers.
lessons.excerpt: When one provider bans or cuts off a key, ARTEX moves to the next to continue activity.

actionable.title: Hunt ARTEX-style agent activity in CloudTrail
actionable.detail: Query CloudTrail and S3 access logs for anonymous GetObject/ListObjects bursts, requests for placeholder object names (zzz_nonexistent_abc.txt, Notexist-xyz) before guessing bursts, FilterLogEvents calls with limit=1000 from long-term keys, Cognito SignUp followed by CognitoIdentityCredentials sessions running broad List/Describe calls, and the ARTEX user agents from the post. Then rotate or remove long-lived access keys and scope Cognito authenticated roles to the minimum.

entries.verify_note: Independent verifier found every lesson supported by the source.
entries.prior_art: Check Point and Microsoft ARTEX reports in the pool cover the campaign and identity view; new here is the AWS control-plane behavior (FilterLogEvents limit=1000, S3 placeholder probes, Cognito identity-pool chain).
entries.threat: An LLM-agent attack framework that uses leaked long-term AWS keys or open Cognito self-sign-up to enumerate resources and mine logs for secrets and financial data.
entries.conditions: Leaked long-lived IAM access keys, public S3-hosted front ends exposing configuration, or Cognito user pools that allow self-registration with an over-permissive authenticated role.
entries.mitigations: Remove or rotate long-lived access keys, disable or gate Cognito self-sign-up and scope its authenticated role tightly, alert on anomalous AccessDenied volumes and multi-region enumeration, and block known ARTEX IPs and user agents.

issues: mild: sentence_words 49 > 45 (Query CloudTrail and S3 access logs for anonymous GetObject/ListObjects bursts, requests for placeholder object names (z)

entries.title: OpenSSH ships an emergency workaround for a critical musl-specific vulnerability
entries.summary: OpenSSH 10.6p2 adds a workaround for a critical vulnerability. It affects Linux systems that use the musl C library and do not use PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules) for password authentication. Alpine Linux is one example. Damien Miller, an OpenSSH developer, says the root cause is outside OpenSSH and withheld details. He says the project released the fix the day after it learned of the bug because AI agents have been rediscovering bugs within hours, which makes long embargoes dangerous.

lessons.point: If you cannot upgrade right away on musl systems without PAM, turn off SSH password authentication or SSH itself.
lessons.excerpt: If you operate a Linux system that uses musl libc without PAM (Alpine Linux is one example) then stop reading and set PasswordAuthentication=no or disable SSH for these systems IMMEDIATELY.

lessons.point: The exposure is narrow. glibc systems, non-Linux systems and systems that use PAM for password authentication are not affected.
lessons.excerpt: This vulnerability does not exist on non-Linux systems, Linux/glibc systems and Linux systems that use PAM for password authentication.

lessons.point: A maintainer of core infrastructure has cut embargo time because AI agents rediscover bugs quickly. Defenders should expect less warning before disclosure.
lessons.excerpt: we have recently observed multiple cases of rapid bug rediscovery by AI agents, sometimes within hours

entries.takeaway: Find every musl-based SSH host, especially Alpine containers and appliances, and turn off password authentication now, because maintainers no longer wait out long embargoes.

actionable.title: Inventory musl-based sshd hosts and disable password authentication
actionable.detail: List hosts and images running OpenSSH on musl libc, such as Alpine-based images and embedded or appliance builds. Upgrade them to OpenSSH 10.6p2 or the patched Alpine package. Until then, set PasswordAuthentication no in sshd_config explicitly, or disable SSH.

entries.verify_note: Independent verifier supported all three lessons, which match Damien Miller's post closely; 'PAM-using' means PAM actually used at runtime.
entries.prior_art: Product-security pool entry 'PHP says Chainguard broke the PHP2Shell embargo with patched images', which covers AI rediscovery shortening embargoes, and an earlier OpenSSH 10.6 hardening entry. No prior entry covers this musl/no-PAM bug.
entries.threat: A critical, undisclosed vulnerability reachable through SSH password authentication on Linux systems that use musl libc without PAM.
entries.conditions: Linux with musl libc (for example Alpine Linux), OpenSSH password authentication enabled, and PAM not used for password authentication.
entries.mitigations: Upgrade to OpenSSH 10.6p2 or the patched distribution package, set PasswordAuthentication=no, or disable SSH on affected systems.
entries.author: Animux

editorial.reason: Critical OpenSSH bug on musl/no-PAM hosts (Alpine) with a fix released a day after discovery and a one-line mitigation (PasswordAuthentication=no) to apply now; the maintainer cites AI rediscovery as the reason for skipping a long embargo.

entries.title: Microsoft FORGE Lab finds soundness bugs in Rust's standard library
entries.summary: Microsoft's FORGE Lab reports memory-safety bugs in Rust's core and standard (std) libraries, some of which were found with help from Hyenas, a research version of its AI vulnerability scanner codenamed MDASH; humans did the investigation and impact assessment. The bugs include cases where purely safe Rust triggers undefined behavior. The bugs fall into three patterns of misplaced trust in unsafe code: assuming code will not panic (MapWindows::clone, BTreeMap::insert with unwinding allocators), trusting user-provided trait implementations (str::replace with a custom Pattern producing non-UTF-8 (Unicode Transformation Format 8-bit) strings), and trusting process-wide system state (process::exit from a child thread unmapping the main thread's signal stack). The team says AI agents make the third, environment-dependent class practical to search where static analyzers struggled.

lessons.point: Unsafe-code bugs in the standard library (std) cluster into three trust failures, which make a useful review checklist for any unsafe Rust.
lessons.excerpt: three recurring patterns of misplaced trust in unsafe code: trusting code not to panic, trusting user-provided implementations to be correct, and trusting the underlying system

lessons.point: For panic safety, either do all panicking work before breaking an invariant or make the half-built state safe to unwind (ManuallyDrop or a guard).
lessons.excerpt: Either finish the work that may panic before breaking an invariant, or make the broken state safe to unwind through

lessons.point: When unsafe code depends on a property of a caller-supplied implementation that cannot be validated, the trait should be unsafe to implement.
lessons.excerpt: If none of those work, make the trait unsafe so implementors explicitly promise to uphold it.

lessons.point: The authors claim, without comparison evidence, that AI agents make OS-boundary bugs such as signal stacks and memory mappings practical to search where static analyzers struggled.
lessons.excerpt: AI agents change the picture: they understand enough about the environment the code runs in to make this area practical to search.

entries.takeaway: Even Rust's standard library has soundness bugs of the three kinds the post names, and the authors say agents make the environment-dependent OS-boundary area practical to search.

actionable.title: Unsafe Rust misplaced-trust review checklist
actionable.detail: For every unsafe block, check (1) each call to code you don't control (clone, drop, comparisons, closures, iterator methods, allocators) as a possible early exit (panic), and confirm the state is safe to unwind (ManuallyDrop or a restore-on-drop guard); (2) every value from a safe user trait (AsRef, Borrow, Pattern, ExactSizeIterator, Ord) is called once and validated, or the property is encoded in a type; if neither works, make the trait unsafe; (3) every assumption about process-wide state (signal stacks, mmaps, env, which thread is running) holds when called from other threads. Use it as a prompt for an AI code reviewer or a human audit.

entries.verify_note: Verifier found the title, summary and takeaway over-credited the AI scanner (the source says only some bugs were found with Hyenas, with humans doing investigation), so those and lesson 4 were reworded.
entries.prior_art: Rudra (2021) and CVE-2020-36323 by the same team covered Rust ecosystem and std soundness bugs; the tracker has no prior entry on AI-assisted std-library soundness findings (nearest: 'Google brings Rust (memory safety) to the Pixel baseband', archive.json). New here is the three-pattern taxonomy with fresh 2026 std bugs and the claim that agents make OS-boundary unsafe bugs searchable. Verifier's closest: OpenAI pipeline for Linux kernel root bugs; the team's earlier Rudra work.
entries.threat: Safe Rust code that calls affected std APIs with adversarial or buggy trait implementations, panicking clones, unwinding allocators, or child-thread process::exit can reach undefined behavior.
entries.conditions: Mostly nightly or newly stabilized APIs (map_windows, Pattern, Allocator) or uncommon call patterns; two issues remained open at publication.
entries.mitigations: Track and upgrade to fixed Rust releases, avoid unwinding from custom allocators as the Rust 1.100 stabilization requires, and apply panic-safety guards and once-and-validate handling to user-supplied implementations in your own unsafe code.

issues: mild: sentence_words 59 > 45 (The bugs fall into three patterns of misplaced trust in unsafe code: assuming code will not panic (MapWindows::clone, BT)

entries.title: SafeDep tracks wfx stealer pushed into 8,093+ repos, likely via stolen tokens
entries.summary: Between November 10 and 12, 2026, an attacker pushed the wfx credential stealer into at least 8,093 public repositories, likely using stolen GitHub tokens (unsigned commits point to them). The count is a lower bound (public default branches only, campaign still active); most pushes injected steps into existing workflows, 771 used an npm `postinstall` hook, and the attacker usually reverted the commit minutes later so the branch looked clean. The payload exfiltrates all repository secrets, Actions runtime tokens, in-memory API keys and local credential files, requests OpenID Connect (OIDC) tokens for AWS, Azure and Google Cloud Platform (GCP), and tries to leave AWS access keys and Entra federated credentials as backdoors that would survive secret rotation. Poisoned versions also shipped on Packagist (neuronai-studio v3.14.3) and the Go proxy (gocurl, redock), though normal `composer require` or `go get` does not run the payload.

lessons.point: Push-run-revert hides the compromise from anyone looking at the current branch; detection has to use commit history, Actions run logs and audit events.
lessons.excerpt: In almost all repositories the attacker then reverts the commit, so the branch looks clean.

lessons.point: Rotating secrets is not enough: an OpenID Connect (OIDC) federated credential added to an Entra app keeps granting access to any workflow on main.
lessons.excerpt: Any workflow on the repository’s `main` branch can then log in to Azure as that app, even after you rotate client secrets.

lessons.point: The payload tries cloud OpenID Connect (OIDC) exchange blindly; `id-token: write` appeared in the attacker's new-workflow file, while whether code injected elsewhere gets an OIDC token depends on the host workflow's permissions.
lessons.excerpt: it requests GitHub OIDC tokens for AWS, Azure and GCP and tries to use them, even when the repository has no cloud setup.

lessons.point: The `wfx-docs` probe pull request is itself an indicator of a stolen token, even where no payload followed.
lessons.excerpt: A probe pull request on its own means the account is compromised, even if no payload commit followed.

entries.takeaway: If any repo you own got a wfx-docs PR or a reverted 'ci: refresh build cache' commit, revoke the author's tokens, rotate all reachable secrets and hunt for AWS/Entra backdoors.

actionable.title: Hunt for wfx indicators and cloud backdoors across your GitHub org
actionable.detail: Search org repos and audit logs for `wfx-docs` branches, PRs titled 'docs: dependency audit notes', and commits 'ci: refresh build cache', 'chore: add ci helper', 'chore: add dependency audit workflow', 'ci: restore' and 'ci: cleanup'. For hits, revoke the commit author's tokens, OAuth grants, SSH keys and sessions, rotate every secret the repo can read, and check AWS for new access keys, edited role trust policies and `wfx-<pid>` sessions and Entra app registrations for federated credentials named `wfx-ci-<n>`. Block neuronai-studio v3.14.3, the gocurl pseudo-version and redock v1.0.278/280/282, and treat any machine that ran `npm install` on an affected commit as compromised.

entries.verify_note: Verifier found stolen tokens and completed cloud backdoors were stated as fact and 8,093 as a total; the text now says likely stolen tokens, payload tries to leave backdoors, 8,093 is a lower bound, and lesson 3 notes OIDC token access depends on workflow permissions.
entries.prior_art: Wiz's Gheist campaign (stolen GitHub tokens pushing secret-dumping workflows across 850+ accounts), Shai-Hulud worms and tj-actions/changed-files secret exfiltration already in the tracker. New here: commit-then-revert concealment at 8,000+ repo scale, blind OIDC exchange to AWS/Azure/GCP/Vault/Kubernetes, and rotation-surviving Entra federated-credential and AWS key backdoors, plus poisoned Packagist/Go releases. Verifier's closest: Wiz Gheist entry (stolen GitHub tokens dumping secrets via Actions); GhostAction; Mini Shai-Hulud.
entries.threat: Likely stolen GitHub tokens are used to inject a CI and npm postinstall stealer that exfiltrates repository secrets and cloud credentials and tries to leave persistent AWS and Azure backdoors, then reverts the commit to hide it.
entries.conditions: A GitHub account token with write access to a repository; workflows that run on push, or npm install of an affected commit; cloud OIDC trust configured for the repository increases impact.
entries.mitigations: Revoke the commit author's tokens and sessions and enforce 2FA, rotate all repository, environment and organization secrets, delete wfx-docs branches and probe PRs, republish packages built during the window from clean commits, audit AWS keys and trust policies and Entra federated credentials, and treat machines that ran npm install on affected commits as compromised.

issues: mild: sentence_words 47 > 45 (The payload exfiltrates all repository secrets, Actions runtime tokens, in-memory API keys and local credential files, r)

editorial.reason: Live supply-chain campaign across 8,093+ repos that reverts its own commits and grabs cloud OIDC tokens; teaches what to audit in Actions logs and federated credentials now.

entries.title: Datadog reproduces pre-auth MongoDB crash planted with two ping requests
entries.summary: CVE-2026-118383 (CVSS v4.0 score 9.5) is a use-after-free bug in MongoDB Server's replica set primary catch-up: two unauthenticated `ping` requests with `readConcern.afterOpTime` plant stale waiters, and the member crashes when it later wins an election while lagging. Datadog reproduced the crash on 8.0.34 but did not achieve the code execution the vendor lists as possible. Standalone `mongod` is unaffected, enabling authentication does not prevent the setup, and fixed releases include 9.0.7, 8.0.37, 7.0.48 and 6.0.30. Depending on logging settings, the planted requests can appear in slow-query logs that may predate the crash.

lessons.point: Commands accepted before login (here `ping`) are pre-auth attack surface, so turning on authentication is not a mitigation for this bug.
lessons.excerpt: An unauthenticated client can set up the crash with two `ping` requests, because vulnerable servers accept `ping` before login. Turning on authentication does not prevent this.

lessons.point: The attacker plants the trigger in advance and must wait for a natural lagging-member election, so exploitation is opportunistic rather than on-demand.
lessons.excerpt: Remote unauthenticated exploitation is possible, but only during a specific window that the attacker does not have visibility into.

lessons.point: Detection must look back before the crash: hunt for unauthenticated ping commands with afterOpTime and expired waits in older logs of the same member.
lessons.excerpt: The requests may arrive before the failover. Review earlier logs from the same member, not just events around the crash.

lessons.point: The demonstrated impact is denial of service; code execution remains a vendor-stated possibility, not a reproduced result.
lessons.excerpt: The vendor also identifies arbitrary code execution as a possible impact under certain conditions; our tests did not demonstrate it.

entries.takeaway: Patch every MongoDB replica set member now; auth does not block the pre-login setup, and network restriction only narrows who can plant it.

actionable.title: Upgrade replica set members and hunt for planted waiters
actionable.detail: Upgrade every replica set member (including shard and config server members) to the fixed release for its branch and verify the running version on each. Until then, restrict network access to MongoDB. Search slow-query events (ID 51803) for unauthenticated `ping` commands with `readConcern.afterOpTime` that failed with MaxTimeMSExpired, and for catch-up exits (ID 21363) logged twice in one transition followed by a crash in `CatchupState::abort_inlock()`.

entries.verify_note: Verifier confirmed the claims; the summary's slow-query log statement was qualified as depending on logging settings.
entries.prior_art: No prior MongoDB server entry in the tracker; general pattern of critical pre-auth memory-safety bugs in network daemons (e.g. CVE-2025-14847-style MongoDB pre-auth issues, OpenSSH regreSSHion). The plant-then-wait election trigger and the log-level detection guidance are the specific new content. Verifier's closest: no MongoDB entries in the tracker; generic pre-auth memory-safety bugs in network daemons.
entries.threat: An unauthenticated network client can plant two waiters on a reachable replica set member that crash it when it next completes primary catch-up, potentially leaving the cluster without a primary.
entries.conditions: Vulnerable MongoDB replica set member reachable on the network; the member must later win an election while behind another member, which the attacker cannot cause.
entries.mitigations: Upgrade to 9.0.7, 8.3.16, 8.0.37, 7.0.48, 6.0.30, 5.0.35 or 4.4.32 or later, verify versions on all members including containers and offline members, restrict network access to MongoDB, and retain command objects in logs to detect afterOpTime ping requests.

editorial.reason: CVSS 9.5 pre-auth MongoDB bug with fixed versions and concrete log-based detection; authentication does not block the setup.

entries.title: Microsoft sees attack agents turn leaked GitHub secrets into Azure breaches
entries.summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence saw threat actors use agentic offensive frameworks, such as ARTEX, to search public GitHub repositories for secrets, then use the leaked application credentials to sign in as service principals (application identities) across Entra ID tenants. In one case an agent went from searching GitHub to exfiltrating data from Azure Key Vault in five minutes. When a cloud API call failed, the agents fixed the API version and retried, in one case about 28 seconds later. Microsoft recommends rotating any exposed secret, moving apps to managed identities, hunting on behavior, and using decoys and tarpits to slow autonomous attackers.

lessons.point: Agentic tooling shrinks the time from a leaked secret to cloud data theft to minutes, which leaves no window for a manual response.
lessons.excerpt: In at least one case, Microsoft observed an AI agent advance from scanning GitHub for secrets to exfiltrating data from Azure Key Vault in just five minutes.

lessons.point: The agents troubleshoot failed cloud API calls on their own: a 400 error is followed shortly by a corrected request that succeeds. This is a behavioral signature defenders can hunt for.
lessons.excerpt: Approximately 28 seconds after the first failed response, a batch rerun began against the same vault resource paths using the ARM API version 2023-07-01 and returned HTTP 200.

lessons.point: Deception works well against autonomous attackers. Fake wins can make an agent stop because it thinks its goal is done, and Microsoft says these controls helped reduce attack traffic reaching real assets in its testing.
lessons.excerpt: Fake wins present convincing evidence that the agent’s objective is complete, which can cause it to stop on a false success.

lessons.point: Deleting a leaked secret from the repository does not fix the exposure. Only revoking or rotating it does.
lessons.excerpt: Publicly exposed credentials remain usable until revoked or rotated; removing the original disclosure alone does not remediate the exposure.

entries.takeaway: Treat any secret that reaches a public repository as compromised within minutes. Detect agentic attackers by their machine-speed retry behavior, not by IP addresses or user agents, which they change easily.

actionable.title: Hunt for agentic credential abuse by behavior and rotate exposed app secrets
actionable.detail: Enable GitHub secret scanning, push protection and public leak monitoring. Rotate any exposed client secret and move OAuth apps to managed identities. In Entra sign-in logs, alert on AADSTS7000215/AADSTS7000222 failures followed by a success, on one IP authenticating to three or more service principals, and on one app requesting tokens for ARM, Key Vault, Storage and Graph in a short window. In ARM logs, flag HTTP 400 responses followed within seconds by the same request with a different api-version that returns 200. Deploy honeytokens and decoy resources so you get high-confidence alerts.

entries.verify_note: Claims match after softening the retry timing and the deception result; extends already-tracked ARTEX material with concrete hunting signatures.
entries.prior_art: Microsoft's Storm-0940/ARTEX report and Check Point's ARTEX operator research (both tracked); GitHub secret scanning and Entra workload identity guidance
entries.threat: Agentic offensive frameworks harvest application secrets from public GitHub and use them right away for service principal sign-ins, cloud resource discovery, Key Vault and Storage exfiltration, VM Run Command execution and abuse of AI services.
entries.conditions: Long-lived OAuth client secrets, storage keys or connection strings committed to public repositories, combined with over-privileged service principals and no Conditional Access for workload identities.
entries.mitigations: Rotate exposed secrets immediately and treat them as compromised, migrate apps to managed identities, apply least privilege and Conditional Access to workload identities, enable secret scanning with push protection, hunt sign-in and ARM logs for machine-speed retry patterns, and deploy honeypots, tarpits and decoy credentials.

issues: mild: jargon_chain 8 > 7 (controls helped reduce attack traffic reaching real assets)

entries.title: Attackers used Ethersphere's own release pipeline to ship backdoored bee-js and Swarm Desktop
entries.summary: On November 9, 2026, an attacker with two compromised GitHub accounts published a malicious @ethersphere/bee-js 13.3.0 to npm and a trojanized Swarm Desktop 0.56.2, both through the project's legitimate GitHub Actions workflows. The npm package added a postinstall loader that runs JavaScript fetched from api[.]frameworkmetrics[.]xyz. It carried valid SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts) provenance, because the publish job accepted any release event with tests skipped and no branch, reviewer or tag check. The desktop build was signed, notarized and pushed through the auto-updater, and the later stages reuse the Ethereum-contract command-and-control (C2) of the earlier SleepyDuck Open VSX campaign.
entries.takeaway: Trusted publishing and valid provenance prove where a package was built, not that its source was reviewed, so release workflows need branch, tag and reviewer gates of their own.

lessons.point: Valid provenance from a legitimate trusted-publishing workflow could not tell the malicious release from a good one.
lessons.excerpt: The legitimate 13.2.0 attestation has exactly the same shape, so provenance alone could not have told the two releases apart.

lessons.point: Provenance attests to the build location, not to code review.
lessons.excerpt: It proves where a package was built, not that the source was reviewed.

lessons.point: The publish job ran on any release event with CI skipped and no check that the commit came from the protected branch.
lessons.excerpt: Nothing in the workflow checks that the released commit belongs to the protected `upcoming` branch

lessons.point: Without a long-lived token, the attacker simply drove the project's own OIDC trusted-publishing workflow.
lessons.excerpt: No npm token was needed: the legitimate workflow, running legitimate workflow code from the tag

lessons.point: Newer package managers that skip dependency install scripts by default would not have run the loader.
lessons.excerpt: npm 12, pnpm 10 and later, Yarn Berry 4.14.0 and later, Bun and Deno skip unreviewed dependency scripts by default

lessons.point: A manually dispatched workflow with a free-form branch input and no environment protection exposed code-signing secrets.
lessons.excerpt: a manually triggered workflow that takes a free-form branch input, has no environment protection and hands the build the Apple and Windows signing certificates

lessons.point: Commit author fields prove nothing. Push events tied to the authenticating credential identify the actor.
lessons.excerpt: Author fields are client-set and worthless as evidence

actionable.title: Gate release-triggered publish and signing workflows
actionable.detail: In publish workflows, require that the released tag points to a commit on the protected branch. Do not skip tests on release events. Add required reviewers and a tag policy to the publish environment. Never pass signing secrets to workflow_dispatch jobs that accept a free-form branch. On the consumer side, move to npm 12, pnpm 10+, Yarn Berry 4.14.0+ or Bun, so dependency postinstall scripts do not run unless allowlisted. Also flag a first-ever install hook in a package's history.

entries.verify_note: Independent verifier found every lesson supported by the source.
entries.prior_art: The @asyncapi npm compromise and the SafeDep/StepSecurity npm worm entries already showed poisoned builds shipped with valid trusted-publishing provenance; new here are the release-event CI bypass, the signed auto-updated desktop build and the reuse of SleepyDuck's Ethereum C2.
entries.threat: An attacker with maintainer and release-bot GitHub access publishes a remote-code loader through the project's own trusted-publishing and code-signing workflows.
entries.conditions: Publish workflows that accept release events with CI skipped and no branch or reviewer gate, unprotected default branches, dispatchable workflows holding signing secrets, and clients that run dependency postinstall scripts by default.
entries.mitigations: Pin publishing to commits on protected branches, require reviewers on publish environments, restrict signing secrets to protected workflows, require signed commits, use package managers that skip install scripts by default, and remove bee-js 13.3.0 and Swarm Desktop 0.56.2 and rotate Bee node keys and passwords on affected hosts.

editorial.reason: Live npm and desktop-updater compromise reported by Socket, StepSecurity and SafeDep; teaches that valid trusted-publishing provenance does not prove review, and gives concrete release-workflow gates.

entries.title: Trojanized Claude Code extension on Cursor Marketplace plants persistent SSH backdoor
entries.summary: Phorion found that Claude Code for VS Code version 2.1.313 on the Cursor Marketplace carried injected code. The code runs as soon as the extension file loads, appends an attacker key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys and opens a reverse SSH tunnel to 134.209.82.225. It also sets up persistence on macOS, Linux and Windows and sends a report on the host back to the operator. That report includes the names, but not the values, of environment variables that look like secrets. A bug in the macOS check often stops it from turning on SSH, but the key and persistence still get installed, and removing the extension does not remove them.

lessons.point: The payload is an immediately invoked function prepended to extension.js. It runs when Node loads the module, before activate(), and needs no user action.
lessons.excerpt: executes as soon as Node loads the file, before the extension’s normal `activate` callback even runs

lessons.point: Rules that only watch processes miss this, because the key is written with Node's fs API rather than shell tools. Defenders need file telemetry that flags IDE helper processes writing to authorized_keys.
lessons.excerpt: process-only rules watching for shell commands like `echo` or `tee` touching `authorized_keys` won’t catch it

lessons.point: Hunt by key fingerprint, not by the 'svc-telemetry' comment, because the malware itself only checks the comment string.
lessons.excerpt: When hunting for this activity, it’s worth checking the public-key fingerprint rather than relying solely on the comment string.

lessons.point: Uninstalling the extension does not clean up. Responders must kill the tunnel loop, remove the LaunchAgent, cron or scheduled-task persistence, remove the planted key and rotate credentials.
lessons.excerpt: uninstalling the extension alone won’t remove the backdoor

entries.takeaway: An AI coding-assistant extension from the official vendor, served by an editor marketplace, ran with full user rights when loaded, so hunt for integrated development environment (IDE) extension hosts writing to ~/.ssh and LaunchAgents and do not treat uninstalling as remediation.

actionable.title: Hunt for and clean up Claude Code 2.1.313 extension backdoor artifacts
actionable.detail: Across the fleet, look for anthropic.claude-code-2.1.313 extension directories. Search authorized_keys for the key fingerprint SHA256:0Z6R+DF64Do2nwQic8a7kkfDLNNk4IiK+2U2Rci4htk, not just the svc-telemetry comment. Look for ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist, ~/.config/.smt and ~/.config/.smtk, $TMPDIR/.stk_* files, ssh or autossh running with '-R *:0:localhost:22', and traffic to 134.209.82.225 on port 22 or 8099. Add an EDR rule for Code Helper or Cursor Helper processes writing to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys or creating com.apple.* LaunchAgents. Check SSH logs for logins from localhost using that key, then rotate credentials if any are found.

entries.verify_note: Verifier: all four lessons and the IOCs supported by the Phorion writeup (port 8099 is the beacon port). Novelty lowered to the verifier's 55.
entries.prior_art: The nearest pool entries are archive 'Cursor's VS Code import drops extension versions and installs latest' (Open VSX identity and versions), archive 'Markdown Preview Enhanced, a VS Code extension, chained flaws into RCE' and product-security 'OVHcloud CLI GitHub releases carried attacker binaries ... GlassWorm'. None covers a trojanized official AI coding-assistant extension with this kind of detection detail.
entries.threat: A backdoored official Claude Code extension bundle (2.1.313) on the Cursor Marketplace runs a payload when the module loads. The payload plants an attacker SSH key, opens a reverse SSH tunnel to 134.209.82.225 for interactive access, persists through a LaunchAgent, cron job or scheduled task, and reports host details and the names of secret-looking environment variables.
entries.conditions: A developer installs or auto-updates to Claude Code for VS Code 2.1.313 from the Cursor Marketplace. Full inbound access on macOS also needs Remote Login (SSH) to be already on or turned on later, or passwordless sudo.
entries.mitigations: Find and remove 2.1.313. Kill the tunnel processes. Remove com.apple.sysmond.plist, the @reboot cron entry or the SysMon task and Startup script, and the ~/.config/.smt, .smtk and /tmp/.stk_* files. Remove the svc-telemetry key and confirm Remote Login is off. Rotate credentials if SSH was on or an inbound login appears. Alert on IDE extension hosts modifying ~/.ssh.
entries.author: _chall

editorial.reason: A trojanized official AI coding-assistant extension, covered by six outlets, with concrete hunting steps (key fingerprint, persistence paths, an EDR rule) and the lesson that uninstalling does not remediate.

entries.title: pwn.ai found a new Linux networking bug class escaping KVM guests
entries.summary: pwn.ai researchers, working in Vercel's sandbox challenge, found that guest-controlled checksum metadata can rewrite an IPv4 header after the host kernel has validated it. The bug is in Linux networking, not in KVM itself, so many hypervisors are affected. In their lab they turned a memory disclosure into selected 64-byte host-kernel writes and a host-root helper run. They credit GPT-5.6 Sol as the main reasoning engine inside a long-running research harness. The upstream fix validates checksum_start before completing the checksum.

lessons.point: The authors call it a new class: untrusted checksum metadata edits packet fields after validation.
lessons.excerpt: untrusted checksum metadata can rewrite security-sensitive packet fields after the kernel has already validated and acted on them

lessons.point: The bug is outside the hypervisor, so KVM-only audits miss it.
lessons.excerpt: the vulnerability wasn't even in the hypervisor, it was in the Linux networking stack.

lessons.point: An LLM provided source-level analysis within a human-directed harness.
lessons.excerpt: served as the primary reasoning engine for source-level analysis, exploring attack paths, and challenging assumptions

lessons.point: The accepted fix validates the checksum start.
lessons.excerpt: ipv4: validate checksum_start before completing checksum

entries.takeaway: VM isolation depends on the kernel's networking code, so patch KVM hosts and sandbox providers.

actionable.title: Patch hypervisor hosts and sandbox providers
actionable.detail: Apply the kernel fix on every KVM host (and nested or microVM sandboxes), and ask your sandbox provider for their patch status; treat guest-originated packet metadata as untrusted in custom kernels.

entries.prior_art: Earlier VM-escape work targets hypervisor device emulation; this reaches the host through guest-controlled metadata in core networking, with LLM-assisted discovery. Verifier: Checksum offload/virtio_net metadata bugs (virtio-net GSO/csum handling fixes); Google Big Sleep and XBOW LLM-driven vuln finds; kvmCTF KVM escapes
entries.verify_note: Independent fresh-context verifier re-read the source; discrepancies it found (title/summary overstatements) were corrected before merge.

entries.title: Claude wrote machine-checked no-crash proofs for 239 OSS-Fuzz entry points
entries.author: Keane Lucas et al. (Anthropic, Theorem)
entries.summary: Anthropic and Theorem had Claude prove, in Rocq, that 239 OSS-Fuzz entry points in 123 open-source libraries never crash (no memory-safety error or failed assertion) for any input up to 64 MB, after patching the bugs it found along the way. The spec is derived mechanically from the existing fuzz harness plus formal RISC-V and Linux-process semantics, so the ~180M lines of proof need no human review: trust reduces to the semantics, the theorem statements and the Rocq checker. Scope is narrow (single-threaded static RISC-V binaries, fixed memory budget) and compute is large, but it moves formal verification from niche to a pipeline step.

lessons.point: LLM-written formal proofs now scale to production libraries at the binary level, not just toy programs.
lessons.excerpt: proved that there are no crashes on any input (up to 64 MB) for 239 entry points across 123 different OSS-Fuzz libraries

lessons.point: The spec problem is sidestepped by reusing what developers already wrote: an existing fuzz harness becomes the property to prove.
lessons.excerpt: automatically converting their preexisting compilable test suites into a spec

lessons.point: Machine checking replaces review of the AI output: the trusted base is the semantics, the theorem statements and the checker, not the 600k-line proofs.
lessons.excerpt: virtually none of it needs to be manually reviewed

lessons.point: The guarantee is scoped: it holds only for single-threaded static RISC-V binaries on Linux under a memory budget, and bugs may remain in the trusted components.
lessons.excerpt: assume that the program runs as a single-threaded static binary with a fixed memory budget on a RISC-V CPU using Linux OS

lessons.point: Attempting proofs is itself a bug finder: failures pointed at real bugs that fuzzing had missed.
lessons.excerpt: the process of attempting to prove these specs discovered hundreds of bugs

entries.threat: AI-accelerated bug discovery and exploit chaining outpacing test-based assurance for memory-unsafe code.
entries.conditions: C/C++ libraries with existing fuzz harnesses; proofs currently limited to single-threaded static RISC-V Linux binaries.
entries.mitigations: Turn fuzz harnesses into no-crash specs and have an LLM produce checker-verified proofs; review the theorem statements and trusted semantics rather than proof text.
entries.takeaway: If you maintain C/C++ with fuzz harnesses, those harnesses are now candidate proof specs: an LLM plus a proof checker can turn 'fuzzed a lot' into 'proved no crash' for the covered scope.

actionable.title: Fuzz-harness-to-proof pipeline
actionable.detail: For a C/C++ library already in OSS-Fuzz, try Theorem's published add-project Claude skill and pipeline on one entry point; review only the generated theorem statement and assumptions, and treat proof failures as bug reports.

entries.prior_art: seL4 and CompCert (human-written verification at 10x code effort), binary-level verifiers like Alive2, LLM proof assistants (Baldur, AlphaProof), and AI bug finding (Big Sleep, AIxCC). None showed LLM-written, machine-checked binary-level proofs at this scale.
entries.verify_note: Independent verifier: all excerpts verbatim; novelty 78 vs 75 (kept 75); relevance 72; noted trusted components may hold bugs and the compute cost is large.

entries.title: Chainguard details wfx stealer that backdoors cloud roles and can forge checks
entries.summary: Starting November 10, 2026, an attacker used stolen GitHub tokens to open probe pull requests in 61,764 repositories from 4,837 accounts (Aikido's count). It pushed wfx, a 1,500-line shell stealer, wherever it could, then reverted the commit and deleted the workflow run within about a minute. The stealer takes Actions secrets, OIDC and runtime tokens, cloud, SSH and AI-tool credentials and runner memory. It swaps GitHub OIDC tokens for AWS, GCP and Azure sessions, and it carries code to post forged success results under the names of required checks, though StepSecurity found that feature switched off in all 101 copies it examined. For persistence it rewrites AWS role trust policies to allow any AWS account and adds wfx-ci federated credentials to Azure AD apps, both of which survive secret rotation.

lessons.point: Required status checks are not a reliable gate against a token holder. The payload has code to post fake passing results under the required check names, so branch protection would let the change through; StepSecurity found it not yet switched on.
lessons.excerpt: posts forged success status checks against the commit using the names of the repository's required checks

lessons.point: The attacker deletes the workflow run and its logs, so detection depends on a gap in run numbers rather than on log content.
lessons.excerpt: A missing run number in a workflow's history is often the only trace left.

lessons.point: Rotating secrets is not enough. Response has to audit cloud configuration too: AWS trust policies set to Principal * and Azure federated credentials let the attacker back in after rotation.
lessons.excerpt: Rotating secrets alone does not remove a trust policy or a federated credential.

entries.takeaway: With a stolen write token, pinning and pull request review do nothing, so limit what a CI runner holds and audit cloud trust after any wfx hit.

actionable.title: Detect deleted wfx runs and forged checks, then audit cloud trust
actionable.detail: For each repository, list Actions run numbers per workflow from November 10 onward and flag any gaps. For commits in that window, list status checks and flag success results posted by an app or token other than your CI. In AWS, query IAM for role trust policies containing "Principal": {"AWS": "*"}, STS sessions named wfx-*, and access keys you did not create. In Azure, list federated identity credentials named wfx-ci-*. In GCP, look for generateAccessToken or signJwt calls from GitHub OIDC principals you did not configure. Block egress to 194.150.166.244 and 18.143.168.96 on port 8080, and note that StepSecurity reports later variants send data only to Telegram.

entries.verify_note: Verifier confirmed counts, IPs and persistence; forged required checks is a built-in capability StepSecurity saw switched off, now worded that way. Novelty taken as the verifier's 30.
entries.prior_art: SafeDep's 'wfx stealer pushed into 8,093+ repos, likely via stolen tokens' (push-revert, OIDC exchange, Entra and AWS backdoors). Adds Aikido's larger count, forged required status checks, run deletion detectable by missing run numbers, and AWS Principal * trust rewrites.
entries.threat: An attacker holding stolen GitHub tokens pushes a CI stealer into every repository the tokens can write to, dumps secrets and runner memory, trades OIDC tokens for cloud sessions, forges required checks, plants cloud backdoors that survive rotation, and deletes its workflow runs.
entries.conditions: The attacker needs a GitHub token with write access to the repository. The repository's workflows must hold secrets or have id-token permission and cloud roles that trust GitHub OIDC.
entries.mitigations: Search for wfx-docs branches and the probe pull request title. Treat any probe author as compromised and revoke its tokens and grants. Rotate every secret the workflow could reach. Restore AWS trust policies, delete rogue IAM keys and Azure wfx-ci federated credentials, and re-run required checks. Block the exfiltration hosts.
