Give GITHUB_TOKEN minimal scope, keep long-lived credentials off runners, and restrict OIDC trust to specific repositories and branches.

editorial.reason: Live campaign across 60,000+ repositories; concrete detection steps (missing run numbers, AWS Principal * trust, Azure wfx-ci credentials) and the lesson that secret rotation alone leaves cloud backdoors.

entries.title: Citrix NetScaler CVE-2026-88771 is a pre-auth command injection zero-day in default configuration
entries.summary: CVE-2026-88771 lets an unauthenticated attacker run commands as root on Citrix NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway in the default configuration, and it was exploited in the wild before a patch existed. The bug is in a crash-reporting Perl script (ns_monuploadd_err.pl) that reads appliance logs, pulls a core-file name out of them without validating it, and passes it to a shell command. Any request field that ends up in the logs, such as a login name or User-Agent header, can carry the attack, and the fix builds the name only from strictly matched fields and calls find without a shell.

lessons.point: The flaw affects the default configuration and was exploited as a zero-day before Citrix shipped a fix, so any unpatched internet-facing appliance should be treated as possibly compromised.
lessons.excerpt: It affects the default configuration and was exploited in the wild as a zero-day, before any fix existed.

lessons.point: Root cause: a log-parsing script trusts whatever text follows NSPPE in a log line as a core-file name and process ID, then interpolates it into a shell command.
lessons.excerpt: The problem is that the script never verifies that those first two fields are really an `nsppe` core file name and a numeric process ID.

lessons.point: The attack surface is any input that gets logged, not one endpoint, so blocking a single URL is not a complete mitigation; patching is required.
lessons.excerpt: Any endpoint or port that logs data controlled in an HTTP header can trigger this vulnerability.

lessons.point: The fix builds the value only from tightly matched captures. It runs external commands in list form, so no shell interprets metacharacters.
lessons.excerpt: Perl does not build a command string and does not start `/bin/sh`, so shell metacharacters cannot be interpreted as commands.

lessons.point: The same bulletin (CTX697096) has a sibling bug, CVE-2026-88778, that the upgrade alone does not fix; it needs a configuration change.
lessons.excerpt: Fixed by enabling Enhanced ISN Generation, not by the upgrade alone.

entries.takeaway: Patch NetScaler ADC and Gateway to 14.1-73.37 / 13.1-64.23 (or the FIPS/NDcPP equivalents) now, enable Enhanced ISN Generation, and hunt for compromise, because this root-level pre-auth bug was exploited before a fix existed.

actionable.title: Patch, harden and hunt on NetScaler ADC/Gateway for CVE-2026-88771 and siblings
actionable.detail: 1) Inventory all NetScaler ADC and Gateway appliances, including management interfaces. 2) Upgrade to 14.1-73.37+, 13.1-64.23+, 14.1-73.37 FIPS+, or 13.1-37.279+ (13.1-FIPS/NDcPP) per Citrix bulletin CTX697096; if you cannot patch at once, take internet-facing appliances offline or restrict access, as watchTowr advised. 3) Enable Enhanced ISN Generation for CVE-2026-88778, which the upgrade alone does not fix. 4) Hunt: because exploitation went through logged fields, review appliance logs (AAA/SSLVPN login records, User-Agent and request-parameter entries) for usernames or headers containing 'pitboss' or 'NSPPE' text alongside shell metacharacters such as semicolons or backticks, and check for unexpected files in temp directories and unexpected processes running as root. 5) Because the bug was exploited before disclosure, treat unpatched exposed appliances as possibly compromised: rotate credentials and session secrets handled by the appliance and review downstream access from it.

entries.prior_art: Earlier NetScaler pre-auth bugs in the archive, e.g. 'Citrix NetScaler Pre-Auth Heap Overflow (CVE-2026-8452) ... SAML Signature Canonicalization' (memory corruption in nsppe); this one is a different class (shell injection via log content in a Perl helper script) outside nsppe. Verifier's closest: watchTowr Citrix NetScaler CVE-2026-8452; known appliance command-injection patches.
entries.verify_note: Verifier: versions, CVE-2026-88778, zero-day and default-configuration claims match; lessons 3-4 slightly over-generalize.
entries.threat: Unauthenticated remote attacker runs arbitrary commands as root on the NetScaler appliance, the front door for enterprise remote access; exploited in the wild as a zero-day alongside the DTLS memory overflow CVE-2026-88772.
entries.conditions: NetScaler ADC / NetScaler Gateway in default configuration on builds before the fixed versions (watchTowr diffed vulnerable 14.1 build 73.30 against fixed 73.37). Attacker-controlled text must reach appliance logs that ns_monuploadd_err.pl later parses, which login fields, headers and the management interface all allow.
entries.mitigations: Upgrade to 14.1-73.37+, 13.1-64.23+, 14.1-73.37 FIPS+, or 13.1-37.279+ for 13.1-FIPS/NDcPP; enable Enhanced ISN Generation for CVE-2026-88778; take unpatched exposed appliances offline or restrict access; hunt logs for shell metacharacters in logged usernames and headers; assume compromise on appliances that were exposed and unpatched.

issues: mild: sentence_words 49 > 45 (4) Hunt: because exploitation went through logged fields, review appliance logs (AAA/SSLVPN login records, User-Agent an)
mild: acronyms 6 > 3 (ADC, FIPS, ISN, NSPPE, AAA, SSLVPN)

editorial.reason: Pre-auth root command injection in NetScaler ADC/Gateway exploited as a zero-day in default configuration; concrete fixed builds, a sibling bug the upgrade alone doesn't fix, and log-hunting guidance.

entries.title: Compromised Qubole credentials let attackers raid over a dozen customer cloud accounts
entries.summary: A threat actor used compromised identity and access management (IAM) credentials for an AWS account tied to the big-data platform Qubole to assume the cross-account roles customers had created for Qubole, and pulled data from more than a dozen organizations between October 14 and 26. Many of those roles were still in place long after customers stopped using Qubole and could read most of the data taken; the actor enumerated resources, harvested secrets from common AWS storage locations, tested them with TruffleHog, and copied whole Amazon S3 buckets. Sentra and Wiz analyzed the campaign; Wiz also found a separate October 8-11 campaign that tested customer-owned AWS access keys for Qubole integrations.

lessons.point: A software-as-a-service (SaaS) vendor's cross-account role is a standing trust path: whoever holds the vendor's credentials can assume it in every customer account that trusts that vendor.
lessons.excerpt: The credentials allowed the attackers to assume IAM roles organizations had set up for Qubole

lessons.point: Integration roles left behind after a vendor is offboarded were the main exposure, and they had broad read access to data.
lessons.excerpt: Qubole roles were still in place long after companies had stopped using Qubole, and those roles could read nearly all of the data the attacker went after

lessons.point: Activity came from rented hosting and a commercial virtual private network (VPN), not the vendor's network.
lessons.excerpt: The attacks came from a rented OVH server and the Mullvad VPN, and none of the observed activity originated from Qubole

lessons.point: The actor used a consistent role session name prefix, which gives defenders a concrete CloudTrail hunting indicator.
lessons.excerpt: The threat actor used role session names that followed a consistent format of the prefix quiam-, followed by a suffix describing the actions taken.

entries.takeaway: Every cross-account role you granted a vendor is a standing door into your AWS account, so remove the ones for vendors you no longer use and alert on sessions from outside the vendor's network.

actionable.title: Audit stale vendor cross-account roles and hunt their sessions
actionable.detail: List every IAM role whose trust policy names an external AWS account, map each account to a current vendor, and delete roles for vendors no longer in use. For the rest, scope permissions to least privilege and add source-IP or VPC conditions to the trust policy. For Qubole specifically, search CloudTrail from October 1 for AssumeRole events from Qubole's account (805246085872 per Wiz) or session names starting with quiam-, review each session's Secrets Manager, SSM Parameter Store, Lambda and S3 activity, rotate every secret the role could read and revoke active role sessions.

entries.verify_note: Removed a counterfactual sentence not in the source.
entries.prior_art: AWS confused-deputy and ExternalId guidance; research on SaaS vendor cross-account roles left after offboarding.
entries.threat: An actor holding a SaaS vendor's leaked AWS IAM credentials assumes the cross-account roles customers granted that vendor, then enumerates resources, harvests and validates secrets, and exfiltrates S3 data across many customers at once.
entries.conditions: Customer AWS accounts that still trust the vendor's account through an integration role, often after the vendor is no longer used, with broad read access to S3 and secret stores and no source restrictions in the trust policy.
entries.mitigations: Remove integration roles for vendors no longer in use, grant least privilege, add source-IP conditions to trust policies, review CloudTrail for AssumeRole calls from the vendor account and quiam- session names, rotate every secret a compromised role could read, and revoke active role sessions since rotation alone does not end issued temporary sessions.

issues: mild: sentence_words 47 > 45 (For Qubole specifically, search CloudTrail from October 1 for AssumeRole events from Qubole's account (805246085872 per )

entries.title: Wiz turned PHP memory bugs into unauthenticated RCE on WordPress using AI
entries.summary: Wiz Research reported memory-safety bugs in the PHP engine itself (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, up to CVSS 9.2), so every PHP version back to 5.4 is hit by at least one of them. The bugs sit in how PHP handles fatal errors such as out-of-memory, so a hello-world app is exposed. The bugs had existed for years; frontier models made the multi-step exploit chain practical to build and adapt per target in hours. PHP shipped the patch on October 21, 2026.

lessons.point: The bugs are in core PHP, so every app on an affected version is exposed, including a plain Hello World app.
lessons.excerpt: Every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities, going back to version 5.4.

lessons.point: The root cause is stale internal state left behind after fatal errors such as out-of-memory, which a later request or worker reuses.
lessons.excerpt: All of the disclosed vulnerabilities are memory-safety issues that stem from bugs in how PHP handles fatal errors while processing requests, particularly out-of-memory errors.

lessons.point: Frontier models made the exploit chain practical: they adapted exploits to different targets in hours.
lessons.excerpt: Frontier models were critical to making this process practical, enabling us to develop and adapt working exploits across multiple applications in hours.

lessons.point: Exploit complexity may no longer be a reliable barrier, so old memory bugs deserve faster patching.
lessons.excerpt: As the time and expertise required for this work decrease, complexity may no longer provide a meaningful barrier, changing how we define what is vulnerable in practice.

entries.takeaway: Patch PHP now: the flaws are in the engine, not your app, and AI has cut the cost of turning old memory bugs into working exploits.

actionable.title: Patch PHP and inventory PHP runtimes
actionable.detail: Upgrade every PHP runtime to the October 21, 2026 release, including PHP bundled in container images. If you cannot patch yet, apply your WAF or CDN vendor's PHP2Shell rule as a stopgap and treat memory disclosure as a credential-rotation trigger on exposed hosts.

entries.prior_art: Core-language RCE disclosures exist (for example PHP-CGI), but a core PHP memory-corruption chain exploited pre-auth across three CMSs with frontier-model-built exploits has no equal in the pools. Verifier: Google Big Sleep / Project Zero AI-found bugs, DARPA AIxCC, XBOW; earlier frontier-model exploit-development reports. Delta is AI-built multi-bug chain on core
entries.verify_note: Independent fresh-context verifier re-read the source; discrepancies it found (title/summary overstatements) were corrected before merge.

editorial.reason: Core PHP RCE chain built with frontier AI; patched October 21 with broad vendor mitigations.

entries.title: PortSwigger's Gareth Heyes bypassed six of eight popular vector-image sanitizers
entries.summary: Gareth Heyes tested eight sanitizers for Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) uploads and bypassed six, using tricks such as switching one element's namespace to XHTML, animating a link into a JavaScript URL, and pointing a stylesheet instruction at a data URL. He also showed Firefox running JavaScript from a stylesheet delivered in a `Link` response header over a harmless XML body, and Safari importing a GIF as SVG through `<use>`. DOMPurify and darylldoyle/svg-sanitizer resisted every technique.

lessons.point: Two libraries held up against every technique in the post.
lessons.excerpt: Both DOMPurify and darylldoyle/svg-sanitizer held up against everything in this post, which is quite impressive.

lessons.point: A namespace switch on one element brings HTML into an SVG without foreignObject.
lessons.excerpt: Switch the XML namespace on a single element to XHTML and the browser renders it as HTML directly inside the SVG.

lessons.point: Response headers can load stylesheets in Firefox, so a clean body is not enough.
lessons.excerpt: Firefox lets you load external CSS files using a Link response header.

lessons.point: An uploaded GIF can carry an SVG payload that Safari imports.
lessons.excerpt: if you can upload a GIF that contains the payload, it won't render when you open it in the browser, but it can still be imported with a `<use>` element!

entries.takeaway: If you accept SVG uploads, sanitize with DOMPurify or darylldoyle/svg-sanitizer, serve user files from a separate origin, and never let users influence response headers.

actionable.title: Audit which SVG sanitizer you use
actionable.detail: If your app uses mattkrick/sanitize-svg, Borewit/svg-sanitizer, bgalek/safe-svg, alnorris/SVG-Sanitizer, cloudflare/svg-hush or jams2/py-svg-hush, switch to DOMPurify or darylldoyle/svg-sanitizer. Serve uploaded images from a separate cookieless origin with a strict CSP, and make sure no user input reaches Link headers.

entries.verify_note: All claims supported; 'held' covers only these techniques and the GIF is SVG text under a .gif name. Novelty lowered to its 62.
entries.prior_art: SVG XSS and sanitizer bypasses are a long-running topic, and the post cites Kevin Mizu's animateTransform trick; the Link-header stylesheet execution in Firefox and Safari's GIF-as-SVG import are new.
entries.threat: Stored XSS through uploaded SVG or image files that pass a sanitizer.
entries.conditions: Applications that accept SVG or image uploads and serve them from the main origin using one of the six bypassed sanitizers.
entries.mitigations: Use DOMPurify or darylldoyle/svg-sanitizer, serve uploads from a separate origin with a strict CSP, and keep user input out of response headers.

entries.title: Midnight Blizzard hit iOS and Android users through watering-hole exploit chains
entries.summary: Sekoia reports that the Russian state group Midnight Blizzard (APT29) planted malicious JavaScript on hacked or cloned websites, including a Ukrainian web analytics tracker (Plerdy) that exposed hundreds of sites for a week. The script fingerprinted each visitor and then served one of three zero-click exploit chains, two for iOS and one for Android. Every chain used already-patched bugs. Both iOS chains reused the DarkSword exploit kit, and one also used CVE-2024-27834 to bypass Pointer Authentication Codes (PAC). The Android chain used Chrome CVE-2026-3910 and Qualcomm CVE-2025-27038 to steal cookies, passwords and Wi-Fi keys.

lessons.point: The campaign used only n-day bugs, so devices that were not patched were the ones exposed. Patch speed on mobile fleets is the main control.
lessons.excerpt: Sekoia identified three exploit chains (two targeting iOS and one targeting Android) used across the campaign. All three target previously patched vulnerabilities,

lessons.point: Ready-made exploit chains built by commercial surveillance vendors make advanced mobile exploitation cheaper, and state groups are expected to reuse them more often.
lessons.excerpt: The adoption of packaged n-day exploit chains lowers the cost and technical threshold required to conduct advanced mobile exploitation.

lessons.point: Compromising one shared third-party script, here a web analytics tracker, spreads the exploit kit to every site that loads it.
lessons.excerpt: The hackers also targeted Ukrainian web analytics service Plerdy in a supply chain attack, adding their malicious code to the tracker file.

lessons.point: The injected script profiled each visitor's browser and device before sending an exploit, which keeps the chains away from people who are not targets.
lessons.excerpt: The code was designed to fingerprint visitors, harvesting browser and device configuration data and sending it in JSON format before the exploit is delivered.

entries.takeaway: Patched mobile bugs still get used against devices that have not been updated, so slow patching on high-risk staff devices is what the attacker exploits.

actionable.title: Enforce minimum OS and browser versions on high-risk mobile devices
actionable.detail: Use MDM to block or quarantine iOS devices below 17.5 / 16.7.8 and Android devices missing the August 2025 security patch or running Chrome older than the March 2026 fix (CVE-2026-3910). Turn on Lockdown Mode for diplomatic and defense staff. Pin or apply Subresource Integrity (SRI) to third-party analytics scripts, and check Sekoia's indicators of compromise (IOCs), including the Plerdy tracker, against proxy logs.

entries.verify_note: Independent verifier supported all four lessons and every version in the action; corrected: only the first iOS chain used CVE-2024-27834.
entries.prior_art: Google TAG's 2023-2024 reporting (cited in the article) on APT29 reusing NSO and Intellexa exploits in watering holes; Citizen Lab Candiru ad-delivered spyware entry in the pool. No DarkSword or Midnight Blizzard mobile entry found in the pool.
entries.threat: Visiting a compromised or cloned site, or any site that loads the infected Plerdy tracker, on an unpatched iPhone or Android phone gives the attacker code execution and full data theft without any click.
entries.conditions: The device runs iOS older than the May 2024 fixes, or Android/Chrome without the March 2026 Chrome and August 2025 Qualcomm patches, and passes the attacker's fingerprinting filter.
entries.mitigations: Keep iOS, Android and Chrome fully updated. Enable Lockdown Mode for high-risk users. Pin third-party scripts or use Subresource Integrity, and hunt for Sekoia's published indicators.

entries.title: Google DeepMind's AI agents cut the cost of attacking 1024-bit RSA
entries.summary: Google DeepMind, with cryptographers from UC San Diego and Inria, says supervised AI agents found two cheaper attacks on legacy 1024-bit RSA. First, PKCS#1 v1.5 signature padding (used by the PKCS#11 interface of hardware security modules, or HSMs) gives no protection once an attacker controls about half the signed block; agents re-ran a known forgery 3.5 times cheaper (391 versus 1,380 CPU core-years) in under four days with about 20 human messages. Second, a theoretical batch-factoring method makes each additional 1024-bit key about 30 times cheaper, but it is not implemented, and 2048-bit keys are not affected.
entries.takeaway: Treat any remaining RSA-1024 keys as weaker than assumed and retire them, especially hardware security module (HSM) signing keys that sign attacker-influenced data.

lessons.point: Padding stops helping against chosen-message forgery once the attacker controls about half of the signed block.
lessons.excerpt: Once they control roughly half of the block or more, padding adds no protection at all

lessons.point: The forgery result hits the PKCS#1 v1.5 format used by HSM signing interfaces.
lessons.excerpt: this applies to the PKCS#1 v1.5 format used by the PKCS#11 signing interface of cryptographic devices such as hardware security modules (HSMs).

lessons.point: Agents carried out the heavy engineering of a cryptanalytic computation with minimal human input.
lessons.excerpt: Two AI agents designed, ran and debugged the forgery computation in under four days, with approximately 20 messages from the human researcher, mostly approvals.

lessons.point: The signature attack has steep preconditions and does not recover the key.
lessons.excerpt: It requires roughly 4 billion signing queries made in advance, and does not work against devices that hash messages internally.

lessons.point: The batch-factoring gain is a theoretical estimate only.
lessons.excerpt: makes factoring each additional 1024-bit key roughly 30 times cheaper on average than the best previous approach

actionable.title: Inventory and retire RSA-1024 signing keys
actionable.detail: Find any remaining 1024-bit RSA keys, prioritizing HSM or PKCS#11 signing keys that sign data an outsider can influence without hashing it inside the device. Move them to 2048-bit or larger keys. In the meantime, rate-limit or audit raw signing queries on HSMs.

entries.verify_note: Independent verifier found every lesson supported by the source.
entries.prior_art: Earlier academic RSA-1024 signature forgery (1,380 core-years) and batch NFS 'factorization factory' work; pool has AI-assisted vulnerability research but no AI-driven cryptanalysis result.
entries.threat: Cheaper chosen-message signature forgery and batch factoring against legacy 1024-bit RSA.
entries.conditions: RSA-1024 keys still in use, an attacker who controls about half or more of the signed block, and roughly 4 billion signing queries on a device that does not hash internally.
entries.mitigations: Retire RSA-1024 keys for 2048-bit or larger, hash messages inside the signing device, and limit and monitor raw signing access to HSMs.

entries.title: Microsoft sees attackers keep Linux server access via GSocket relays after patching
entries.summary: Microsoft reports multiple unrelated threat actors installing GSocket, an open-source relay-based remote access tool, on Linux servers compromised through web application remote code execution (RCE). Access survives patching of the original bug. Both the host and the operator connect outbound to the public Global Socket Relay Network and authenticate with a shared secret, which leaves no attacker-owned IP or domain to block. Deployments use /dev/shm for staging, process names that look like kernel threads, and layered cron, systemd and shell-profile persistence. GSocket-related detections rose 356.2% from March to August 2026, mostly on PHP (Hypertext Preprocessor), cPanel and Apache hosting. In a few observed incidents, attackers attempted to gain root through CVE-2026-43284 (Dirty Frag).

lessons.point: Patching the exploited web app is not remediation: the relay client and its persistence live independently of the vulnerable application.
lessons.excerpt: Because GSocket runs independently of the exploited application, patching the vulnerability does not remove the relay client or its persistence.

lessons.point: A relay command-and-control (C2) channel keyed by a shared secret has no attacker-owned IP or domain to block and the operator can reconnect from anywhere, but defenders can still restrict access to the relay itself, and Microsoft publishes hashes, paths and distribution hosts.
lessons.excerpt: GSocket identifies endpoints by a shared secret instead of an IP address or hostname.

lessons.point: Egress control is the lever: inbound rules never see the traffic, so deny-by-default outbound plus monitoring of relay endpoints is the network defense.
lessons.excerpt: Apply deny-by-default egress rules, allow only required destinations, and monitor connections to relay infrastructure.

lessons.point: This is a growing, multi-actor trend rather than a single campaign.
lessons.excerpt: From March through August 2026, devices with GSocket-related detections increased 356.2%, although the increase was not consistent month to month.

entries.takeaway: After any web remote code execution (RCE) on a Linux server, hunt for GSocket and layered persistence and enforce egress filtering; a patch alone leaves the attacker in.

actionable.title: Add GSocket hunting to Linux web remote code execution (RCE) incident response
actionable.detail: For any compromised internet-facing Linux host: search process command lines for gs-netcat/gsocket and gsocket.io or gsgg.b-cdn.net downloads, check /dev/shm/.gs-* and files like systemd-remount-d, defunct.service or /tmp/.gsn_ora, and audit cron, systemd units and shell startup files for layered persistence. Mount /dev/shm and temp dirs noexec where feasible, apply deny-by-default egress, and patch local privilege escalation bugs such as CVE-2026-43284 on internet-facing servers.

entries.verify_note: Verifier found lesson 2 overstated that no IOCs exist to block and the summary implied Dirty Frag escalation was common; the lesson now notes relay restriction and published hashes, paths and hosts, and the summary says a few observed incidents.
entries.prior_art: Abuse of legitimate relay/tunnel tools for C2 (ngrok, Cloudflare Tunnel, gs-netcat use reported in earlier cryptojacking and Linux intrusions) and generic 'patching is not eviction' guidance; tracker has related relay-network entries (Volt Typhoon relays) but nothing on GSocket. New: Microsoft telemetry on scale and sector, concrete deployment tradecraft and KQL hunts. Verifier's closest: CL-UNK-1211 Linux persistence entry; Volt Typhoon rotating relays.
entries.threat: After exploiting an internet-facing web application, attackers deploy GSocket for encrypted outbound relay C2 with masquerading and redundant persistence, retaining access after the vulnerability is patched and attempting local root escalation.
entries.conditions: Linux server with an exploitable internet-facing application (commonly PHP, cPanel or Apache hosting); outbound traffic to the Global Socket Relay Network permitted; writable or memory-backed staging paths such as /dev/shm.
entries.mitigations: Remediate the host and not just the app by removing the GSocket client, persistence and staged files, enforce deny-by-default egress and monitor relay connections, mount temp and memory-backed directories noexec, audit cron, systemd and shell profiles, and prioritize kernel privilege-escalation patches on internet-facing servers.

editorial.reason: Microsoft telemetry shows GSocket relays keep attackers on Linux servers after the entry bug is patched; actionable hunts and egress advice.

entries.title: PortSwigger turns its CRLF desync research into an automated Burp AT skill
entries.summary: PortSwigger added a scan check for HTTP request header injection. It also added a Burp AT skill that takes one of these findings and tries to escalate it to a CRLF-powered desync, where injected line breaks (carriage return and line feed) split one request into two upstream. The skill runs four phases: find where the injection lands upstream, prove request splitting, crawl for an open-redirect gadget, then confirm a redirect to the tester's collaborator server across connections. When a phase fails it falls back to a tentative finding or a request-tunnelling skill.

lessons.point: An injection point in the path may be rewritten into a custom header upstream, so testers must work out where it lands relative to the Host header before request splitting will work.
lessons.excerpt: Just because your insertion point is the path, doesn’t mean that your injected header ends up in the path upstream.

lessons.point: The skill confirms a desync by fuzzing request-splitting prefixes until 2 or 3 distinct upstream status codes come back.
lessons.excerpt: The skill will fuzz several different prefix payloads in order to try and produce unique status codes.

lessons.point: PortSwigger left response queue poisoning out of the automated exploit because it was too dangerous for real users. The redirect it uses instead still gives a cache-poisoning primitive.
lessons.excerpt: we chose err on the side of caution and opted for an exploit that would be less catastrophic if it happened to impact real users

lessons.point: The agent skill degrades gracefully. If a later phase fails, it hands the tester a partial but validated finding.
lessons.excerpt: if the gadget phase fails, you’ll still get a validated desync finding without evidence of an exploit

entries.takeaway: Header injection findings used to be triaged as low severity, but tools can now escalate them to critical desyncs automatically, so they deserve full follow-up.

actionable.title: Re-triage open header injection findings as possible desyncs
actionable.detail: For any reported HTTP request header injection, especially behind nginx-style proxies that URL-decode the path, test whether encoded CRLF (%0d%0a) can split the upstream request. Check whether a Host or X-Forwarded-Host driven redirect exists as a gadget. If either holds, rate it critical rather than low. Run active exploitation only against targets you are authorized to test, because desync payloads can affect other users.

entries.verify_note: Independent verifier supported all four lessons; it judged the delta over PortSwigger's archived CRLF-Powered Desync paper to be mostly tool packaging, so novelty takes its lower score.
entries.prior_art: PortSwigger's 'CRLF-Powered Desync Attacks' research (archive: 'CRLF header injection escalates to CDN-wide response queue poisoning') and the CL.0/browser-powered desync entry. New here is only the automated agent-skill packaging of that methodology.
entries.threat: An HTTP request header injection that lets an attacker insert CRLF sequences upstream can split requests and desync the connection, so other users are served attacker-controlled redirects. Chained with cache poisoning, this can lead to full-site takeover.
entries.conditions: The front-end forwards attacker-controlled input (often a URL-decoded path) into the upstream request without stripping CRLF, and the back-end reuses connections across users.
entries.mitigations: Reject or strip CR and LF characters in any value forwarded upstream, avoid passing decoded paths such as nginx $uri into proxy_pass, and do not build redirects from Host or X-Forwarded-Host.

entries.title: 38.9% of agent-generated PRs carry a security smell
entries.author: A H M Nazmus Sakib et al.
entries.summary: A large-scale study of the AIDev dataset classified security smells across 16,112 file changes in 4,022 agent-generated pull requests. 38.9% of agent PRs contain at least one security smell and supply-chain integrity issues make up 82.3% of them - but the counterintuitive result is that human collaborators introduce 67.6% of the genuine leaked secrets in these agent-assisted workflows, and review catches almost none of them. All percentages are downstream of an LLM-as-a-judge classification pipeline plus manual review, so treat the precision of the figures accordingly.

lessons.point: Supply-chain integrity dominates the detected smell taxonomy (82.3%); the abstract does not enumerate the remaining categories, so everything else combined is a small residual - point provenance and dependency controls at agent output.
lessons.excerpt: 38.9% of agent-generated PRs contain at least one security smell, with supply chain integrity issues accounting for 82.3% of all detected security smells

lessons.point: Blaming the agent misreads the data: humans introduced most genuine leaked secrets, which the authors describe only as suggesting a *potential* reduction in developer vigilance - an association, not a causal finding.
lessons.excerpt: human collaborators are responsible for introducing 67.6% of genuine leaked secrets within these agent-assisted workflows

lessons.point: Existing review is not a control here - automated and human review together missed 81.1% of these credentials before integration.
lessons.excerpt: existing automated and human review processes fail to detect 81.1% of these credentials prior to integration

entries.threat: Security debt accumulates in high-impact file paths faster than human review capacity, with hard-coded credentials making up 99.6% of critical-severity smells.
entries.conditions: Repositories that accept autonomous coding-agent pull requests through a conventional human review process.
entries.mitigations: Enforce secret scanning as a merge gate rather than a review step; apply provenance/dependency-integrity checks to agent PRs; add context-aware guardrails at the human-AI collaboration point rather than at final review.
entries.takeaway: Gate agent PRs with automated secret and dependency-integrity checks - human review demonstrably does not catch this class, and the humans are introducing most of it.
entries.prior_art: That LLM-generated code contains vulnerabilities is well documented (Copilot-era studies onward). The delta is scale and attribution on real agent PRs - the 67.6% human-origin secrets finding inverts the 'the agent is the risk' framing. Methodologically it applies an existing technique (LLM-as-judge + manual coding) to a new dataset rather than introducing a new method. Accepted at the KDD 2026 AgenticSE workshop.
entries.verify_note: Independent verifier: removed invented contrast categories (injection/logic bugs); restored the authors' 'potential' hedge on developer vigilance; surfaced that all figures come from an LLM-as-a-judge pipeline; novelty 68->57.

editorial.reason: Large-scale, widely-discussed finding on coding-agent risk with a concrete gate: automated secret + dependency-integrity scanning on agent PRs, because human review misses 81%.

entries.title: Trail of Bits: only Go and vcpkg verified every downloaded package
entries.summary: Trail of Bits built a Docker and mitmproxy harness that played a compromised package repository and injected malware into real packages. Of 25 package managers, fewer than half verified lockfile hashes by default, and only Go and vcpkg verified every package they downloaded. Some lockfiles carry hashes that don't protect integrity: Pub warns on a mismatch but installs anyway, Conan's MD5 revision is an identifier, and CocoaPods and Composer hashes don't cover the fetched code.
entries.takeaway: A committed lockfile doesn't protect you from a compromised registry unless your package manager actually enforces its hashes; check yours and turn on the strict flag.

lessons.point: Integrity by default is rare: only two of 25 package managers verified every package they downloaded.
lessons.excerpt: fewer than half used lockfiles that checked for tampering by default, and only two verified the integrity of every package they downloaded

lessons.point: A hash in the lockfile is not enough: Pub detects a mismatch, rewrites the lockfile and installs the tampered package unless you pass --enforce-lockfile.
lessons.excerpt: If there is a mismatch, Pub detects the error, but installs the package anyway.

lessons.point: pnpm had the same overwrite-on-mismatch default until version 11.4 in May 2026.
lessons.excerpt: Overwriting the lockfile after a hash mismatch was also the default behavior in pnpm until version

lessons.point: Commit or tag hashes that don't cover the downloaded artifact give no protection: Composer pins a commit but downloads a ZIP that can't be checked against it.
lessons.excerpt: Once again, GitHub could serve a malicious ZIP archive without detection by Composer.

actionable.title: Enforce lockfile hashes in CI for every ecosystem you use
actionable.detail: Commit lockfiles for applications and install with the strict mode: npm ci, pnpm install --frozen-lockfile (pnpm 11.4 or later), yarn --immutable, flutter pub get --enforce-lockfile, uv/Poetry lock installs, and pip with hashes (pip --require-hashes). For NuGet set RestorePackagesWithLockFile. Treat Maven, Composer, CocoaPods, Conan, Gem and cpanminus as having no repository-compromise protection, and mirror or vendor their dependencies. Move cpanminus off plain HTTP.

entries.verify_note: Verifier: every fact checks out (source text truncated before the signature section; Table 2 supports the Go claim). Verifier novelty 50, relevance 72; took the lower novelty.
entries.prior_art: Prior work covers maintainer compromise and install-time code execution (pool claim package-installers-run-arbitrary-code-by-default) and the Gamage et al. lockfile study; this is the first cross-ecosystem dynamic test of 25 managers against a malicious repository, with per-manager verdicts.
entries.threat: An attacker who compromises a package repository or its web front end can serve modified packages that most package managers install without detecting tampering.
entries.conditions: Package managers that lack lockfile hashes, don't verify them by default, or whose hashes don't cover the downloaded artifact; cpanminus additionally fetches over plain HTTP.
entries.mitigations: Commit lockfiles and install in strict or frozen mode, enable signature verification where supported, mirror or vendor dependencies for ecosystems without integrity checks, and switch cpanminus to HTTPS mirrors.

editorial.reason: First cross-ecosystem test of package managers against a malicious registry; tells teams exactly which strict lockfile flags to turn on.

entries.title: JFrog Artifactory auth bypass chain exploited in the wild leaves persistent backdoors
entries.summary: Wiz Research saw attackers chain two Artifactory flaws: an exposed anonymous-user token and a token-scope validation bug. They separately abused a critical default-config auth bypass to get admin control. After entry, attackers created admin accounts, deployed Groovy plugins for code execution, and stole Access signing keys. Upgrading therefore does not remove them. Some implants even live only in memory, hide from 2xx-based detection, and wipe logs.

lessons.point: Two individually non-admin bugs combined into an unauthenticated-to-admin path in two requests.
lessons.excerpt: Together, the two can turn an unauthenticated request into an admin-scoped token in two steps.

lessons.point: Patching closes the entry point but not persistence: plugins reload on restart and look like normal API traffic.
lessons.excerpt: are reloaded automatically on restart, and are reachable over ordinary, TLS-wrapped API traffic that is indistinguishable at the network layer from normal registry usage.

lessons.point: Stolen token-signing private keys let attackers mint valid tokens forever, so the token certificate must be reset, not just the software upgraded.
lessons.excerpt: An attacker holding `private.key` can therefore forge valid tokens for any user and any scope, indefinitely, without ever touching the compromised host again

lessons.point: Detections keyed to successful responses miss implants that return output through error responses.
lessons.excerpt: Detection logic that looks for successful (2xx) plugin executions will miss this backdoor entirely.

entries.takeaway: For an exposed artifact registry, patching is not remediation: hunt for rogue admins and plugins and rotate token-signing keys and every stored credential.

actionable.title: Post-exploitation hunt checklist for Artifactory
actionable.detail: If an instance was exposed while vulnerable, assume compromise. Review admin users (including accounts with names like jfrog-insight or repo-service), list Groovy files under the plugins directory, check for requests by token:anonymous to /access/api/v1/tokens and /api/plugins/execute/, look for HTTP 500 responses on plugin endpoints and truncated request logs, reset the Access token certificate and rotate LDAP, proxy and remote-repository credentials.

entries.prior_art: No Artifactory entries found in pool; the nearest are other KEV exploited-appliance entries, which lack this post-exploitation detail (patch-surviving plugins, in-memory servlet filter, key theft). Verifier: No Artifactory entry; nearest is the CISA KEV exploited-appliance entries and 'Wiz scans every new npm version at publish time...'; patch-surviving plugin backdoor plus signing-key theft is a new detail within the known 'patching is not remediation' pattern
entries.threat: Attackers chain Artifactory auth flaws (CVE-2026-42018 anonymous token exposure, CVE-2026-42016 scope validation, CVE-2026-82329 default-config admin bypass) to gain admin, then plant Groovy plugin backdoors, a Rust backdoor, an in-memory servlet filter, and steal Access signing keys and stored upstream credentials.
entries.conditions: Self-hosted Artifactory instances reachable over the network while running vulnerable versions; Wiz reports roughly two thirds of customers running Artifactory had a vulnerable instance at publication of each CVE.
entries.mitigations: Upgrade to fixed versions, hunt for rogue admin accounts and plugins, reset the token certificate and Access keys, rotate stored credentials, and add behavioral detections for low-privilege identities minting tokens or touching the plugins API.
entries.verify_note: All four excerpts are verbatim and claims (67/69% exposure, 2-step chain, in-memory filter, HTTP 500 output, log purge) are supported. Source text is truncated at the CVE-2026-82329 detection section.

issues: mild: sentence_words 52 > 45 (Review admin users (including accounts with names like jfrog-insight or repo-service), list Groovy files under the plugi)

editorial.reason: In-the-wild exploitation of a JFrog Artifactory auth-bypass chain leaving Groovy plugin backdoors; teaches what to hunt for on a core build-infrastructure system.

entries.title: Argus, an open-source security platform, has AI agents that only propose actions
entries.summary: Argus is a self-hosted, MIT-licensed security operations platform. Its nine specialist AI agents triage and investigate with read-only tools. Their only write tool files a pending request with a separate action broker, which applies policy, approvals, dry runs and rollback. It also plants canaries aimed at AI agents (planted prompt injections, a fake MCP server, fake LLM API keys) and runs autonomous response playbooks that start in shadow mode and roll themselves back.

lessons.point: Agents can investigate but cannot act. Their only write path creates a pending request that a separate broker governs.
lessons.excerpt: Agents cannot execute anything; their one write-capable tool creates a pending request.

lessons.point: Telemetry the agent reads is wrapped as untrusted data, so an injection planted in a log becomes a detection signal instead of a command.
lessons.excerpt: Everything they read is treated as untrusted data, so a prompt injection hidden in a log becomes a signal instead of a hijack.

lessons.point: Canaries built for AI agents can catch rogue or attacker-run agents that take the bait.
lessons.excerpt: Plant canaries built for agents: hidden prompt injections, agent rules files, a fake MCP server and fake LLM API keys.

lessons.point: Autonomous response is limited by shadow mode, reversible-only actions, rate and blast-radius caps, and automatic rollback.
lessons.excerpt: They start in shadow mode so you can see what they would do, use only reversible actions, stay within hourly and blast-radius caps, and roll themselves back unless you keep the change.

entries.takeaway: Argus is a concrete reference design for agentic SecOps, with read-only agents, a propose-only path to a policy broker, agent-targeted canaries and autonomy that is reversible and off by default, but all of it is self-described with no independent evaluation.

actionable.title: Copy Argus's propose-only action broker for security agents
actionable.detail: Give investigation agents read-only tools plus a single propose_action tool that creates a pending request. Route that request through a separate broker. The broker checks a kill switch, deny-lists and approvals (approver differs from requester, two approvers for high risk), runs a dry run with blast radius, executes the action, and stores a rollback payload. Mark every tool result as untrusted data in the prompt. Separately, plant a fake MCP server and fake LLM keys as canaries for agents.

entries.verify_note: README supports every claim (nine agents, MIT); the design combines known patterns and has no evaluation.
entries.prior_art: Dual-LLM and human-in-the-loop tool gating, Microsoft spotlighting, Thinkst Canarytokens, LLM agent honeypots (Palisade Research), SOAR playbooks with dry-run and rollback
entries.threat: Prompt injection through ingested telemetry hijacks SOC agents, and rogue AI agents operate inside the environment.
entries.conditions: LLM agents read attacker-influenced logs and evidence, and could take response actions in cloud, identity or endpoint systems.
entries.mitigations: Use read-only agent tools, a propose-only write path to a policy broker with approvals, dry runs and rollback, untrusted-data wrapping of tool results, canaries aimed at agents, and autonomy that starts in shadow mode and is off by default.

entries.title: Imperva tracks StyleSmuggler Magento exploitation dropping the PSK Agent Go RAT
entries.summary: Imperva observed a September 9-13, 2026 automated campaign exploiting StyleSmuggler (CVE-2026-75650) in Magento and Adobe Commerce, where PHP in a /paypal/transparent/response/ query string is written to a var/report/ file and then evaluated via GraphQL styles parameters. Payloads pipe psk_agent.sh into bash, which installs a 10.5 MB obfuscated Go RAT (chi_down) with SOCKS5 proxying and persistence, and sometimes a 910-line AES-encrypted PHP webshell that can call libc via PHP FFI. Victims are beaconed back through hostname-bearing DNS lookups, the dropper had 0% VirusTotal detection, and Imperva assesses a likely Chinese-speaking operator with moderate confidence.
entries.takeaway: Patching StyleSmuggler does not evict PSK Agent, so hunt for the dropper, webshell and DNS beacons on any Magento host that was exposed.

lessons.point: The vulnerability is a two-step log-poisoning gadget: attacker PHP is persisted to an error report file, then a GraphQL request loads and evaluates it.
lessons.excerpt: A second request to /graphql uses attacker-controlled styles parameters to load the poisoned report file and evaluate the embedded PHP.

lessons.point: DNS lookups alone confirm successful execution to the operator, so blocking HTTP egress does not hide which hosts were compromised.
lessons.excerpt: the lookup alone could confirm that code execution had succeeded—even if the HTTP connection was blocked or failed

lessons.point: The webshell uses PHP FFI to call libc directly, which survives disable_functions hardening of the usual exec primitives.
lessons.excerpt: One of the more notable uses PHP’s Foreign Function Interface to call functions in libc directly

lessons.point: File reputation is useless here; detection has to cover the chain from the exploit request through shell spawning, egress and persistence.
lessons.excerpt: The dropper’s 0% VirusTotal detection rate shows why file reputation alone is insufficient.

actionable.title: Hunt Magento hosts for PSK Agent artifacts after patching
actionable.detail: Apply Adobe's VULN-39341 hotfix. Then search writable/executable dirs ($HOME, /tmp, /var/tmp, /dev/shm) for psk_agent.sh and chi_down, check cron and systemd for persistence, look for processes masquerading as kworker, fc-cache or chronyd, and look for zer4.php or other new PHP files under pub/media/. Alert on DNS lookups under 0f851bdc9d.ddns.1433.eu.org and on web-server processes contacting dynamic DNS domains or UDP/123. Disable PHP FFI where not needed, and rotate the Magento encryption key, DB, admin, payment-gateway and integration secrets on any host with indicators.

entries.verify_note: Lesson 3 says the FFI webshell survives disable_functions hardening; Imperva only says it is 'potentially preserving command execution'.
entries.prior_art: Core claim: StyleSmuggler is a shared access vector with multiple operators deploying distinct post-exploitation kits; this one is PSK Agent with DNS success beaconing and an FFI webshell. Nearest existing entry is product-security's 'Exploited Adobe Commerce and Magento upload flaw can lead to code execution' (CVE-2026-48356, a different bug). Earlier StyleSmuggler research documented a Rust backdoor; this post adds a new payload family and IOCs rather than a new technique class.
entries.threat: Opportunistic, automated exploitation of internet-exposed Magento and Adobe Commerce stores via CVE-2026-75650 to install a persistent Go RAT, an encrypted PHP webshell and DNS-based victim tracking, with likely access to payment-gateway and store secrets.
entries.conditions: Magento or Adobe Commerce store without the VULN-39341 hotfix, reachable from the Internet, with writable var/report or log files and a web-server account able to execute shell commands or reach outbound HTTP/DNS.
entries.mitigations: Apply VULN-39341 and verify it; treat hosts with any indicator as fully compromised; hunt for psk_agent.sh, chi_down, zer4.php and masquerading processes; monitor and restrict web-server egress and dynamic-DNS lookups; disable PHP FFI and unneeded exec functions; rotate all secrets accessible to the web-server account; block listed IOCs.

issues: mild: acronyms 9 > 3 (PSK, PHP, MB, SOCKS5, FFI, VULN, HOME, UDP, DB)

entries.title: Microsoft says Storm-0940 used the ARTEX pentest framework against 2,250+ tenants
entries.summary: Microsoft says Storm-0940 used ARTEX, an open-source multi-agent penetration-testing framework, to run password spraying, reconnaissance and OAuth-application abuse at machine speed after the ConnectWise Cloud Backup compromise. The actor tried to sign in to more than 2,250 tenants, and in several cases went from first targeting to privileged cloud access in under 3 hours. Most attempts failed, but the speed left defenders little time to respond.

lessons.point: Agentic tooling is already used by a state-aligned actor to scale known tradecraft such as spraying and OAuth abuse.
lessons.excerpt: ARTEX is an open-source penetration testing framework that can use any AI model to automate a variety of offensive security workflows.

lessons.point: Time to privileged cloud access fell under 3 hours in several cases.
lessons.excerpt: Several of these Storm-0940 ARTEX-driven attacks have resulted in the actor obtaining privileged access to an organization’s cloud infrastructure – including multiple instances where the time from initial targeting to privileged access was less than 3 hours.

lessons.point: Alerts fire, but the pace outruns coordinated response.
lessons.excerpt: the speed of the activity allows very little time for Defenders to respond to those alerts and remediate the actor’s access in a coordinated fashion.

lessons.point: Hunt for service-principal sign-ins and unexpected credential or privilege changes on applications.
lessons.excerpt: Customers should review service principal sign-ins, investigate unexpected application credential or privilege changes

entries.takeaway: Agent-driven intrusions compress the time from first touch to privileged cloud access to hours, so detection and OAuth-app hygiene must work at machine speed.

actionable.title: Audit OAuth apps and service principals
actionable.detail: List enterprise apps and service principals with tenant-wide consent, review recent credential additions and privilege changes through Microsoft Graph, and alert on bursts of sign-in failures per minute. Rehearse a response that assumes hours, not days.

entries.prior_art: Earlier pool entries cover AI-orchestrated attacks compressing human timelines (claim agent-orchestrated-attacks-compress-human-attack-timelines); this adds a named state actor, a named framework and measured tenant scale. Verifier: Anthropic GTG-1002 (Nov 2025) AI-orchestrated espionage report; Google GTIG AI misuse reports. Delta is a named open-source agentic pentest framework (ARTEX) us
entries.verify_note: Independent verifier found every claim supported by the source.

editorial.reason: Microsoft attributes machine-speed ConnectWise supply-chain follow-on attacks to an agentic pentest framework.

entries.title: ScreenConnect RMM+ extension flaw may have let attackers bypass MFA
entries.summary: Huntress traced a campaign to a possible authentication weakness in the RMM+ extension, a third-party ScreenConnect extension; ConnectWise has not confirmed the initial access method. The campaign pushed the 16-file SCKit malware to 288 endpoints across 48 organizations within 90 minutes. Versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 accept a blank access key when none is configured. Because the extension works outside ScreenConnect's own accounts and multi-factor authentication (MFA), commands reached machines with no matching login activity. ConnectWise disabled five extensions across about 400 installations but says it found no flaw in ScreenConnect itself. SCKit also tries to infect technicians who connect to investigate, though Huntress has not seen that step succeed.

lessons.point: A possible cause, not confirmed by ConnectWise: an unset secret that defaults to accepting a blank value would turn an optional integration into an unauthenticated command channel.
lessons.excerpt: Versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 of the extension contain a flaw that means installations without a configured access key will accept a blank one.

lessons.point: Plugins that expose their own command path sit outside the host product's authentication, so multi-factor authentication (MFA) on the console does not protect them.
lessons.excerpt: Because RMM+ operates independently of ScreenConnect's normal user accounts and authentication controls, an attacker could potentially execute commands without defeating MFA.

lessons.point: Do not investigate a suspected remote-access compromise through the same remote-access tool; the malware is built to attack the responder.
lessons.excerpt: the malware is designed to turn an infected computer into a trap for the technician sent to investigate it

lessons.point: Disabling the vulnerable extension does not evict an attacker who already installed their own remote access client and persistence.
lessons.excerpt: Disabling extensions and resetting credentials alone may not remove unauthorized software, persistence mechanisms, or access already established on endpoints.

entries.takeaway: Audit remote-management extensions as separate auth surfaces, and investigate compromised endpoints out-of-band rather than through ScreenConnect.

actionable.title: Inventory and disable RMM+ ScreenConnect extensions
actionable.detail: On self-hosted ScreenConnect servers, remove or disable the RMM+ extension, RMM Plus, Labtech Plus and related extensions, and confirm any remaining extension has a configured access key. Hunt for rogue ScreenConnect clients and review remote command history; investigate affected machines with other security tools rather than a ScreenConnect session, and fully clean hosts before taking them out of isolation, since Huntress saw reinfection within minutes.

entries.verify_note: Verifier found the blank-key flaw was presented as the confirmed cause though the source calls it a possible weakness and initial access is unconfirmed; title, summary and lesson 1 were hedged and the invented RMM+ expansion removed.
entries.prior_art: Prior ConnectWise/ScreenConnect abuse in the tracker (Storm-0940 ARTEX entry after the ConnectWise Cloud Backup compromise; ScreenConnect named among recurring remote-support appliance flaws) and the 2024 ScreenConnect auth-bypass CVE-2024-1709. New here: the compromise path runs through a third-party extension with a blank-key default rather than ScreenConnect itself, plus responder-targeting malware. Verifier's closest: Storm-0940/ARTEX entry following the ConnectWise compromise; BeyondTrust Remote Support entries.
entries.threat: Attackers issue ScreenConnect remote commands through a third-party extension without valid credentials or MFA, install rogue clients on MSP-managed endpoints, and try to compromise technicians who connect to investigate.
entries.conditions: ScreenConnect installation with RMM+ 1.0.31 or 1.0.32 (or related extensions) and no configured access key; affected ScreenConnect versions included 26.6.6.9747 and 26.7.6.9783.
entries.mitigations: Disable RMM+ family extensions, look for rogue ScreenConnect clients and executed commands, investigate with tools other than ScreenConnect, remove malware and persistence before reconnecting hosts, and reset credentials.

entries.title: StepSecurity finds fake-interview npm look-alikes stayed on npm for seven months
entries.summary: StepSecurity followed up JFrog's report on AccuraSoftHire, a fake company that gave job candidates take-home tests built on look-alike Tailwind plugins carrying the PolinRider loader. Two of the poisoned packages, tailwind-lines-clamps and tailwind-lineclamp, stayed on npm for 211 and 169 days and had more than 4,000 downloads in 2026. StepSecurity also decoded all 609 transactions from the Ethereum wallet the loader uses to find its server (the NullReceiver technique) and recovered eight server IPs, the newest posted on October 19.

lessons.point: The loader runs when Tailwind builds the CSS, not at install time, so controls that only watch or disable npm install scripts miss it.
lessons.excerpt: The loader does not run during `npm install`, so tools that only check install scripts do not see it.

lessons.point: A release-age cooldown would have blocked most of the short-lived look-alikes but not the two that lasted months. Catching those needs an inventory of the packages on developer machines.
lessons.excerpt: A cooldown that blocks packages published in the last few days would have held back most of the short-lived ones, but not the two that lasted months.

lessons.point: Because the server address comes from public blockchain transactions, the attacker can move servers without republishing anything, and defenders can read back the full server history to build a complete blocklist.
lessons.excerpt: To change servers, the attacker only has to send a new transaction. No package needs to change.

entries.takeaway: Interview assignments run on work laptops are an employer supply-chain risk, and the malware hides in build-time code and blockchain-resolved servers that install-script controls and static blocklists both miss.

actionable.title: Hunt for fake-interview loaders on developer machines
actionable.detail: Inventory node_modules and global installs on developer laptops for the IOC packages (tailwind-lines-clamps, tailwind-lineclamp, tailwind-forms-kit, tailwind-custom-forms and the rest of the table). Search for .vscode/tasks.json files with runOn folderOpen and for unpacked Chrome extensions from a job-new-alerts folder. Block and search egress logs for all eight decoded server IPs, plus Ethereum RPC lookups from build processes. Rotate every credential on any machine that ran an interview assignment.

entries.verify_note: Verifier confirmed every number and the package-to-dwell-time pairing; the wallet was already public via OpenSourceMalware. Novelty taken as the verifier's 30.
entries.prior_art: JFrog's AccuraSoftHire research; OpenSourceMalware's NullReceiver and PolinRider write-ups; EtherHiding blockchain C2; the Binance theft entry citing fake recruitment interviews. New: measured npm dwell times (169 and 211 days) and the decoded eight-server history.
entries.threat: North Korea-linked operators pose as employers and get developers to run take-home projects on work laptops; a blockchain-resolved loader then steals browser, wallet, SSH, cloud and git credentials.
entries.conditions: A developer runs a recruiter-supplied project build, a curl one-liner or an unpacked extension on a company machine that holds deployment or cloud credentials.
entries.mitigations: Ban interview work on company devices, inventory packages on developer machines, alert on VS Code folderOpen tasks and unpacked extensions, apply release-age cooldowns, block all eight decoded server IPs, monitor build-time egress, and rotate all credentials on any exposed machine.

editorial.reason: Live DPRK fake-interview campaign whose loader runs at CSS build time, so install-script controls and short cooldowns miss it; gives an IOC hunt for developer laptops.

entries.title: With ChatGPT, ITRES rebuilt two BruCON techniques whose source was never released
entries.summary: A researcher with no recent kernel experience used ChatGPT, conference slide photos, Git history and a compiled executable to rebuild two Windows kernel execution-redirection techniques shown at BruCON 2026. The original author had spent about four months on them and never released source. Both techniques reached SYSTEM on Windows 11 with VBS (virtualization-based security), HVCI (hypervisor-protected code integrity) and kernel shadow stacks enabled, after about 24 hours of recorded work. The model refused 39 times and broke working code late in the project, so the last integration step was finished by hand.

lessons.point: Partial public material (slides, Git history, a compiled binary) was enough to reconstruct unreleased techniques with LLM help.
lessons.excerpt: Using public research, Git history and a compiled executable, we went on to reconstruct and reproduce two of his techniques: Native SSDT and Shadow SSDT.

lessons.point: The author argues researchers should rethink how hard it is for others to weaponize partial disclosures.
lessons.excerpt: But the assumptions about how difficult it is for someone else to turn partial published information into custom working code may no longer be valid.

lessons.point: Model refusals were frequent but inconsistent: it helped build similar functionality earlier, then refused the final integration.
lessons.excerpt: That is approximately 13.8% of the 282 final assistant responses.

lessons.point: Offline test harnesses validated parsing logic only; real kernel effects needed a protected Windows lab with A/B/A restore checks.
lessons.excerpt: They didn’t prove that we could modify kernel execution, restore the original state or obtain a SYSTEM identity.

entries.takeaway: The author argues LLMs make partially disclosed exploit research much cheaper to reproduce, so release decisions for talks, binaries and repos should assume others can rebuild it.

actionable.title: Treat released binaries and slides as reproducible source
actionable.detail: Before publishing exploit research, assume a compiled PoC, slide photos and Git history can be turned into working code by an LLM-assisted non-expert within days. Scrub binaries and history you do not intend to release (deleting a repo late does not undo earlier clones), and plan defender guidance (detections, patches) to land with the talk, not after.

entries.prior_art: Closest pool work covers frontier AI agents compressing intrusion timelines (archive: 'Frontier AI Agents Compress a Two-Week Intrusion Into 10 Hours') and LLM research harnesses finding bugs (PwnEscape); this adds a measured case of LLM-assisted reproduction of unreleased kernel exploitation research from partial artifacts, plus refusal counts. Verifier: Earlier work showed LLMs speeding up exploit reproduction from partial information (e.g., GPT-4 one-day exploitation from CVE descriptions, Fang et al. 2024; AI-assisted n-day patch-diff reproduction). This adds a concrete kernel/HVCI case study with refusal counts, but the thesis itself is not new.
entries.verify_note: Independent fresh-context verifier re-read the source; the overstatements it flagged were corrected before merge.
entries.threat: Attackers with modest expertise can rebuild unreleased exploitation techniques from conference talks, deleted repos and compiled PoCs using general-purpose LLMs.
entries.conditions: Partial technical material is public (slides, Git history, a compiled executable); the reproduced techniques still require administrator privileges to load or use the tooling.
entries.mitigations: Researchers: avoid publishing compiled PoCs or history you do not intend to release; coordinate defensive guidance with disclosure. Defenders: keep VBS/HVCI enabled and monitor for vulnerable driver loading and admin-to-kernel paths.

editorial.reason: tl;dr sec-featured case of an LLM-assisted researcher rebuilding Windows kernel techniques from slides and a binary in about 24 hours; it changes how to weigh partial disclosure.

entries.title: Valid SQL crashes SQLGlot and SQLFluff with huge memory amplification
entries.summary: SQLGlot and SQLFluff parse deeply nested or very wide but syntactically valid SQL with no depth or node limit: about 50 nesting levels hits Python's recursion limit, and a sub-2MB query builds an abstract syntax tree (AST) using over 1.5GB of RAM. Because apps parse before executing, one authenticated Superset SQL Lab user can kill or pin the shared worker pool, a Dify plugin query broke the daemon-to-worker bridge for about 60 seconds, and Pathway was OOM-killed at 8GB+. The same flaw shows up in Neo4j Cypher, graphql-js and graphql-core.
entries.takeaway: Treat any parser that consumes user or LLM-generated text as a trust boundary: cap bytes, depth and node count before parsing, and upgrade SQLGlot/SQLFluff to versions with limits.

lessons.point: Recursive-descent parsers without a depth cap fail on modest nesting.
lessons.excerpt: At 50+ levels of nesting, the recursive descent parser exhausts the call stack.

lessons.point: The DoS fires in the pre-execution parse step, so database-side limits and query timeouts don't help.
lessons.excerpt: An authenticated user with ordinary SQL Lab access is enough; the query never has to run.

lessons.point: Client-side input limits are not a control; enforce size caps on the server.
lessons.excerpt: The frontend enforces a 3,000-character input limit. The backend does not.

lessons.point: The bug class is generic to parsers that build rich object trees, not specific to SQL.
lessons.excerpt: Any parser that turns untrusted text into a rich object tree without bounding depth or node count is exposed.

actionable.title: Bound parser input before parsing
actionable.detail: Upgrade SQLGlot (limit merged ahead of v30.5.0) and SQLFluff to patched releases and keep default limits on. Where a parser takes user or LLM-generated SQL/GraphQL/Cypher, reject on cheap pre-parse checks on the server (byte size, token count, parenthesis depth, column count), run parsing with a timeout in a memory-capped worker or subprocess, and rate-limit submissions. For graphql-js and graphql-core, set an explicit max token/depth limit since none is on by default.

entries.verify_note: Excerpts verbatim. Verifier: the two CVEs were assigned to the SQLFluff findings only, and ~750x was measured on SQLGlot. Verifier novelty 55.
entries.prior_art: Classic algorithmic-complexity and deep-nesting DoS (billion laughs, JSON/YAML nesting bombs, GraphQL depth/complexity limits, Imperva's own graphql-java DoS write-up). New here: CVEs in the two main Python SQL parsers, measured amplification ratios, and concrete cascades into Superset, Dify and Pathway.
entries.threat: An authenticated low-privilege user (or anyone reaching an exposed parse endpoint) sends a valid but deeply nested or very wide query that exhausts memory or CPU in the parser, crashing or hanging shared workers.
entries.conditions: Application passes untrusted or LLM-generated SQL to unpatched SQLGlot or SQLFluff (or graphql-js/graphql-core/Cypher without limits) with no server-side size or depth cap.
entries.mitigations: Upgrade parsers and keep recursion/node limits enabled; server-side byte/token/depth/column caps before parsing; parse timeouts; container memory limits; rate limiting; isolate plugin processes.

entries.title: Unit 42: ransomware groups try PAN-OS CVE-2026-0257 to bypass GlobalProtect MFA
entries.summary: Unit 42 updated its report on CVE-2026-0257, a GlobalProtect authentication bypass fixed in May 2026. Unit 42 saw exploitation attempts by ransomware operators including Qilin and Inc against unpatched devices; successful ones open VPN sessions that skip MFA, followed by RMM tools, RDP and SMB. In one notable case the attackers pivoted to vCenter and ESXi and dumped domain-controller credentials offline from the virtual disk, bypassing in-guest EDR.

lessons.point: Exploitation yields an MFA-free VPN foothold.
lessons.excerpt: Attackers are leveraging this vulnerability to gain an initial foothold into corporate networks, subsequently bypassing multi-factor authentication (MFA) controls to establish a VPN session.

lessons.point: The key change is going to the virtualization layer.
lessons.excerpt: The most significant evolution in tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) following successful exploitation of CVE-2026-0257 is the direct pivot to the virtualization layer.

lessons.point: Offline credential theft sidesteps in-guest detection.
lessons.excerpt: This tactic bypasses in-guest endpoint detection and response (EDR) and security controls

lessons.point: A fix has existed for months.
lessons.excerpt: Fixes for this vulnerability have been available since May 2026.

entries.takeaway: Patch GlobalProtect and protect the hypervisor management plane: in one case attackers read virtual disks to go around endpoint tools.

actionable.title: Close the hypervisor blind spot
actionable.detail: Patch PAN-OS or apply the mitigations (dedicated Authentication Override certificate or disable the option), isolate vCenter and ESXi management, and alert on execInstalledOnly changes and VMDK reads outside backup tools.

entries.prior_art: Ransomware targeting ESXi is established; the offline VMDK credential-dumping pivot after a VPN bypass is the new detail. Verifier: Hypervisor-targeting ransomware (ESXi encryptors, Scattered Spider vCenter/ESXi pivots, Mandiant UNC3944 reports); offline NTDS extraction from VMDK is document
entries.verify_note: Independent fresh-context verifier re-read the source; discrepancies it found (title/summary overstatements) were corrected before merge.

editorial.reason: Ransomware groups attempting a PAN-OS MFA bypass and pivoting to the hypervisor layer.

entries.title: Citizen Lab: Candiru spyware reached Al Jazeera devices through targeted ads
entries.summary: Citizen Lab reports AdFection: Candiru spyware infected Al Jazeera devices through targeted advertisements, which it calls the first public technical confirmation of zero-click mercenary spyware delivered through ads. Discover-Tech, an Israeli firm that looks like a normal ad company, ran a platform that fingerprints devices and infects them when an ad renders. Four billion bidding records show its ads on almost 200,000 sites and apps. Google, IAB Europe, Beeswax, Vungle and Eskimi cut its access after disclosure.

lessons.point: Ads delivered a zero-click mercenary spyware attack.
lessons.excerpt: first public technical confirmation of a zero-click mercenary spyware attack delivered via targeted advertising, which we call AdFection

lessons.point: Ad industry vendor lists failed to catch the abuse.
lessons.excerpt: Discover-Tech has appeared on lists of “certified” and “approved” vendors maintained by Google and advertising industry association IAB Europe

lessons.point: Scale: ads reached nearly 200,000 sites and apps in four months.
lessons.excerpt: Analysis of four billion Discover-Tech bidding records shows that during a four-month period, the company’s ads were shown on almost 200,000 unique websites and Android/iOS apps in dozens of countries.

lessons.point: Disconnecting the vendor was possible after disclosure.
lessons.excerpt: Google, IAB Europe, Beeswax, Vungle (Liftoff), and Eskimi took action to disconnect Discover-Tech’s access to the digital advertising ecosystem.

entries.takeaway: Real-time ad bidding can deliver zero-click spyware; ad vendors cut off the abuser only after Citizen Lab disclosed it.

actionable.title: Reduce ad-delivery exposure for at-risk staff
actionable.detail: For journalists and executives, enable lockdown or hardened modes, use a content blocker or DNS filtering for ad networks, and keep mobile OS updates current; add ad-exchange vendor review to threat models.

entries.prior_art: Zero-click mercenary spyware via messaging apps is well documented; ad-based delivery confirmed technically is new. Verifier: Intellexa Predator/Aladdin ad-based zero-click infection (Amnesty/Haaretz 2023-2024); ADINT surveillance research (Citizen Lab PenLink, Patternz)
entries.verify_note: Independent fresh-context verifier re-read the source; discrepancies it found (title/summary overstatements) were corrected before merge.

entries.title: EDK2 network boot flaw lets attackers run code before Secure Boot
entries.summary: CVE-2026-97631 (severity 9.5) is a 16-year-old buffer overflow in the network boot (PXE) driver of TianoCore EDK2. EDK2 is the open source base most UEFI (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface) firmware is built on. During network boot, an oversized ICMP error message overflows a 504-byte field, which can let an attacker run code at the highest CPU privilege before Secure Boot and TPM (Trusted Platform Module) protections apply. The planned coordinated disclosure broke early when a vendor's public pull request published the fix, and the article says an attacker needs some control over a local network and an exploit tuned to each target.

lessons.point: The bug is a bounds error in copying ICMP error messages during PXE boot.
lessons.excerpt: for a message longer than 504 bytes it still copies bytes into the field

lessons.point: Fuzzing campaigns started after the similar PixieFail bug did not find this flaw.
lessons.excerpt: It appears those efforts failed to find this latest flaw.

lessons.point: Exploits must be tuned to each firmware build, which limits mass exploitation.
lessons.excerpt: but it needs to be tuned for each target model/version/configuration since the addresses will change based on those

lessons.point: Turning off network boot is the main interim mitigation, since Secure Boot and TPM do not stop this bug.
lessons.excerpt: they should consider turning off network boot capabilities at least temporarily if possible

entries.takeaway: Any server fleet that network-boots on EDK2-based firmware has a pre-OS code-execution hole, so disable PXE where you can and push your firmware vendors for updates.

actionable.title: Inventory PXE-booting EDK2 machines and disable network boot
actionable.detail: Identify servers and storage that boot from the local network on EDK2-derived firmware (AMI, Insyde, Phoenix, Project Mu). Disable PXE where it is not needed, ask each firmware vendor for a fixed BIOS/UEFI update for CVE-2026-97631, and watch for oversized ICMP error traffic on boot network segments.

entries.prior_art: No UEFI, EDK2 or PXE entries in the pools. The source names PixieFail, an earlier EDK2 PXE flaw class, as the closest precedent.
entries.threat: An attacker on the local network sends an oversized ICMP error during PXE boot and overflows the driver buffer. This gives ring-0 code execution before Secure Boot and TPM protections, which could defeat disk encryption, or simply hangs the boot.
entries.conditions: Machines whose firmware is built on EDK2 with PXE network boot enabled (on by default) and that boot from the network, with the attacker on the network and knowing the target firmware build. Machines that boot only from disk are not affected.
entries.mitigations: Apply the BIOS/UEFI update from your firmware vendor, temporarily disable network boot where possible, keep TPM and Secure Boot enabled, and monitor logs for exploitation attempts.

entries.title: GitHub Security Lab found 24 Android vulnerabilities with its AI agent
entries.summary: GitHub Security Lab extended its open-source Taskflow Agent with Android-specific audit steps. One taskflow separates mobile from non-mobile entry points, and another checks a fixed list of vulnerability classes against each entry point. Together they found 24 vulnerabilities, including OsmAnd location tracking and a WebView account-takeover chain. The post is candid that LLMs over-report low-severity bugs, misjudge severity, and need PoC runs plus expert review.

lessons.point: Give the model a per-entry-point checklist of vulnerability classes so non-determinism doesn't skip the essential bug classes on less familiar platforms like Android.
lessons.excerpt: Since mobile application vulnerabilities are less widely known and LLMs are non-deterministic, we should ensure the LLM checks for certain essential vulnerabilities classes.

lessons.point: Run a strict checklist prompt several times alongside a broad open-ended prompt: the first catches the obvious bugs and the second finds the creative ones.
lessons.excerpt: By combining both prompts across multiple runs, we get the best of each

lessons.point: LLM auditors over-report low-impact or unrealistic-state bugs, even when told not to, so every finding needs expert triage.
lessons.excerpt: it often reported low-severity vulnerabilities, even when specifically told not to do so

lessons.point: Making the model write a proof of concept surfaces mitigating factors it otherwise misses; a debugger is the stronger fix for the false positives that remain.
lessons.excerpt: the only way to fix these issue is to give the LLM a debugger to run the proof of concept and original code

entries.takeaway: Scaffolded, platform-specific taskflows make LLMs effective Android bug hunters, but severity and exploitability still need a PoC and a human.

actionable.title: Two-stage Android audit: classify entry points, then checklist per entry point
actionable.detail: Stage 1: enumerate exported activities, services, receivers, deeplinks and JS bridges, and separate mobile from non-mobile entry points. Stage 2: for each entry point, prompt for its class-specific checklist (intents: confused deputy, insecure broadcast; WebView: XSS, exposed bridges; files: path traversal). Run that strict pass several times plus one open-ended pass, then require a PoC for every finding before human triage.

entries.prior_art: Earlier GHSL Taskflow Agent posts on generic audit taskflows, and LLM-assisted SAST triage; the delta is the Android-specific entry-point and checklist decomposition plus its field results.
entries.verify_note: Independent verifier: all lessons supported; novelty 45 (vs 50), relevance 80.

editorial.reason: 24 real, disclosed Android vulnerabilities (OsmAnd location tracking, a WebView account-takeover chain) found with an open-source agent you can run today, plus candid lessons on LLM severity misjudgment and false positives.

entries.title: Attackers used AhsayCBS zero-days to plant a host-locked Python backdoor
