entries.summary: Huntress saw attackers chain CVE-2026-105133 and CVE-2026-105134 in AhsayCBS backup servers. Both are assessed to have been exploited as zero-days to bypass authentication and run commands. The attackers left five Jakarta Server Pages (JSP) web shell families, two XMRig miners, tunneling tools and a Python implant. The implant runs only on its intended host, because it checks for a marker file named after the SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm 256) hash of the host's MachineGuid. In the same environment, a Veeam server was queried for stored credentials, which suggests the operator deliberately targeted backup infrastructure.

lessons.point: Attackers hit backup servers with zero-days before patches existed. Treat them as tier-zero assets.
lessons.excerpt: The two vulnerabilities are assessed to have been weaponized as zero-days

lessons.point: The implant is tied to its host. It runs only when a marker file derived from the host's MachineGuid sits next to it. A sample copied into a sandbox stays inert, so analysts need the marker file or the original host.
lessons.excerpt: looks for a marker file with the same name in the same directory housing the Python implant

lessons.point: One web shell hid encrypted payloads in the pixel data of PNG (Portable Network Graphics) images and ran them from memory. The payload is hidden in PNG pixels, while the AhsayCBS.jsp loader itself sits on disk.
lessons.excerpt: a loader that hides encrypted payloads in the pixel data of PNG images and runs them from memory

lessons.point: Backup software stores credentials for hypervisors, repositories and domain accounts, so compromising backup systems opens a path to the wider estate.
lessons.excerpt: Backup software holds credentials for hypervisors, repositories and domain accounts.

entries.takeaway: Backup servers hold the keys to the estate, so patch AhsayCBS and hunt for JSP shells, Defender exclusions and Veeam credential queries.

actionable.title: Hunt backup servers for the AhsayCBS intrusion pattern
actionable.detail: On AhsayCBS hosts, look for unexpected .jsp files (including st_*.jsp and status_*.jsp), PNG files served from web roots, new Microsoft Defender exclusions, SYSTEM scheduled tasks restarting kvm-agent.exe, GOST/Chisel binaries, and AnyDesk, Atera or Splashtop installs. On Veeam servers, alert on WMI-launched PowerShell querying the VeeamBackup PostgreSQL database.

entries.verify_note: Overstated scanning lesson corrected.
entries.prior_art: Host-keyed malware such as Gauss; Veeam backup credential theft (CVE-2023-27532).
entries.threat: An attacker who exploits AhsayCBS gets command execution on backup servers, then plants persistent web shells, miners and tunnels, and steals backup-stored credentials for hypervisors and domain accounts.
entries.conditions: AhsayCBS without the mid-October 2026 patches is reachable by the attacker; co-located backup products such as Veeam store recoverable credentials.
entries.mitigations: Apply the October 2026 AhsayCBS patches, keep backup consoles off untrusted networks, alert on Defender exclusion changes and new remote-access tools, rotate credentials stored in backup products after any compromise, and keep the host-locked implant together with its marker file for analysis.

entries.title: Engineer lists three AWS IAM anti-patterns coding agents keep writing
entries.summary: A practitioner reviewing agent-written AWS IAM policies names three recurring patterns the author considers wrong. They are extra Deny statements in identity policies, permissions boundaries used as a generic restriction rather than to constrain delegated IAM administration, and explicit Allow statements for sts:GetCallerIdentity, which needs no permission. The post argues extra Deny statements add complexity without being load-bearing; for permissions boundaries it says there is mostly no harm, but they misuse their purpose. It says Deny belongs in service control policies (SCPs) and resource control policies (RCPs) for organization-wide invariants. It is an opinion piece from experience, with no measurement of how often agents do this.

lessons.point: Agent-written identity policies often pair an Allow with a broad Deny to 'lock things down'; the author says to think twice before using Deny in identity policies, since it adds complexity that is not load-bearing. Deny still fits service control policy (SCP) and resource control policy (RCP) invariants and unusual carve-outs (e.g. revoking role sessions).
lessons.excerpt: seen a lot of over-zealous AWS IAM policies that use `Deny`.

lessons.point: Permissions boundaries exist to cap roles created by delegated administrators, not as a general way to restrict a principal.
lessons.excerpt: The predominant use case for permissions boundaries is to limit privileges available to IAM roles created by developers

lessons.point: Coding agents misuse permissions boundaries as a generic restriction tool, which signals they reproduce a defense-in-depth habit without understanding the mechanism.
lessons.excerpt: But coding agents miss the nuance - they use permissions boundaries as just

lessons.point: The author's personal 'Van Halen' test: an Allow for sts:GetCallerIdentity is pointless, since that action is always allowed and cannot be blocked.
lessons.excerpt: one of the few AWS IAM actions that are always allowed and cannot be blocked - `sts:GetSessionToken` is the only other one I know of

entries.takeaway: Review agent-generated IAM for cargo-cult patterns: needless Deny, misused permissions boundaries and no-op GetCallerIdentity grants.

actionable.title: Add an IAM review checklist for agent-written policies
actionable.detail: When an agent edits IAM JSON or Terraform, flag: Deny/NotAction statements inside identity policies (move invariants to service control policies (SCPs) or resource control policies (RCPs)), permissions boundaries on roles not created by delegated admins, and any Allow for sts:GetCallerIdentity or sts:GetSessionToken. Ask the agent to justify or remove each before merge.

entries.verify_note: The verifier confirmed the entry; the summary no longer genders the author or lumps permissions boundaries with Deny, and lessons 1 and 4 were softened to match the post.
entries.prior_art: Pool covers LLM-generated code hallucinating APIs and packages, and LLM-proposed AWS attacks with stolen keys (Adan Alvarez), plus Datadog pathrunner for IAM privilege escalation; nothing specifically on IAM-policy anti-patterns produced by coding agents. The IAM facts themselves are long-standing AWS guidance. Verifier's closest: no direct equivalent; Datadog pathrunner IAM escalation entry.

entries.title: SOCRadar: INC and The Gentlemen ransomware affiliates ran intrusions through AI agents
entries.summary: SOCRadar found an exposed command-and-control server holding the session logs, knowledge base and source code of Phantom, a framework affiliates of INC and The Gentlemen ransomware used. They exploited edge systems such as FortiClient EMS, SimpleHelp and cPanel, tracked victims in AI-managed knowledge bases, and staged 46 INC encryptor builds.

lessons.excerpt: Operators ran intrusions through OpenCode with OpenRouter-hosted commercial models, logging 8,257 messages across 133 sessions

lessons.point: Targets were edge and remote-access systems.
lessons.excerpt: The operators exploited edge and remote-access systems at scale, including FortiClient EMS, SimpleHelp, cPanel and VPN gateways.

lessons.point: AI also handled victim tracking and credential bookkeeping.
lessons.excerpt: They used AI-managed knowledge bases to track victims, stolen credentials and campaign progress.

entries.prior_art: CrowdStrike and NorForge describe criminals' agent harnesses; this adds ransomware affiliates, a deployment wave and spend figures from the operators' own logs. Verifier: Anthropic GTG-1002 / threat intel reports on AI-orchestrated intrusion; Gambit Security staging-server report; CrowdStrike agentic campaigns. Delta: exposed ope
