entries.title: Alpine Linux rebuilt GitLab after its upgrade missed a Ruby patch
entries.summary: On October 20 and 21 a newly registered account sent crafted CI configurations to Alpine Linux's GitLab to exploit CVE-2026-97229, a CVSS 10.0 bug in Ruby's Onigmo regular expression engine, crashing workers 8 times. Alpine's upgrade to GitLab 19.3.6 did not fix it, because the fix is a patch GitLab applies to Ruby only in its official packages and Alpine's image used stock Ruby; self-built installs also need Ruby 3.3.13, 3.4.12 or 4.0.9. Alpine found no evidence of code execution but could not rule it out, so it rebuilt the instance, reset all passwords and secret keys, and verified packages and releases against records outside GitLab.

lessons.point: A vendor's fix can live in a patched runtime it bundles, so upgrading the application alone leaves source or self-built installs vulnerable.
lessons.excerpt: The fix isn’t in GitLab’s own code but in a patch to Ruby, which GitLab applies only in its official packages.

lessons.point: The attacker pulled Alpine's public container image, likely to tune the exploit to the exact build, so publishing your images helps attackers fit exploits to you.
lessons.excerpt: The attacker also downloaded our GitLab container image, which suggests they were tuning the exploit to our exact build.

lessons.point: Without outbound connection logs, Alpine could not prove the exploit failed, which forced a full rebuild.
lessons.excerpt: We had no logging of outbound network connections, and our hosting provider keeps none either.

lessons.point: Keeping signing keys off the forge and checking commits against independent records let Alpine clear its packages and releases despite the uncertainty.
lessons.excerpt: The keys that sign Alpine packages and releases are not, and never have been, stored on the GitLab server.

entries.takeaway: If you build GitLab yourself, check what runtime patches its official packages carry, and log outbound traffic so you can rule a compromise in or out.

actionable.title: Check bundled-runtime patches when you self-build vendor software
actionable.detail: For self-managed GitLab built from source or on your own image, confirm Ruby is 3.3.13, 3.4.12, 4.0.9 or later, not just the GitLab version. For each critical release, read whether the fix sits in a bundled component your build must apply. Record outbound connections from the host, keep logs longer than 14 days, and keep signing keys off the forge.

entries.verify_note: Verifier upheld all four lessons (novelty 55 vs 50, lower kept).
entries.prior_art: The pool has GitLab's advisory for a different CVSS 10.0 regex RCE (CVE-2026-110264, 19.5.1 patch release), which is a vendor patch notice. This entry adds a first-hand incident: the fix lived in a bundled Ruby patch that self-built installs missed, plus the forensic limits that forced a rebuild.
entries.threat: An attacker with a self-registered account submits crafted CI configurations that trigger an Onigmo regex engine bug for possible code execution on the GitLab server, exposing user data, password hashes, two-factor authentication secrets, CI/CD variables, runner tokens and private repositories.
entries.conditions: Self-managed GitLab without the October 12 fix, or GitLab built on standard Ruby older than 3.3.13, 3.4.12 or 4.0.9, with open account registration.
entries.mitigations: Use GitLab's official packages or upgrade Ruby to a fixed release, apply critical GitLab releases within a day, log outbound and database connections and keep logs longer, keep signing keys off the forge, and sign release tags so releases can be verified outside GitLab.
entries.author: sashk

editorial.reason: First-hand incident on a CVSS 10.0 GitLab bug: the fix lived in a bundled Ruby patch that self-built installs miss, and missing egress logs forced a full rebuild.

entries.title: CrowdStrike: four newly seen actors ran agentic Claude Code intrusions
entries.summary: CrowdStrike analyzed four previously unreported actors (not all clearly criminal) that left offensive agent frameworks exposed (May to August 2026). One built a Supervisor and Executor pair of Claude Code agents derived from PentestGPT and hit at least 15 healthcare entities; one used two harnesses and a China-based API proxy; one used 819 skills from GitHub and had to coax the model past guardrails; one used a single slash command with a seven-step workflow. CrowdStrike judges that agentic AI commoditizes baseline offensive operations.

lessons.point: Agentic AI lowers the cost of baseline offensive operations.
lessons.excerpt: The four cases documented in this report likely demonstrate that agentic AI commoditizes baseline offensive cyber operations.

lessons.point: A supervisor/executor split with a state machine structures the attack.
lessons.excerpt: a “Supervisor” Claude Code agent selects the next task from a state machine (i.e., a predefined workflow of attack stages) and an “Executor” agent performs the task.

lessons.point: Guardrails slowed but did not stop the weakest actor, who nudged the model.
lessons.excerpt: the threat actor periodically had to intervene to overcome the model’s safety guardrails or to exhort Claude Code to keep trying to overcome a particular barrier.

lessons.point: CrowdStrike forecasts that low-skill actors will reach a higher capability level.
lessons.excerpt: Agentic AI will reduce barriers to effective intrusions

entries.takeaway: CrowdStrike expects low-skill actors to reach organized-crime-level effectiveness within 12 months, so harden against basic tradecraft now.

actionable.title: Plan for agent-speed basic attacks
actionable.detail: Close commodity paths (exposed services, weak creds, unpatched edge) and tune detections for rapid, systematic enumeration; add endpoint telemetry for coding-agent CLIs run by non-developers.

entries.prior_art: Anthropic and OpenAI threat reports describe misuse; this adds four exposed harness architectures with named designs. Verifier: Anthropic GTG-1002 disclosure (Nov 2025) and later Anthropic threat reports; PentestGPT, PentAGI; Gambit and SOCRadar reports from the same period. Delta: four
entries.verify_note: Independent fresh-context verifier re-read the source; discrepancies it found (title/summary overstatements) were corrected before merge.

editorial.reason: Four exposed agentic Claude Code intrusion harnesses documented by CrowdStrike.

entries.title: Microsoft finds 78% of exploited CVEs are takeover-class bugs
entries.summary: Microsoft analyzed about 383,000 published CVEs against roughly 2,000 exploited in the wild and found exploitation concentrates in server-side RCE, local privilege escalation, client-side RCE and auth bypass, while XSS and DoS shrink sharply in the exploited set. Its own exposure-management data shows median patch times of about two weeks on Windows workstations, over a month on Windows servers, 10+ weeks on Linux servers and over a year on network appliances, while CISA KEV timelines have collapsed to a 3-day median in 2026. The second half of the post is a pitch for Defender EASM, MDVM and attack-path analysis.
entries.takeaway: Prioritize takeover-class bugs on exposed, highly privileged servers and appliances first, because those are both the most exploited and the slowest patched.

lessons.point: The exploited set is a tiny and differently shaped slice of the CVE population, so CVSS-wide patch queues waste effort on classes attackers rarely use.
lessons.excerpt: Server-side RCE rises from 20% of published CVEs to 37% of exploited CVEs, local privilege escalation from 11% to 18%, and client-side RCE from 4% to 13%.

lessons.point: Patch latency is worst exactly where exposure is highest, with network appliances lagging by more than a year at the median.
lessons.excerpt: It stretches to 10+ weeks on Linux Servers and for applications running on MacOS, and beyond a year on network appliances.

lessons.point: Time from CVE publication to KEV listing has collapsed in 2026, which Microsoft partly attributes to AI-assisted exploit development.
lessons.excerpt: 2026 data up to September already have that number dropping to 20 days, with a median of only 3 days since publication.

lessons.point: Takeover classes dominate real-world exploitation and are the earliest place to break an attack chain.
lessons.excerpt: account for 78% of real-world exploited vulnerabilities

actionable.title: Rank patch queues by impact class and asset exposure
actionable.detail: Score each open CVE by whether it is a takeover class (server-side RCE, auth bypass, LPE, client-side RCE) and by the exposure of the asset (internet-facing, privileged service identities, reach to critical data). Patch or compensate for takeover bugs on exposed servers and appliances first, and set explicit service-level agreements (SLAs) for appliances since their median patch time is the longest. Use KEV and exploit-availability signals rather than CVSS alone.

entries.verify_note: Lesson 3 attributes faster KEV listing partly to AI-assisted exploit development as Microsoft's finding; the post only says 'industry research suggests' it, and the timing figures come from CISA data.
entries.prior_art: Core claim: exploitation concentrates in a small set of takeover-class CVEs, so prioritize by impact and exposure. This restates well-known findings from VulnCheck State of Exploitation, EPSS research and CISA KEV analyses (which the post itself cites). The product-security corpus has many individual KEV and exploited-CVE entries (Ivanti, F5 BIG-IP, Cisco ASA, Plex) and a 'Prioritize edge exposure' actionable, but no aggregate dataset entry; the new data is Microsoft's own patch-latency medians by platform.

issues: mild: sentence_words 46 > 45 (Its own exposure-management data shows median patch times of about two weeks on Windows workstations, over a month on Wi)

entries.title: Google PageBreak finds 500+ XSS bugs with near-zero false positives
entries.summary: PageBreak is Google Product Security's internal agent, mostly running on Gemini models, that hunts bugs in Google's own web apps. The agent only proposes a bug. Hand-written (not AI-written) validators then fire a real payload per bug class (XSS, SQL injection, path traversal, RCE, server-side request forgery) against a running environment, and only confirmed findings reach product teams. That produced 500+ XSS bugs at near-zero false positives, while apps built on Google's secure-by-design frameworks yielded just 2.

lessons.point: The agent only proposes a bug. A separate deterministic validator confirms it by actually running an exploit payload.
lessons.excerpt: When the agent identifies a potential flaw, it passes the hypothesis to a validator which then executes a real payload to confirm the exploit.

lessons.point: Testing against a running environment cuts false positives and keeps 'AI slop' away from product teams.
lessons.excerpt: This approach results in a near-zero false positive rate, ensuring that we avoid overloading product teams with unverified vulnerability reports.

lessons.point: Unverified findings are not thrown away. They seed later runs and show where validators are missing, but they never go to developers.
lessons.excerpt: Crucially, we do not send these unverified candidates to product teams, preserving their focus for high-confidence alerts.

lessons.point: Asking the agent to report which capability or access it lacked turns failed validations into a roadmap for the harness.
lessons.excerpt: We let the PageBreak agent report what capabilities or environment access it is missing in order to validate a report.

lessons.point: Secure-by-design web frameworks held up against the agent: only 2 XSS bugs across hundreds of apps built on them, both in internal or debug endpoints.
lessons.excerpt: As of September 4, 2026, the scanner identified only 2 XSS vulnerabilities across hundreds of web applications built on these frameworks and those were limited to internal applications or debug endpoints with hardening gaps.

entries.takeaway: Let the AI agent propose bugs, report only what a non-AI validator confirms by exploitation, and treat safe-by-default frameworks as the stronger defense.

actionable.title: Put a per-bug-class exploit validator between your AI scanner and your bug tracker
actionable.detail: For each bug class you hunt, write a deterministic validator that is not AI-written. XSS: load the URL in a headless renderer and detect execution of a unique JavaScript marker. SQL injection: check output or timing differences. Path traversal: plant a file in a world-readable location and read it back through the app. RCE: sleep delay, file write, or outbound DNS/HTTP callback. Server-side request forgery (SSRF): detect an internal request reaching a canary. File only the confirmed findings. Keep unconfirmed ones as seeds for later runs, and log the capability or access the agent says it lacked.

entries.prior_art: Chainguard Athena write-up ('Gate agent-found vulnerabilities on host-side replay', archive.json); the general generate-then-verify pattern used by AI pentest agents such as XBOW and Google Big Sleep. New here: production-scale numbers (500+ XSS) and the framework-hardening comparison. Verifier's closest: Chainguard Athena host-side replay gate; XBOW and Big Sleep generate-then-verify.
entries.verify_note: Verifier: excerpts verbatim; 'near-zero false positives' is Google's own unquantified claim.
entries.threat: Noisy, unverified LLM vulnerability reports overwhelm product teams. Real XSS and similar bugs remain in large first-party web estates.
entries.conditions: Needs running test environments, scanning infrastructure that can authenticate to the apps, and validators for each bug class. Google also relies on its mono-repo and traffic-to-code mapping (Security Signals), which most organizations do not have.
entries.mitigations: Use secure-by-design web frameworks. Gate AI findings on deterministic exploit validation. Run agents across many iterations with identical seeds to improve the odds of finding a working exploit path.

editorial.reason: Google's production-scale numbers for AI web testing gated by non-AI exploit validators (500+ XSS, near-zero false positives, only 2 on its high-assurance frameworks) teach how to make agent-found bugs trustworthy.

entries.title: SenTrojan researchers hid analog hardware Trojans in sensors triggered by physical signals
entries.summary: SenTrojan is a framework, accepted at the NDSS 2027 conference, for hiding malicious analog circuitry inside sensors before they are deployed. A crafted external physical signal turns the Trojan on, and it can then disable the sensor or feed it fake readings. The authors tested two designs on 14 sensors. They report trigger success above 95%, zero false triggers for the logic-based design, and less than 5% average deviation in drift, noise floor and response time, which makes the Trojan hard to spot.

lessons.point: The Trojan sits in analog signal circuitry that many sensor types share, so one technique works across sensor architectures. Earlier sensor attacks were specific to one sensor.
lessons.excerpt: SenTrojan embeds malicious functionality into analog signal circuitry commonly shared across diverse sensor architectures, and activates the hidden behavior through crafted external physical signals.

lessons.point: Infected sensors behave almost exactly like clean ones until triggered, so standard functional testing is unlikely to catch them.
lessons.excerpt: SenTrojan achieves an average successful trigger rate above 95%, maintains over 97% similarity to benign behavior, incurs zero false-trigger rate for LRD designs

lessons.point: The work turns sensor security from a question of accidental physical flaws into one of hardware supply-chain trust.
lessons.excerpt: broadening sensor security from unintended physical vulnerabilities to intentional supply-chain compromise.

entries.takeaway: In safety-critical cyber-physical systems, a sensor's readings can only be trusted as far as its hardware supply chain can be trusted, and functional tests alone may not reveal an implanted analog Trojan.

actionable.title: Treat sensor sourcing as part of the threat model for cyber-physical systems
actionable.detail: For safety-critical sensing, source from vetted suppliers, cross-check readings from redundant sensors that use different transduction principles, and add plausibility checks so a single spoofed or failed sensor cannot drive actuation.

entries.verify_note: Independent verifier supported all three lessons; zero false triggers holds for the LRD design only, and the trigger and similarity figures are averages.
entries.prior_art: None found in the pool. The closest known academic work is A2 analog malicious hardware (IEEE S&P 2016) and earlier unintended-effect sensor attacks such as acoustic and EMI injection, which the abstract positions itself against.
entries.threat: An attacker in the hardware supply chain implants a dormant analog Trojan that a remote physical signal can later trigger to disable a sensor or spoof its readings.
entries.conditions: The attacker can change the sensor's analog circuitry before deployment, and can later deliver a physical trigger signal with the right frequency and amplitude features.
entries.mitigations: Vet the hardware supply chain, use redundant sensors with different transduction principles, and check readings for plausibility at the system level.

issues: mild: jargon_chain 9 > 7 (sensors behave almost exactly like clean ones until triggered)

entries.title: Nuxt Content query endpoint lets unauthenticated users stall servers with SQLite functions
entries.summary: @nuxt/content v3 before 3.15.2 exposes POST /__nuxt_content/<collection>/query by default with no authentication. It runs a client-supplied SQL string after a keyword denylist check, and that check ignores SQLite built-in functions. A WHERE clause such as length(hex(randomblob(200000000))) passes the check and forces hundreds of megabytes of allocation. better-sqlite3 runs queries synchronously, which blocks the Node.js event loop, so one request stalls every other request (reported slowdown 1339x). Version 3.15.2 rejects function calls. Version 3.16.2 only accepts WHERE clauses that exactly match the query builder's output.

lessons.point: A keyword denylist on client-supplied SQL misses expensive built-in functions, so it is not a safe validator for raw queries.
lessons.excerpt: SQLite resource-consumption functions (`randomblob`, `zeroblob`, `hex`, `length`) are not keywords matched by the regex and therefore pass validation unconditionally.

lessons.point: A synchronous database driver in Node.js turns one slow query into a server-wide denial of service, because the event loop cannot serve other requests meanwhile.
lessons.excerpt: is a synchronous call that blocks the Node.js event loop for the entire duration of the SQLite query

lessons.point: Framework-registered internal endpoints can be public by default; inventory them, because this one shipped for every collection with no authentication.
lessons.excerpt: This endpoint is enabled by default for every collection and requires no authentication.

lessons.point: The fix was an allowlist that accepts only the exact shape the client-side query builder emits, not a longer denylist.
lessons.excerpt: only accepts `WHERE` clauses matching the exact output of the query builder (#3862, #3877)

entries.takeaway: Any endpoint that accepts raw SQL from the browser needs an allowlist of exact query shapes, plus query time and memory limits, not a keyword denylist.

actionable.title: Upgrade @nuxt/content to 3.16.2 or later, or block its query route
actionable.detail: Check package lockfiles for @nuxt/content >= 3.0.0, < 3.15.2 and upgrade to >= 3.16.2. If you cannot upgrade, block POST /__nuxt_content/*/query at the reverse proxy or web application firewall, or prerender the site so the route is not deployed. In your own code, grep for handlers that pass request-body SQL to a driver and replace denylist checks with a builder-shape allowlist plus a query timeout.

entries.verify_note: Lessons match the advisory.
entries.prior_art: SQLite randomblob/zeroblob resource-exhaustion denial of service; Node.js event-loop blocking.
entries.threat: An unauthenticated remote attacker sends a single POST with a crafted WHERE clause that allocates hundreds of megabytes and blocks the Node.js event loop, and repeats it to keep the site down.
entries.conditions: Server-rendered @nuxt/content v3 before 3.15.2 using the default SQLite or D1 adapter with the query route reachable; fully prerendered static deployments are not affected.
entries.mitigations: Upgrade to 3.16.2 or later; block or restrict POST /__nuxt_content/*/query at the proxy or web application firewall; prerender the site; set request and query time limits.

entries.title: Sentry's tunnelRoute skipped middleware for the whole tunnel path, not just rewrites
entries.summary: @sentry/nextjs's tunnelRoute option forwards browser events through a path on your own Next.js server and tells the SDK to skip middleware for them. The skip matched every path under the tunnel prefix, while the rewrite only served the exact tunnel path with the o and p parameters, so any app route that resolves under that prefix (a direct collision or a root dynamic segment like app/[locale]) ran without middleware. It is only an authorization bypass where middleware is the sole authz layer; fixed in 9.47.2, 10.75.2 and 11.0.0-rc.1.

lessons.point: The bug is a scope mismatch: an exemption (skip middleware) was matched more broadly than the thing it existed to protect (the rewrite).
lessons.excerpt: The middleware skip was wider than the rewrite.

lessons.point: Requests in the gap reach application routes with middleware never executed.
lessons.excerpt: Requests in that gap go to your application instead of Sentry, and your middleware never runs on them.

lessons.point: It is only exploitable when middleware is the sole authorization layer for the colliding routes; server-side session checks still hold.
lessons.excerpt: your middleware is the only place that enforces authorization for those routes

lessons.point: The durable fix is defense in depth: enforce authorization in the route, layout or data-access layer as well as middleware.
lessons.excerpt: Enforce authorization in the route, layout or data-access path as well as in middleware.

lessons.point: Only webpack builds are affected.
lessons.excerpt: Turbopack builds are not affected

entries.threat: Unauthenticated access to Next.js routes whose only authorization check lives in middleware, by requesting them under the Sentry tunnel prefix.
entries.conditions: tunnelRoute set; webpack build; an app route resolving under the tunnel path (including a root dynamic segment); middleware-only authorization.
entries.mitigations: Upgrade @sentry/nextjs to 9.47.2 / 10.75.2 / 11.0.0-rc.1; move tunnelRoute to a path no route can resolve under; build with Turbopack; enforce authz in routes or data access, not only middleware.
entries.takeaway: Any SDK or framework that exempts paths from middleware is a potential authz bypass: if middleware is your only authorization check, grep your dependencies for middleware skips.

actionable.title: Audit middleware exemptions and add route-level authz
actionable.detail: Upgrade @sentry/nextjs; then list every matcher/skip that bypasses Next.js middleware (Sentry tunnel, static assets, health checks) and confirm each protected route also checks the session server-side in its layout, route handler or data-access layer.

entries.prior_art: Next.js CVE-2025-29927 (x-middleware-subrequest middleware bypass) established that middleware-only authorization in Next.js is fragile; this is a new, SDK-introduced instance of the same class.
entries.verify_note: Independent verifier: all excerpts verbatim; novelty 40 (same); stressed the route-collision precondition and that server-side session checks still protect routes.

editorial.reason: Critical GHSA in a ubiquitous Next.js SDK with a transferable lesson: middleware exemptions are authz bypasses wherever middleware is the only authorization check.

entries.title: VOLTA infostealer uses an LLM to rank victims' assets by value
entries.author: khalidkhair
entries.summary: Cisco Talos describes VOLTA, a self-deleting Windows infostealer that, after stealing credentials, sessions and wallets, builds an evidence bundle about the victim and sends it through OpenRouter to an LLM that ranks the victim's assets by monetization value. If the default model refuses, VOLTA detects refusal phrases and falls back to two other models. Talos reads it as a builder sold to customers, which makes the AI triage step available to low-skill operators.
entries.takeaway: Crimeware now uses LLMs as the analyst who decides which victims to work first, and is built to route around refusals.

lessons.point: The LLM is used for post-theft triage, ranking a victim's assets by how much they are worth.
lessons.excerpt: VOLTA sends a structured evidence bundle to an LLM to rank the victim’s assets by monetization value.

lessons.point: The malware expects refusals and string-matches them to fail over to other models, so a single provider's refusal does not stop it.
lessons.excerpt: checking each response for phrases like “I can’t” or “I’m not able,” before passing on to a chain of up to three models.

lessons.point: Stolen live sessions are reused to enrich the dossier, for example searching the victim's Gmail for receipts to confirm a home address.
lessons.excerpt: using the victim's own authenticated Gmail tokens, it queries their inbox for receipts from Amazon, DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub, Walmart, and PayPal

lessons.point: Talos says blocking headless Chrome launches would stop the App-Bound Encryption bypass that much of the token theft relies on.
lessons.excerpt: An application control policy that restricts which processes may launch Chrome with `--headless` would block the ABE decryption path entirely.

actionable.title: Detect headless Chrome launches and outbound LLM API calls from non-developer endpoints
actionable.detail: Alert when Chrome starts with --headless from an unexpected parent process, and flag traffic to openrouter.ai or other LLM APIs from hosts that have no business reason to call them. If compromised, preserve %APPDATA%\volta_debug.txt, revoke tokens and treat plaintext wallet seeds as lost.

entries.prior_art: Talos's CLOSEDQUORUM AI-driven C2 implant and SOCRadar's report of INC and The Gentlemen affiliates running intrusions through OpenRouter models; VOLTA applies the LLM to post-theft victim appraisal with a refusal-fallback chain.
entries.threat: Infostealer operators using LLMs to prioritize and profile victims, including physical address inference.
entries.conditions: Windows endpoints where an infostealer can run and reach LLM APIs over the victim's own connection.
entries.mitigations: Application control on headless Chrome, hardware-backed credential storage, egress monitoring for LLM APIs, and fast token revocation after infection.

entries.title: IBM Aspera Faspex authorization bypass gives full admin, exploited in the wild
entries.summary: The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-123218, an incorrect-authorization flaw (CWE-863, from the Common Weakness Enumeration) in IBM Aspera Faspex 5.0.0 through 5.0.19, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on November 9, 2026. A user can craft a specific message to bypass authorization and gain full administrative privileges; IBM's CVE Numbering Authority (CNA) vector rates it network-reachable with no privileges required. CISA set a due date of November 12, 2026, only three days after listing.

lessons.point: A crafted message lets a user skip authorization checks and become a full Faspex administrator, so a single foothold account (or less) becomes control of the file-transfer server.
lessons.excerpt: IBM Aspera Faspex 5.0.0 through 5.0.19 could allow an authorized user to craft a specific message to bypass user authorization and gain full administrative privileges.

lessons.point: IBM's own Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) vector says no privileges are required (PR:N), which conflicts with the description's 'authorized user'; treat it as potentially reachable without an account until the vendor clarifies.
lessons.excerpt: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H

lessons.point: The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) set a remediation due date only three days after listing the flaw.
lessons.excerpt: IBM Aspera Faspex Incorrect Authorization Vulnerability | November 09, 2026 | November 12, 2026

entries.takeaway: Patch internet-facing Aspera Faspex 5.0.0 through 5.0.19 per IBM's advisory now and review admin accounts for unexpected changes.

actionable.title: Patch and hunt on Aspera Faspex
actionable.detail: Inventory IBM Aspera Faspex instances, upgrade any on 5.0.0-5.0.19 per IBM advisory node 7295921, and audit Faspex admin accounts, role changes and recent transfers for signs of privilege escalation; restrict internet exposure until patched.

entries.verify_note: Verifier confirmed the lessons; removed two inferences it flagged (exploitation severity from the due date, a fixed version the source does not name).
entries.prior_art: Routine CISA KEV listings already tracked (e.g. Plex Media Server, Fortinet, GitLab KEV entries in product-security.json); file-transfer appliance exploitation is a well-known pattern. No prior Aspera Faspex entry.
entries.threat: An attacker with a Faspex account (possibly none, per the CNA vector) sends a crafted message to gain full administrative privileges on the file-transfer server.
entries.conditions: IBM Aspera Faspex versions 5.0.0 through 5.0.19 reachable by the attacker.
entries.mitigations: Apply IBM's fix per its vendor advisory, limit internet exposure of Faspex, and audit admin accounts and transfer logs for abuse.

editorial.reason: Exploited file-transfer admin takeover with a three-day CISA deadline; the vector-vs-description contradiction is a useful triage lesson.

entries.title: Microsoft Outlook spoofing flaw that skips unsafe-action warnings is exploited
entries.summary: The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-124194 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on November 10, 2026: Outlook's UI fails to warn users of unsafe actions (CWE-356, from the Common Weakness Enumeration), letting an unauthorized attacker perform spoofing over a network. The CVE Numbering Authority (CNA) vector requires user interaction and impacts confidentiality only. Affected products include Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and Office Long-Term Servicing Channel (LTSC) 2021 and 2024, and the federal due date is November 24, 2026.

lessons.point: The bug is a missing warning, not memory corruption: Outlook lets a potentially unsafe action proceed without telling the user, which enables spoofing.
lessons.excerpt: Product ui does not warn user of unsafe actions in Microsoft Office Outlook allows an unauthorized attacker to perform spoofing over a network.

lessons.point: Exploitation needs the victim to interact and has high confidentiality impact, with no integrity or availability impact.
lessons.excerpt: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N

lessons.point: Fixed builds are version-specific per channel, so check that Office Long-Term Servicing Channel (LTSC) installs reach the listed build.
lessons.excerpt: Microsoft Office LTSC 2024 | Affected 16.0.0 < 16.0.17932.21140

entries.takeaway: Move every Outlook client to Microsoft's fixed builds for this CVE; it is an exploited spoofing bug that needs user interaction.

actionable.title: Confirm Outlook clients are on fixed builds
actionable.detail: Query endpoint management for Microsoft 365 Apps, Office Long-Term Servicing Channel (LTSC) 2021 (below 16.0.14334.21048) and Office LTSC 2024 (below 16.0.17932.21140) and force the update; warn users about spoofed messages until coverage is complete.

entries.verify_note: Verifier found two lessons went beyond the NVD text (phishing framing, auto-update advice) and a named November update the source lacks; text trimmed, held for a human check.
entries.prior_art: Outlook client attack surface already covered (product-security.json 'Sanitized webmail CSS steals tokens and keylogs Outlook'); KEV listings are routine news. The NVD text gives no technique detail.
entries.threat: An attacker crafts content that makes Outlook perform a potentially unsafe action without warning the user, enabling spoofing and data disclosure.
entries.conditions: Unpatched Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise, Office LTSC 2021 or Office LTSC 2024 Outlook clients and a user who interacts with attacker content.
entries.mitigations: Apply Microsoft's security update for this CVE per its security update guidance and reinforce phishing awareness until patched.

entries.title: NorForge found exposed Cairn AI-pentest panels used by criminals and red teams
entries.summary: NorForge found more than 20 open Cairn panels, a web front for a state-based multi-agent engine that works from an origin to a goal using a shared blackboard of facts and operator hints. Many were tied to malicious activity and showed targets, found weaknesses, secrets and whether the target was compromised. A number of apparently legitimate red-team operations were exposed too, which can put clients at risk. NorForge withheld panel addresses until takedown.

lessons.point: Open agent panels give an unusually detailed view of attacker workflow.
lessons.excerpt: More than 20 exposed Cairn panels were identified as likely associated with malicious activity, providing an unusually detailed view of how threat actors select targets, direct autonomous agents, exploit vulnerabilities, and establish persistent access to compromised systems.

lessons.point: Legitimate red teams are exposed the same way, which endangers client data.
lessons.excerpt: In addition, a considerable number of apparently legitimate red team operations were also exposed this way, potentially placing clients at risk.

lessons.point: Cairn organizes work as projects with a start point and an end goal.
lessons.excerpt: In Cairn, each separate task is considered a project.

lessons.point: Agents share findings through a blackboard that humans can also edit.
lessons.excerpt: The agent posts every fact onto a project-internal blackboard.

entries.takeaway: AI pentest harnesses leak the targets and secrets they hold; lock down their UIs, and treat open panels as both an attacker intel source and a client-data risk.

actionable.title: Secure your own offensive tooling
actionable.detail: Put any AI pentest or agent harness UI behind authentication and a VPN, never on the open internet, and scan your own ranges on Shodan/Censys for such panels. Defenders can search for open panels to learn about active targeting.

entries.prior_art: Earlier reporting (Gambit Security, September) noted AI harnesses on attacker servers; NorForge gives the first panel-level view. Verifier: Gambit Security September 2026 report on AI harnesses (Hermes, Strix, Cairn) on an attacker staging server; classic exposed C2 and open-directory research. Delt
entries.verify_note: Independent verifier found every claim supported by the source.

editorial.reason: Exposed Cairn AI-pentest panels reveal attacker workflow and risk to legitimate red-team clients.

entries.title: Callix finds 819 access-control flaws at sensitive callsites in Android firmware apps
entries.summary: An NDSS 2027 paper argues that prior analyses of pre-installed Android apps miss bugs because they only flag calls to a fixed list of sensitive APIs, while generic APIs like database reads become sensitive when they touch protected data. Callix scores callsite sensitivity from both the API and the data involved, recovers each security check on the path as an explicit property, and uses a 'restriction context' to judge whether those checks are sufficient. On 1,750 pre-installed apps from 10 top vendors it found 819 vulnerable paths at 95.1% sampled precision, with many confirmed through vendor bug bounties.
entries.takeaway: Checking that an access check exists in original equipment manufacturer (OEM) firmware apps is not enough; judge whether it is strong enough for the data a generic call operates on.

lessons.point: Sensitive-API allowlists produce a blind spot: generic operations such as database reads become dangerous only because of the data they touch, and existing tools exclude them to avoid false positives.
lessons.excerpt: a generic API, such as a database read, appears benign in general but becomes security-sensitive when operating on protected data, yet is left without sufficient access control

lessons.point: Presence of a permission check is the wrong question; the analysis has to ask whether the check matches the sensitivity of the operation at that callsite.
lessons.excerpt: existing studies focus only on the presence of checks, not on whether those checks enforce sufficient protection for the operation at a given callsite

lessons.point: The bug class is widespread in vendor firmware, and a large share of findings expose private user data through generic database operations.
lessons.excerpt: Callix discovered 819 vulnerable paths across these vendors, 42.1% of which allow reading or modifying private user data through generic database operations

lessons.point: Sensitive-API lists miss generic APIs that become sensitive because of the data they operate on.
lessons.excerpt: this misses a class of vulnerabilities in which a generic API, such as a database read, appears benign in general but becomes security-sensitive when operating on protected data, yet is left without sufficient access control

lessons.point: Prior analyses only asked whether a check exists, not whether it is strong enough for that operation.
lessons.excerpt: existing studies focus only on the presence of checks, not on whether those checks enforce sufficient protection for the operation at a given callsite

lessons.point: Of the 819 vulnerable paths found, 42.1% allow reading or modifying private user data through generic database operations.
lessons.excerpt: Callix discovered 819 vulnerable paths across these vendors, 42.1% of which allow reading or modifying private user data through generic database operations

actionable.title: Review exported components by data sensitivity, not by API name
actionable.detail: When auditing pre-installed or privileged Android apps (or any IPC-exposed service), enumerate exported entry points that reach generic data operations (ContentProvider queries, SQLite reads/writes, file access) and check whether the guarding permission or caller check is proportionate to the data being read or modified. A signature-level permission guarding a low-value table is fine; a normal-level permission or a package-name check guarding contacts, messages or account data is a finding.

entries.prior_art: Core claim: access-control analysis of Android firmware must judge check sufficiency per callsite, including generic APIs on protected data. Nearest entries are GitHub Security Lab's AI-agent Android audit (24 Android vulns, two-stage entry-point checklist) in product-security, which is about audit workflow rather than sensitivity-aware sufficiency analysis. Academic prior work on pre-installed app analysis (sensitive-API-list approaches and permission-check presence analysis) is what this paper extends; the restriction-context sufficiency model is the delta.
entries.threat: Malicious or compromised third-party apps on a device calling exported components of vendor pre-installed apps that perform generic database or file operations on private data behind missing or insufficient access checks.
entries.conditions: A pre-installed vendor app exposes a component that performs a generic operation on protected data, and the check on that path is absent or weaker than the data warrants (for example a normal-level permission or bypassable caller check).
entries.mitigations: Vendors should guard exported components that touch private data with signature-level permissions or strict caller verification, and review checks for sufficiency relative to the data. Users and fleet managers should apply vendor firmware updates that address bounty-reported issues.
entries.verify_note: Verifier found lessons supported; flagged 'common in vendor firmware' as an inference beyond the 819 count. Lesson 3 restated as the measured figure. Novelty agreed at 62.

entries.title: F5 BIG-IP APM pre-auth heap overflow RCE (CVE-2026-94127) is exploited
entries.summary: watchTowr Labs patch-diffed F5's fix for CVE-2026-94127 (advisory K000162605), an unauthenticated heap overflow in BIG-IP APM's traffic manager (tmm) that F5 reports as exploited in the wild. When an APM OAuth profile is configured, the HTTP Authorization header was copied into a fixed-size heap buffer with no length check, so an oversized header on an OAuth endpoint corrupts memory and, per the researchers, leads to remote code execution despite ASLR, NX and SELinux. Affected: BIG-IP APM 21.1.0, 17.5.0-17.5.1 and 17.1.0-17.1.3; other modules and BIG-IQ are not affected.

lessons.point: The root cause is a decades-old bug class: an attacker-controlled HTTP header was copied into a fixed-size heap buffer without a length check, and the fix only adds that check. Any code path that parses credentials before authentication needs explicit bounds checks.
lessons.excerpt: It is simple: before the patch, there was no size check before copying the value to the heap buffer, and now there is one.

lessons.point: The bug sits on an edge appliance that terminates TLS and brokers authentication, so a pre-auth memory-corruption flaw there exposes plaintext traffic and credentials. Patch it as an emergency.
lessons.excerpt: In other words, it lives at the very edge of your network, terminates your TLS, sees all of your traffic in plaintext, and holds the keys to your authentication.

lessons.point: The vendor advisory reported in-the-wild exploitation before the public technical analysis came out, so patch timelines should assume attackers are already using it.
lessons.excerpt: Even more scary, though: this wasn't just any vulnerability. There were bad people on the Internet exploiting it.

entries.takeaway: Edge appliances keep shipping pre-auth memory-corruption bugs in authentication paths (here, a missing length check on an Authorization header), so they need emergency patching, minimal exposure and crash-based detection.

actionable.title: Apply F5 K000162605 hotfixes on BIG-IP APM with OAuth profiles and hunt for compromise
actionable.detail: Find BIG-IP systems running APM 21.1.0, 17.5.0-17.5.1 or 17.1.0-17.1.3, especially those with an APM OAuth profile on a virtual server, and apply the engineering hotfixes in F5 advisory K000162605. Because the flaw was exploited in the wild, also hunt for compromise. Look for unexpected tmm crashes or restarts and for requests to /f5-oauth2/ endpoints with abnormally large Authorization headers. Check the integrity of the tmm crash hook script (/etc/bigstart/scripts/tmm.finish), which the researchers abused to get command execution. Until the patch is in, limit who can reach the OAuth endpoints.

entries.prior_art: watchTowr Citrix NetScaler pre-auth heap overflow CVE-2026-8452; Kemp LoadMaster pre-auth RCE CVE-2026-8037.
entries.threat: An unauthenticated remote attacker can get code execution on the BIG-IP traffic manager (tmm), which sees decrypted traffic and handles authentication.
entries.conditions: BIG-IP APM on an affected version with an OAuth profile configured on a reachable virtual server.
entries.mitigations: Apply the K000162605 hotfixes, limit exposure of the OAuth endpoints, monitor for tmm crashes and oversized Authorization headers, and check the integrity of tmm.finish.

issues: mild: sentence_words 46 > 45 (When an APM OAuth profile is configured, the HTTP Authorization header was copied into a fixed-size heap buffer with no )

editorial.reason: Pre-auth RCE in an internet-facing BIG-IP edge appliance, exploited in the wild; teaches emergency patching and minimal exposure for auth-path parsing on edge devices.

entries.title: GitHub Security Lab's Fuzzing Taskflow has an LLM agent write AFL++ harnesses
entries.summary: GitHub Security Lab released a Fuzzing Taskflow that takes a C/C++ GitHub repo and autonomously writes fuzzing harnesses, runs AFL++, reads coverage to chase gaps, improves the harnesses, and triages crashes into reports. The agent makes decisions while MCP tools do the execution, and a coverage loop with doubling time budgets stops once gains plateau. The author warns that the agent runs LLM-chosen build commands on the host with no container. It should only run in a throwaway environment, and its crash verdicts still need human review.

lessons.point: Split authority: the LLM picks what to fuzz and which gap to chase, while narrow tools perform execution and state lives in a database rather than in the agent.
lessons.excerpt: the **LLM agent owns the decisions, and the MCP tools own the execution**

lessons.point: Bound agent compute with plateau detection: stop iterating when coverage gains fall below a small threshold for two rounds.
lessons.excerpt: once two consecutive iterations each gain less than a configurable threshold (1% absolute line coverage by default)

lessons.point: Coverage-driven dictionary enrichment pulls magic constants from the comparisons that guard unreached code, helping the fuzzer pass hard checks.
lessons.excerpt: Then, after every coverage step, the pipeline looks at the guards near the uncovered lines

lessons.point: An agent that runs LLM-chosen build commands on the host is a prompt-injection risk; contain it in a disposable environment.
lessons.excerpt: A prompt-injected agent could, in principle, do anything your user can.

entries.takeaway: LLM agents can now take over the labor-intensive parts of fuzzing (harness writing, coverage chasing, triage), but they need containment and human review of verdicts.

actionable.title: Run seclab-taskflows-fuzzing against a C/C++ project in a Codespace
actionable.detail: Start a Codespace from github.com/GitHubSecurityLab/seclab-taskflows-fuzzing and run ./scripts/fuzzing/run_fuzzing.sh owner/repo (try DaveGamble/cJSON first as a smoke test). Do not run it on a workstation with credentials or elevated privileges. Watch the dashboard on port 8765, and treat every 'vulnerability' verdict and suggested diff as a draft to confirm by hand.

entries.prior_art: GitHub Security Lab Taskflow Android audit (24 vulnerabilities); OSS-Fuzz-gen.
entries.threat: The agent executes arbitrary LLM-chosen build commands on the host; a prompt-injected agent (for example via hostile content in the target repo) could act with the user's privileges.
entries.conditions: Running the taskflow outside a disposable environment, or with elevated privileges.
entries.mitigations: Run only in a Codespace or throwaway VM without elevated privileges; keep human review on verdicts and suggested patches.

entries.title: tensorlake@0.5.144 npm worm spread from a hijacked admin account
entries.summary: On 7 October 2026 an attacker using a tensorlake repository admin account committed a Mini Shai-Hulud payload to main through the GitHub web UI (so every commit showed as 'verified'), then started the release workflow by hand. Version 0.5.144 (about 106,000 monthly downloads) shipped through npm trusted publishing with valid provenance and no stolen npm token. Its preinstall loader skips CI, downloads Bun, and runs an 856 KB worm. The worm steals cloud, GitHub, npm, SSH, browser and wallet credentials and republishes the victim's npm packages. It plants Claude Code and VS Code hooks, resolves its command-and-control (C2) server through an Ethereum contract, and installs a gh-token-monitor service that runs rm -rf ~/ when the stolen GitHub token stops working.
entries.takeaway: Provenance attestations and 'verified' commit badges prove where a build came from, not that the source is clean; and in this worm family, revoking the stolen GitHub token before removing gh-token-monitor wipes the victim's home directory.

lessons.point: No registry credential was needed: control of a repo admin account plus the project's own release workflow was enough to publish.
lessons.excerpt: The attacker did not need an npm token. They used a repository administrator account to commit the payload to `main` through the GitHub web interface.

lessons.point: Trusted publishing and SLSA provenance faithfully attest a poisoned build; they do not indicate the source is safe.
lessons.excerpt: The provenance is valid for a build of poisoned source.

lessons.point: Commits made in the GitHub web UI are signed by GitHub, so the 'verified' badge gives no signal about account compromise.
lessons.excerpt: GitHub signs web interface commits, so all eight show as verified.

lessons.point: Incident response order matters: the dead-man switch fires on revocation, so remove the monitor service first, then rotate tokens.
lessons.excerpt: If GitHub returns 40x, for example after revocation, it deletes the home directory.

actionable.title: Remove gh-token-monitor before revoking tokens, and gate release workflows on reviewed commits
actionable.detail: On any machine that installed tensorlake@0.5.144 (or another Mini Shai-Hulud package), first disable and delete gh-token-monitor (systemd user service, macOS LaunchAgent com.user.gh-token-monitor, or Windows scheduled task; files under ~/.config/gh-token-monitor/ and ~/.local/bin/gh-token-monitor.sh), then rotate GitHub, npm, cloud, SSH, AI-tool and browser-saved credentials. Hunt for public repos described 'Shai-Hulud: Here We Go Again', commits authored as claude, and unexpected .claude/settings.json or .vscode/tasks.json. For your own packages: require PRs and reviews on the branch your publish workflow builds from, require a second approver (GitHub environment protection) for manually dispatched releases, and alert on direct pushes to main by admins. Block iseekaigogo.com and Ethereum RPC egress from developer machines where feasible.

entries.verify_note: Excerpts verbatim. Verifier: the token-revocation wiper arms only on some machines (accounts with no organizations, 24-hour watch), and the workflow was started on 8 Oct 00:08 UTC. Novelty lowered to the verifier's 40.
entries.prior_art: Same worm family as the keyv/cacheable Mini Shai-Hulud compromise and ChainDrop already in the archive (valid provenance, Bun loader, Ethereum-resolved C2, Claude Code/VS Code hooks). New here: delivery through an admin account's web-UI commits and a manually started trusted-publishing run instead of a stolen npm token, a new C2 domain and Ethereum contract, a browser password stealer, eval of C2 responses, and an identified rm -rf ~/ handler that arms only for tokens whose account has no organizations.
entries.threat: Compromised maintainer/admin GitHub account publishes a credential-stealing, self-propagating npm worm through the project's legitimate release pipeline.
entries.conditions: Developer workstation (loader exits on CI) runs npm install of tensorlake@0.5.144 with install scripts enabled; the destructive watcher arms when a stolen GitHub token belongs to an account with no organizations.
entries.mitigations: Pin tensorlake to 0.5.143 or upgrade to the reverted 0.5.145; set ignore-scripts for installs; remove gh-token-monitor before rotating credentials; enforce branch protection and release approvals so an admin account alone cannot ship from main.

editorial.reason: Live npm worm (two independent write-ups, SafeDep and StepSecurity) that published through the project's own trusted-publishing workflow and arms a home-directory wiper on token revocation: a concrete lesson that valid provenance doesn't…

entries.title: Oracle PeopleSoft zero-day used by ShinyHunters was three chained flaws
entries.summary: The PeopleSoft bug that ShinyHunters has exploited since May, patched as CVE-2026-35273 (CVSS 9.8), is really three flaws chained together. A server-side request forgery (the server can be made to send requests for the attacker) in the Integration Gateway reaches the internal Environment Management Hub. That hub trusts 127.0.0.1 by default, and from there an attacker can write a web shell or plant a malicious XML file, giving remote code execution with no login. Attackers got past web application firewall rules by URL-encoding one character of the blocked path.

lessons.point: A default allowlist entry for the loopback address turns any server-side request forgery into full access to internal admin interfaces.
lessons.excerpt: That file ships with the local loopback address, 127.0.0.1, already on the list.

lessons.point: Path-matching web application firewall rules can be bypassed by URL-encoding a single character, because the server decodes the path before serving it.
lessons.excerpt: Many WAF rules match the path's plain text, while the PeopleSoft server decodes it and serves the page.

lessons.point: The XMLDecoder code-execution path leaves no web shell behind, so web-shell hunting alone can miss it.
lessons.excerpt: The second path leaves less for standard detection to catch.

lessons.point: Patching does not remove an attacker who is already inside. Hunt for web shells and rotate credentials as well.
lessons.excerpt: Patching closes the door; it does not by itself evict someone already inside.

entries.takeaway: Treating loopback as trusted makes any request-forgery bug a way past the perimeter, so patch rather than relying on path-based firewall rules.

actionable.title: Patch PeopleSoft CVE-2026-35273 and remove PSEMHUB exposure
actionable.detail: Apply Oracle's security alert fix on PeopleTools 8.61/8.62. If you cannot patch yet, disable the Environment Management Hub (multi-server) or remove the PSEMHUB application (single-server). Do not rely on WAF rules that block /PSEMHUB/, since /%50SEMHUB/ gets past them. On hosts that may be compromised, hunt for web shells and unexpected XML files read at service start, and rotate every credential reachable from the PeopleSoft tier.

entries.prior_art: No PeopleSoft or ShinyHunters entries in the pools. Closest: the ai-security entry on loopback MCP servers needing Host/Origin checks, the same loopback-trust failure in a different product.
entries.threat: An unauthenticated attacker chains a server-side request forgery in PSIGW to the PSEMHUB admin interface, which trusts loopback, then gets code execution through a log-write web shell or an XMLDecoder payload. This leads to data theft and extortion.
entries.conditions: PeopleSoft Enterprise PeopleTools 8.61 or 8.62 without Oracle's June 10 fix, with the PSIGW listening connector reachable and PSEMHUB deployed using the default allowedhosts.properties.
entries.mitigations: Apply Oracle's CVE-2026-35273 fix, disable or remove PSEMHUB if you cannot patch, do not treat path-based WAF blocking as a fix, and on suspected hosts preserve evidence, hunt for web shells and rotate all reachable credentials.

editorial.reason: ShinyHunters has exploited this PeopleSoft chain since May. It teaches two things that transfer: a default loopback allowlist turns server-side request forgery into unauthenticated RCE, and path-matching WAF rules fall to a single…

entries.title: OVHcloud CLI GitHub releases carried attacker binaries for 94 minutes, delivering GlassWorm
entries.summary: An attacker replaced the binaries on five OVHcloud CLI GitHub releases, kept them live for 94 minutes, then deleted the evidence. StepSecurity rebuilt the attacker's build, recovered the GlassWorm loader from an orphaned commit, and ran the full chain in isolation. Their replay shows the install.sh script never served arm64 Linux, Homebrew was not an infection path, and running the CLI's version command was enough to spot the malicious build.

lessons.point: Release assets can be swapped after publication and the evidence deleted, so a short exposure window can leave few traces.
lessons.excerpt: An attacker swapped the binaries on five OVHcloud CLI releases, stayed live for 94 minutes, and deleted the evidence.

lessons.point: Deleted malicious code could still be recovered from an orphaned commit, which made a full detonation possible.
lessons.excerpt: recovered the GlassWorm loader from an orphaned commit, and detonated the full chain in an isolated chamber

lessons.point: Exposure depends on install channel: Homebrew was not affected, and a simple version check identifies the bad build.
lessons.excerpt: Homebrew was never a path in, and a single ovhcloud version command was enough to spot the malicious build

entries.takeaway: Release binaries can be replaced after publication, so pin and verify checksums or provenance for downloaded CLIs instead of trusting the release tag.

actionable.title: Triage OVHcloud CLI installs and verify release-asset integrity
actionable.detail: On hosts and CI images that installed the OVHcloud CLI from GitHub releases or install.sh in the exposure window, run `ovhcloud version` and compare against the vendor's known-good build; treat Homebrew installs as unaffected per the replay. For all CLIs fetched from GitHub releases, pin a SHA-256 or verify signed provenance (e.g. artifact attestations) before execution rather than trusting the release tag.

entries.prior_art: Closest pool entry is the LiteLLM 1.107.0 trojanized PyPI/Docker release (built from a lookalike repo); release-asset swaps on GitHub are a known vector, but the reconstructed detonation and per-channel exposure analysis are new. Verifier: Release/tag tampering of trusted artifacts is well established (tj-actions/changed-files tag repoint 2025, Codecov bash uploader 2021, GlassWorm campaigns on OpenVSX/npm); the delta is a mutated GitHub release asset swap on a cloud vendor CLI plus a forensic replay recovering the loader from an orphaned commit.
entries.verify_note: Independent fresh-context verifier re-read the source; the overstatements it flagged were corrected before merge.
entries.threat: Attacker with release-write access replaces signed-off binaries on existing GitHub releases with builds that drop the GlassWorm loader, then deletes traces.
entries.conditions: Users or CI pipelines that downloaded OVHcloud CLI binaries from the affected GitHub releases (or via install.sh on exposed platforms) during the 94-minute window.
entries.mitigations: Check the installed build with `ovhcloud version`; reinstall from a known-good release; pin checksums or verify provenance for release-asset downloads; restrict and monitor release-edit permissions.

editorial.reason: Live supply-chain incident: OVHcloud CLI release binaries swapped for 94 minutes to deliver GlassWorm; teaches release-asset verification and how to triage installs.

entries.title: Unit 42: CL-UNK-1211 hit government Linux servers with LLM-written payloads
entries.summary: Unit 42 tracked CL-UNK-1211 attacking government and state-affiliated Linux infrastructure from October 2025 to April 2026; payloads carried conversational, step-by-step reasoning comments, which suggests they were produced by an LLM or run by an AI agent. The attackers persisted by setting auto_prepend_file in every PHP config, stole passwords with a .bashrc sudo alias and a PHP login logger, and ran a Go RAT called SysGoRAT over WebSocket C2. They searched qmail mailboxes for social media account emails and tried to kill Cortex XDR processes. One dropped script had a syntax error and would have failed.
entries.takeaway: AI-assisted intrusions still rely on ordinary Linux tradecraft, so defenders should hunt for PHP config tampering, shell rc file aliases and outbound reverse shells, and can treat conversational reasoning comments inside dropped scripts as a triage signal.

lessons.point: LLM-generated payloads leave a fingerprint: conversational reasoning comments addressed to the operator, which can be used as a hunting and triage indicator.
lessons.excerpt: Multiple artifacts deployed throughout the intrusion contained AI-made conversational annotations and developer reasoning comments

lessons.point: Persistence came from editing auto_prepend_file in every PHP config, which loads a web shell before every PHP request. Monitor these directories for integrity changes.
lessons.excerpt: the attackers modified the auto_prepend_file value across all PHP configurations under the directories /etc/php/ and /opt/plesk/php/.

lessons.point: Credentials were harvested by a .bashrc sudo alias that fakes the password prompt, logs the password and then passes it to the real sudo.
lessons.excerpt: In one instance, they created an alias for the sudo command that was designed to execute each time a user attempted to run it.

lessons.point: The attackers planted fake red-team markers so responders would mistake the intrusion for an authorized security assessment.
lessons.excerpt: plant deceptive red-team markers to disguise activity as a legitimate security assessment

actionable.title: Hunt for CL-UNK-1211-style Linux persistence
actionable.detail: Search /etc/php/ and /opt/plesk/php/ for non-empty auto_prepend_file values. Look for sudo aliases or functions in users' .bashrc files. Check for files posing as vendor logs, such as Solarwinds.StatusLog.txt. Alert on php-fpm spawning shells or python3, and on mkfifo/nc, /dev/tcp and python socket reverse shells. Block 104.194.158.65. Enforce default-deny egress on web servers. Treat 'red team' markers found during an investigation as unverified until the engagement is confirmed.

entries.verify_note: Verifier: facts supported; flagged a plural overstatement about broken scripts (fixed to one script). Verifier novelty 42 (closest: Unit 42 TuxBot v3 LLM-assisted malware), relevance 80; took the lower novelty.
entries.prior_art: Closest pool entry is archive 'Measuring AI-enabled malware: ~97% of samples never reach production; AI changes how malware is authored, not how it executes'. This report is a concrete in-the-wild case consistent with that finding: the payloads were AI-authored, but the tradecraft is conventional and one script was broken. What is new is the specific TTP set (auto_prepend_file persistence, sudo-alias stealer, SysGoRAT, mailbox-to-social-media targeting, fake red-team markers). No earlier entry covers CL-UNK-1211 or SysGoRAT.
entries.threat: A state-interest espionage cluster gets into government Linux web and mail servers through web shells, keeps access with PHP config persistence and a Go RAT, steals credentials and mailboxes to take over social media accounts, dumps databases, and tampers with EDR and logs.
entries.conditions: Internet-facing Linux servers running PHP or Plesk and qmail, with cleartext credentials in config and history files, permissive outbound network access and EDR that can be killed by a local process.
entries.mitigations: Monitor PHP configuration and shell rc files for integrity changes, remove cleartext credentials from configs and history, enforce strict outbound firewall rules on servers, enable EDR tamper protection, forward logs off-host, and hunt for the published indicators.

editorial.reason: Live espionage campaign with LLM-written payloads and concrete Linux hunting leads (auto_prepend_file persistence, sudo-alias stealer).

entries.title: Microsoft dissects the SSH backdoor in a trojanized Claude Code extension
entries.summary: Tampered builds 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 of the anthropic.claude-code extension were served from Cursor's extension marketplace on October 29, 2026, from about 2:27 AM to 1:35 PM Pacific time. Microsoft says the Visual Studio Marketplace and the npm package were not affected. The injected loader runs when the extension loads, adds an attacker SSH key tagged svc-telemetry, opens a reverse SSH tunnel and installs startup persistence named like SysMon or com.apple.sysmond.
entries.takeaway: Uninstalling the extension does not clean the machine: hunt for the svc-telemetry key and the disguised startup entries on every developer machine that took the update.

lessons.point: The payload runs as soon as the extension module loads, before the extension's own code, and tries to plant an SSH key, enable SSH, open a reverse tunnel, persist and report the host.
lessons.excerpt: The injected loader runs when the extension module loads and attempts to add an attacker-controlled Secure Shell (SSH) key, enable the local SSH service, establish reverse SSH forwarding, configure persistence, and report host details.

lessons.point: Removing or updating the extension leaves the backdoor in place; keys, tunnel identities, scripts and startup entries must be removed separately.
lessons.excerpt: Removing or updating the extension does not remove artifacts written outside its installation directory.

lessons.point: The loader reports only the names of secret-looking environment variables, not their values, so the report alone shows reconnaissance, not proven secret theft.
lessons.excerpt: The callback sends matching environment-variable names, not values.

lessons.point: The tunnel starts with an outbound connection from the workstation instead of waiting for an inbound one, so egress monitoring matters as much as inbound rules.
lessons.excerpt: This design starts with an outbound connection from the workstation rather than waiting for a direct inbound connection to it.

lessons.point: Microsoft points Cursor users to a publisher allowlist and an install cooldown to limit exposure to newly published malicious versions.
lessons.excerpt: including restricting extensions to approved publishers and configuring an extension installation cooldown to delay installation of newly published versions

entries.threat: A trojanized auto-updating editor extension runs attacker JavaScript at load time on developer machines and installs a persistent reverse SSH backdoor.
entries.conditions: The machine installed or auto-updated anthropic.claude-code 2.1.312 or 2.1.313 from the Cursor marketplace during the October 29 window; remote access also depends on host privileges and SSH configuration.
entries.mitigations: Check authorized_keys for the svc-telemetry key, remove the com.apple.sysmond LaunchAgent, the @reboot crontab entry, the SysMon task and Startup sysmon.cmd and the .smt, .smtk and .stk_ files after preserving evidence, look for connections to 134.209.82.225, rotate credentials where telemetry shows exposure, and set a publisher allowlist and install cooldown for editor extensions.

actionable.title: Hunt for the svc-telemetry key and sysmon persistence on developer machines
actionable.detail: On every machine that ran Cursor on October 29: grep ~/.ssh/authorized_keys (and C:\ProgramData\ssh\administrators_authorized_keys on Windows) for svc-telemetry; check ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist, crontab @reboot entries pointing at ~/.config/.smt, a SysMon scheduled task or Startup sysmon.cmd, and .stk_ files; search network logs for 134.209.82.225. Then configure an extension publisher allowlist and an install cooldown so a freshly published version cannot auto-install.

entries.prior_art: Earlier tracker story on the same incident from a Hacker News report (s-bf5aaab63512); earlier malicious VS Code and Open VSX extension campaigns such as GlassWorm and the 2025 fake Solidity extensions on Open VSX.
entries.verify_note: Independent verifier supported every lesson; two points were softened to match the source (outbound tunnel, allowlist effect). Novelty taken as the verifier's lower 22.

editorial.reason: The week's most widely covered developer-supply-chain incident (Wired, Ars, BleepingComputer, The Register, DoublePulsar), and Microsoft's write-up gives concrete artifacts to hunt and the fact that uninstalling the extension does not…

entries.title: SonicWall SonicOS SSLVPN flaw lets alternate credentials bypass SAML-enforced MFA
entries.summary: CISA added CVE-2026-19868 in SonicWall SonicOS SSLVPN to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on November 6, 2026. The catalog record says a user with valid credentials for another login method can skip SAML login checks, and with them the multi-factor authentication (MFA) that SAML enforces. Federal agencies must apply the vendor's mitigations by November 20, 2026, or stop using the product.

lessons.point: CISA lists this SSLVPN single-factor authentication flaw as exploited in the wild, with a two-week deadline to fix it.
lessons.excerpt: SonicWall SonicOS SSLVPN Use of Single-factor Authentication Vulnerability | November 06, 2026 | November 20, 2026

lessons.point: If no mitigation exists for an affected deployment, CISA's required action is to stop using the product.
lessons.excerpt: discontinue use of the product if mitigations are unavailable

lessons.point: Owners are expected to check how exposed each SSLVPN appliance is to the internet when deciding priority.
lessons.excerpt: Stakeholders are responsible for evaluating each asset's internet exposure

entries.takeaway: Enforcing MFA through SAML on a SonicWall SSLVPN does not protect you if another login method on the same VPN still accepts just a password.

actionable.title: Close alternate login paths on SonicOS SSLVPN and apply advisory SNWLID-2026-0014
actionable.detail: List every SonicOS SSLVPN appliance and check which authentication methods it allows next to SAML, such as local or LDAP accounts. Apply the mitigations in SonicWall advisory SNWLID-2026-0014 by November 20, 2026. Until then, turn off the non-SAML methods and review VPN logins that did not go through the SAML identity provider.

entries.verify_note: The fetched source is only the KEV listing table; the SAML and MFA bypass mechanism in the summary, title and takeaway is not in it.
entries.prior_art: Earlier SonicWall entries (end-of-life GMS won't-fix flaws); no prior entry for this SonicOS SSLVPN SAML/MFA bypass
entries.threat: An attacker with valid credentials for a non-SAML login method can get past SAML authentication and the MFA it enforces on SonicOS SSLVPN.
entries.conditions: SonicOS SSLVPN set up with SAML (and SAML-enforced MFA) while another authentication method still works.
entries.mitigations: Apply the vendor mitigations from SNWLID-2026-0014 by the KEV due date, or stop using the product if no mitigation is available.

entries.title: Binance warns an iOS sandbox escape lets apps read other apps' secrets
entries.summary: Binance warns that 'worse_query', a publicly disclosed iOS sandbox escape affecting iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1 and 27.2, lets a malicious app read other apps' local files, including wallet seed phrases, private keys and login credentials. A public proof-of-concept tool, WQ Files, uses it without a jailbreak but must first be installed, for example by sideloading. Apple's November 9 updates (iOS 27.2.1, 26.7.3, 18.7.12) fix CVE-2026-113963, an app-data access flaw, but it is unclear whether that is the same issue.

lessons.point: Apps that store secrets in local files rely on the OS sandbox. If the sandbox breaks, every app's local secrets are exposed together, not just one vendor's.
lessons.excerpt: allows malicious apps to read local files from other apps, putting seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk across the entire ecosystem

lessons.point: The exploit needs a malicious app on the device. Sideloading and untrusted installs are the delivery path you can control.
lessons.excerpt: The tool must be installed on an iPhone for the attack to work, but an attacker could distribute it through untrusted sources as a sideloaded app

lessons.point: It is not confirmed that Apple's latest patch fixes this flaw, so updating may not be enough by itself.
lessons.excerpt: It is unclear if this is the same security issue Binance is warning of, though.

lessons.point: For suspected compromise, the advice is to move funds to a wallet created on a clean device, because keys that may have leaked cannot be trusted.
lessons.excerpt: Binance advises users to transfer funds to a new wallet created on a clean device and reset all active login sessions

entries.takeaway: Until Apple confirms its November 9 fix covers worse_query, treat secrets in app files on iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1 and 27.2 as readable by other installed apps.

actionable.title: Audit iOS apps for secrets stored in plain sandbox files
actionable.detail: For any iOS app you ship, check that seed phrases, private keys and session tokens are stored in the Keychain with device-only accessibility (or Secure Enclave-wrapped keys), not as plaintext in Documents, Library or App Group containers. Push managed devices to iOS 27.2.1, 26.7.3 or 18.7.12 and block sideloaded apps through MDM (mobile device management).

entries.verify_note: Takeaway limited to what the source supports.
entries.prior_art: Earlier iOS app-sandbox escapes.
entries.threat: A malicious app installed on the iPhone, for example by sideloading, reads other apps' private files and steals seed phrases, private keys and credentials.
entries.conditions: iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1 or 27.2 with an attacker-controlled app installed; secrets stored in files reachable through the flaw.
entries.mitigations: Update to the latest iOS release, remove untrusted or sideloaded apps, store secrets in the Keychain or Secure Enclave rather than plain files, and after suspected compromise move funds to a wallet created on a clean device and reset sessions.

lessons.point: The approach defines security principles for the model instead of targeting known vulnerability classes.
lessons.excerpt: Instead of trying to find specific known vulnerability classes (e.g. XSS, command injection), Kat defined a series of

actionable.title: Give an AI bug-hunting harness explicit design invariants
actionable.detail: Write the security invariants your platform must hold (tenant isolation, who may act on whose resources) and ask the agent to find violations of each, rather than scanning for bug classes.
