entries.title: Wiz CIRT describes what an AI-driven cloud intrusion looks like
entries.summary: Wiz CIRT walks through intrusions where an AI agent system ran the whole operation across cloud, Kubernetes, CI/CD, identity and databases at once. It lists eight traits that separate these from human or scripted attacks, such as hundreds or thousands of actions per hour, credential chaining across platforms, self-repairing scripts, pentest-style naming, task IDs in resource names and heavily commented code. The footprint is loud but split across logs, so no single alert tells the story.

lessons.point: Tempo and absence of working-hour patterns separate agents from human operators.
lessons.excerpt: Activity can reach hundreds or thousands of actions per hour and continues for long periods without the pauses or working-hour patterns typical of a human operator.

lessons.point: Credentials chain across platforms because the agent speaks every platform's API.
lessons.excerpt: Because the agent has native fluency across so many technologies, every credential becomes a stepping stone to the next platform.

lessons.point: Failed attempts are fixed in minutes, so a blocked first try tells you little.
lessons.excerpt: If an attempt fails, the agent immediately reads the error, rewrites its script on the fly, and tries again within minutes

lessons.point: Names like pentest, recon and exfil are an observable tell and a likely guardrail bypass.
lessons.excerpt: Resources, files, and payloads created by the actor are consistently labeled with terms such as `pentest`, `probe`, `recon`, `redteam`, and `exfil`.

lessons.point: The problem is fragmentation, not stealth.
lessons.excerpt: The challenge for defenders isn't that these attacks are invisible.

entries.takeaway: Detect AI-driven intrusions by correlating identity, cloud, CI/CD and workload logs and by hunting the agent's tells.

actionable.title: Hunt the agent's tells
actionable.detail: Add detections for resource names containing pentest, probe, recon, redteam or exfil; numeric task-ID suffixes (-b, -c retries); and bursts of cross-platform API calls from one source. Join identity provider, cloud audit, CI/CD and cluster logs on one timeline.

entries.prior_art: CrowdStrike and Microsoft reports describe attacker use of agent frameworks; this is the first defender-side field guide of observable traits in the pools. Verifier: Sysdig's AI-assisted AWS intrusion write-up (2026), Anthropic GTG-1002, Wiz/Unit42 agentic-attack notes. Delta is the codified 8-trait tell list from a multi-pl
entries.verify_note: Independent verifier found every claim supported by the source.

editorial.reason: Field guide to observable traits of AI-driven cloud intrusions from real investigations.

entries.title: Wiz lists the fingerprints that mark an intrusion as agent-driven
entries.summary: Wiz reviews public agentic intrusions (ARTEX, Hermes, PentestGPT-derived harnesses and Claude Code workflows) and three of its own cases. The three are an exposed Flowise instance turned into a mass-exploitation node, a Java gateway RCE that swept 602 steps across 12 technique families, and an MCP-interface command injection that led to bulk secret and Kubernetes token theft. Wiz distills fingerprints of agent activity: machine-paced iteration whose cadence varies with step complexity, natural-language plans inside scripts, versioned self-correcting tooling, breadth-first technique coverage, noisy parallel lateral movement, and probe-before-payload discipline.

lessons.point: Cadence is a tell: gaps between steps vary with how complex each step is, unlike fixed-interval beacons or millisecond auto-exploit chains, and it continues for many hours without fatigue gaps.
lessons.excerpt: The tell is a variable cadence that tracks step complexity

lessons.point: Agent-generated tooling carries written plans and rationale, which can even name the agent framework.
lessons.excerpt: Scripts and artifacts that carry written rationale (attack plans, explanations of what and why).

lessons.point: Agents read errors and rewrite their approach across numbered script versions, so blocking one path does not stop the intrusion.
lessons.excerpt: A static playbook cannot read an AWS error and re-derive the regional-STS requirement.

lessons.point: Agents try many lateral paths in parallel and keep going without regard to noise, which gives defenders a detection opportunity if signals are correlated.
lessons.excerpt: The loudness is itself a detection opportunity.

entries.takeaway: Agent-driven intrusions are loud and leave readable rationale, so behavioral detections built on cadence, commented /tmp scripts, versioned retries and parallel lateral sweeps can catch them.

actionable.title: Hunt for agentic-intrusion fingerprints in workload telemetry
actionable.detail: Write detections for: (1) many distinct new scripts in /tmp on one workload over hours, appearing about every one to two minutes; (2) scripts with natural-language plan headers or heavy comments; (3) versioned file ladders (x, x2, x3) following 401/403 errors; (4) metadata-endpoint fallback sequences (IMDSv2, then IMDSv1, then ECS credentials, then IPv6 IMDS); (5) parallel port and host sweeps from one workload. Correlate them across identity, cloud and Kubernetes logs rather than alerting on each alone.

entries.verify_note: Verifier upheld all four lessons; incremental over GTG-1002 and earlier Wiz/Microsoft agentic-attack reports (novelty 30 vs 42, lower kept).
entries.prior_art: Wiz CIRT's own 'Anatomy of AI-Driven Cloud Attacks' (2026-10-19, already pooled) listed eight similar traits (tempo, self-repairing scripts, heavy comments); Microsoft's Storm-0940/ARTEX report and the Unit 42 AI-assisted attack investigation. This post adds three new cases and sharper criteria (cadence varying with step complexity, probe-before-payload).
entries.threat: Attackers using agent harnesses that write custom tooling, adapt to errors and escalate from one exposed service to cloud credential theft, Kubernetes token theft, lateral movement and bulk secret exfiltration.
entries.conditions: Internet-exposed services such as unauthenticated Flowise endpoints, Java RCE on gateways, or MCP interfaces that accept attacker-controlled commands, running on workloads with reachable metadata endpoints and Kubernetes service-account tokens.
entries.mitigations: Remove unauthenticated exposure of agent-builder and MCP endpoints, restrict metadata and service-account token access from workloads, and build behavioral detections on script cadence, commented generated tooling, versioned retries and parallel sweeps, correlated across identity, endpoint and cloud signals.

entries.title: Canonical LXD and MicroCloud accepted forged client certificate chains
entries.summary: CVE-2026-112816 (CVSS 10.0) let an attacker log in to the LXD or MicroCloud HTTPS API as a trusted client without its private key, by attaching that client's public certificate behind their own in the TLS chain. The server checked every certificate in the chain against its trust store, but TLS only proves ownership of the first one. Fixed snaps include LXD 6.10.1, 5.21.9, 5.0.11 and 4.0.15 and MicroCloud 3.4.1 and 2.1.5; no exploitation is known.
entries.takeaway: When you pin client certificates in mutual TLS, match only the leaf certificate the client proved it owns, never the extra certificates it chose to send.

lessons.point: The bug: the server compared every certificate the client sent, but a TLS handshake proves key ownership only for the leaf.
lessons.excerpt: It compared every certificate the client sent against the trust store, but a TLS connection only proves the client owns the private key for the first certificate in the chain, the leaf.

lessons.point: Exploitation needs network access to the API and a trusted client's public certificate, which is not secret.
lessons.excerpt: Using the flaw takes two things: network access to the HTTPS API, and the public certificate of a client the server already trusts.

lessons.point: A standalone LXD server is only exposed if an administrator enabled the network API.
lessons.excerpt: It listens only on a local socket unless an administrator turns on the network API with the core.https_address setting.

lessons.point: Neither Canonical nor Incus offers a configuration fix; Incus says restricting network access to the listener is the only step short of patching.
lessons.excerpt: said there is no configuration fix and that the only step is to restrict network access to the listener

entries.threat: Network attackers impersonate a trusted mutual-TLS client, gaining cluster and VM access and possibly root on the host.
entries.conditions: The LXD network API is enabled (core.https_address) or MicroCloud is in use, and the attacker has a trusted client's public certificate.
entries.mitigations: Refresh the lxd and microcloud snaps to the fixed versions and confirm the installed version; move Incus to 7.6.0; restrict network access to the API listener until patched.

actionable.title: Audit mutual-TLS code that matches clients against a trust store
actionable.detail: Patch LXD and MicroCloud now. Then grep your own mutual-TLS services for code that loops over the peer's whole certificate chain when matching pinned client certificates; match only the leaf (PeerCertificates[0] in Go) or the verified chain the TLS library built.

entries.verify_note: Independent verifier supported every lesson; the workaround lesson now attributes the network-restriction advice to Incus. Novelty taken as the verifier's lower 22.
entries.prior_art: Classic certificate-chain validation flaws where unverified intermediate or extra certificates were trusted; Incus advisory GHSA-xg75-xf37-cph9 for the same bug.

entries.title: SAP fixes four maximum-severity unauthenticated takeover flaws
entries.summary: SAP's November 2026 updates fix 35 vulnerabilities. Four are rated 10/10 on the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS). They are: memory corruption (CVE-2026-76964) and missing authentication (CVE-2026-120017) in the Internet Communication Manager (ICM) and SAML2 Service Provider of NetWeaver Application Server ABAP; broken access control in SAP Gateway (CVE-2026-89103); and memory corruption in Web Dispatcher (CVE-2026-89126). Onapsis calls the two memory corruption bugs ICM2SHELL, which gives remote code execution (RCE) on the network-facing component. It calls the Gateway bug PROXYGATE, a pre-authentication RCE that tricks Gateway into treating an outside attacker as an internal application server.

lessons.point: ICM2SHELL needs no SAP user, password or user interaction. It hits a component that is exposed to the network by design, so patch the internet-facing edge first.
lessons.excerpt: ICM2SHELL turns a routine part of web traffic into a point of ingress for attackers.

lessons.point: PROXYGATE is a trust-boundary failure. Gateway accepts an unauthenticated external caller as one of its own internal application servers, giving full system control as the installation owner.
lessons.excerpt: PROXYGATE works by convincing the SAP Gateway that an unauthenticated, external attacker is one of the internal application servers.

lessons.point: Web Dispatcher, a load balancer and reverse proxy, sits in front of almost every enterprise SAP deployment. A bug in it reaches most SAP landscapes.
lessons.excerpt: is a specialized component that acts as a load balancer and reverse proxy for web requests entering an SAP system architecture

lessons.point: SAP bugs have a track record of exploitation, so maximum-severity SAP fixes are a reasonable thing to prioritize even before exploitation is reported. CISA lists 14 exploited SAP flaws, three of them used by ransomware groups.
lessons.excerpt: as actively exploited since November 2021, three of which ransomware groups also abused in the wild.

entries.takeaway: Patch SAP Web Dispatcher, ICM and Gateway now: all four bugs give unauthenticated remote takeover, and SAP flaws have been exploited before.

actionable.title: Prioritize SAP edge components in the November patch cycle
actionable.detail: Inventory every SAP Web Dispatcher and NetWeaver ABAP ICM endpoint reachable from untrusted networks and apply the November 2026 security notes there first. Restrict which hosts can talk to the SAP Gateway as application servers, and watch for unexpected gateway registrations until the fix is in.

entries.verify_note: Figures match.
entries.prior_art: 10KBLAZE Gateway trust abuse; RECON CVE-2020-6287; ICMAD CVE-2022-22536.
entries.threat: An unauthenticated remote attacker who can reach the SAP Web Dispatcher, ICM or Gateway can run code as the SAP installation owner and reach ERP business data.
entries.conditions: The affected component is reachable by the attacker and the November 2026 SAP security notes are not applied.
entries.mitigations: Apply SAP's November 2026 security notes, limit network reach to Web Dispatcher, ICM and Gateway, restrict Gateway application-server registration to known hosts, and monitor those components for anomalous requests.

issues: mild: acronyms 5 > 3 (SAP, SAML2, ABAP, ICM2SHELL, PROXYGATE)

entries.title: Attackers host AntiFox pentest platform on Alibaba Cloud to steal AWS secrets
entries.summary: Arctic Wolf observed self-managed instances of AntiFox, an open-source Chinese-language agentic pentest platform forked from ARTEX 0.1.1, hosted on Alibaba Cloud and tied to confirmed intrusions. The attackers planted an ASPX (Active Server Pages Extended) webshell on an exposed IIS (Internet Information Services) server and accessed and copied config files and connection strings. They also made AWS API calls with valid IAM (Identity and Access Management) users and assumed EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) roles. In one intrusion the attacker cycled through identities and made hundreds of API requests in about 30 minutes, mostly denied but sometimes obtaining production secrets; another case read, copied and deleted S3 (Simple Storage Service) objects. AWS says its services were not compromised and the credentials came from customers' compromised applications.

lessons.point: Open-source agentic pentest frameworks are being self-hosted by attackers for real intrusions, continuing the ARTEX pattern with a new fork.
lessons.excerpt: Attackers are using Alibaba Cloud to host self-managed instances of AntiFox, an open-source agentic penetration testing platform

lessons.point: In this intrusion a dense burst of API calls across several identities was observed, which is a detection signal in itself.
lessons.excerpt: they cycled through multiple identities and made hundreds of API requests in about 30 minutes

lessons.point: Hunt for the rare success inside a denial burst, and correlate it with webshell activity on the web tier.
lessons.excerpt: correlating IIS webshell activity with unusual AWS access and reviewing successful API calls within bursts of denials

entries.takeaway: Hunt for successful AWS calls hidden in bursts of denials that follow web-tier compromise.

actionable.title: CloudTrail alert for one source rapidly switching between identities
actionable.detail: Alert when one source IP or session uses several identity and access management (IAM) principals (users and assumed Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) roles) within a short window with a high AccessDenied ratio, and escalate any successful secret-reading or Simple Storage Service (S3) read/delete calls inside that burst. Join with web-server telemetry for new ASPX (Active Server Pages Extended) files or Internet Information Services (IIS) worker processes spawning shells. On a hit, revoke the affected sessions and keys and rotate credentials found in application files.

entries.verify_note: Verifier found lesson 4 (long-term keys in app config as the root exposure) unsupported by the source and deleted it, and softened lesson 2 and the summary wording.
entries.prior_art: Datadog's 'Datadog traces the ARTEX agentic attack framework inside real AWS accounts', 'Check Point found ARTEX operators letting AI agents run cybercrime campaigns unattended', and 'Microsoft says Storm-0940 used the ARTEX pentest framework against 2,250+ tenants' (product-security.json) already document agentic pentest frameworks used against AWS; AntiFox is a new ARTEX fork with similar tradecraft. Verifier's closest: Datadog ARTEX-in-AWS entry; Storm-0940 ARTEX; Check Point ARTEX operators.
entries.threat: Attackers use a self-hosted agentic pentest platform to exploit internet-facing web services, plant webshells, harvest credentials from application files, and use them against AWS APIs to steal secrets and tamper with S3 data.
entries.conditions: Exposed, exploitable web services (e.g. IIS) storing AWS credentials or connection strings in application files, or EC2 roles reachable from compromised hosts, with over-broad IAM permissions.
entries.mitigations: Correlate IIS webshell activity with unusual AWS access, review successful API calls within bursts of denials, revoke affected AWS sessions and keys, rotate credentials exposed through application files, grant least-privilege permissions, require IMDSv2, keep long-term access keys out of application configurations, and enable GuardDuty.

issues: mild: sentence_words 47 > 45 (Alert when one source IP or session uses several identity and access management (IAM) principals (users and assumed Elas)

entries.title: Google: eight eMudhra CA keys had weak entropy and Chrome blocked them
entries.summary: On October 17, 2026 Google's Chrome Root Program got a report that private keys for eight eMudhra subordinate CA certificates were generated with insufficient randomness, which would let anyone forge trusted HTTPS certificates. Chrome blocked the keys by public-key hash within about 100 minutes, with no browser update needed. No certificates from the intermediates were logged to Certificate Transparency before the block. Chrome will also remove the emSign ECC Root CA - G3 root.

lessons.point: Weak entropy means anyone can derive the CA keys and forge certificates for any site.
lessons.excerpt: The private keys for these certificates were generated with insufficient randomness (i.e., weak cryptographic entropy), enabling anyone to forge trusted HTTPS certificates to impersonate any website

lessons.point: A key-hash block protected users immediately, with no update.
lessons.excerpt: Chrome users were immediately protected against all certificates sharing those keys, without requiring a browser update or restart.

lessons.point: Certificate Transparency enforcement limited the damage window.
lessons.excerpt: no fraudulent certificates issued by these CAs could have been used against CT-enforcing clients.

lessons.point: Site operators must move off the removed root before the Chrome Root Store change.
lessons.excerpt: must immediately acquire and install a new TLS certificate from another PKI hierarchy

entries.takeaway: Weak randomness in CA key generation is catastrophic; Certificate Transparency and fast key-hash blocks are what contained this one.

actionable.title: Check your chains for emSign ECC G3
actionable.detail: Inventory certificates that chain to emSign ECC Root CA - G3, replace them from another root before the Chrome Root Store change lands, and keep CT monitoring on your domains.

entries.prior_art: Past CA incidents (DigiNotar, Symantec) involve compromise or mis-issuance; a weak-entropy intermediate key set blocked in hours is a distinct case. Verifier: Debian OpenSSL weak-key incident (2008); Trustico/DigiCert key-exposure revocation (2018); Symantec and Entrust distrust. Delta: SPKI-hash CRLSet block within ~
entries.verify_note: Independent verifier found every claim supported by the source.

editorial.reason: Weak-entropy CA keys blocked by Chrome within hours; root removal scheduled.

entries.title: 333 Tor exit relays hijacked with the Ebury backdoor to intercept SSH
entries.summary: A researcher who goes by kaba found that attackers had taken over about 333 Tor exit relays (roughly 10% of exits) and set them to redirect SSH on port 22 to 12 interception servers, stealing passwords, watching sessions and infecting the real server with Ebury. They had gained access to the servers in August and deployed Ebury 1.8.3 on them. Tor's network health team flagged the relays as bad exits on October 4 and all were offline by October 5. The attack also favored unencrypted mail traffic.

lessons.point: SSH on port 22 was silently redirected to attacker servers on infected exits.
lessons.excerpt: if you attempt an SSH connection over Port 22, you're unknowingly redirected to one of 12 SSH interception servers.

lessons.point: The infection started two months earlier with a Linux credential-stealing backdoor.
lessons.excerpt: The attackers had gained access to the servers two months earlier, in August, and quietly deployed their Ebury 1.8.3 payload (an OpenSSH backdoor and credential stealer for Linux).

lessons.point: Scale: roughly a tenth of Tor's exit capacity.
lessons.excerpt: To give you a sense of scale, all of Tor has around 3000 exit relays, so roughly 10% were under their control.

lessons.point: A victim who ignored the host-key warning also got their server infected.
lessons.excerpt: Opens a second connection to your server and infects it with Ebury

entries.takeaway: Never accept a changed SSH host key over Tor or any untrusted path; use key auth, and expect backdoored infrastructure hosts to be turned into traffic interceptors.

actionable.title: Treat host-key changes as incidents
actionable.detail: Use SSH keys instead of passwords (especially over anonymizing networks), pin host keys, never click through changed-key warnings, and scan relay or bastion hosts for Ebury indicators.

entries.prior_art: Malicious Tor exit relays are a known threat (sslstrip, bitcoin-swapping); mass port-22 redirection with a backdoored relay fleet is new. Verifier: Malicious Tor exit sniffing/sslstrip (Josh Pitts 2014, 'Spoiled Onions' 2016, KAX17 relays 2020-21); ESET Ebury research (Windigo 2014, 2024 report)
entries.verify_note: Independent fresh-context verifier re-read the source; discrepancies it found (title/summary overstatements) were corrected before merge.

entries.title: Backdoored fragment-api-py release drains users' crypto wallets when the client opens
entries.summary: SafeDep found that fragment-api-py 14.4.2, a PyPI client for Telegram's Fragment marketplace that holds the user's wallet seed for The Open Network (TON), was the old 13.0.0 code with a backdoor in three files and a higher version number, so pip install -U picked it up. On entering the async client context it sends all Tether (USDT) and nearly all TON to a hardcoded attacker wallet, once per client, before any purchase; two wallets lost 0.88 and 43.98 TON. The release had no GitHub tag, and the project publishes with a long-lived PyPI API token from local builds, so a stolen token, compromised machine or insider all fit.

lessons.point: Diffing a suspicious release only against the previous version can mislead; comparing it to every earlier release revealed an old codebase repackaged with a backdoor.
lessons.excerpt: A byte-for-byte comparison of 14.4.2 with every earlier release wheel points to an older base

lessons.point: Bumping the version number past the real latest release makes routine upgrades pull the backdoor in.
lessons.excerpt: with a backdoor in three files and a higher version number

lessons.point: The payload runs at runtime when the client opens, before user code, not at install or import.
lessons.excerpt: The backdoor runs when the client opens, before any user code.

lessons.point: The 14.4.2 release had no matching GitHub tag. Separately, the project publishes with a long-lived PyPI API token from local builds.
lessons.excerpt: The release workflow publishes with a PyPI API token, and the maintainer builds most releases locally.

entries.takeaway: A package that holds secrets such as wallet seeds can steal them through a single version bump, so pin versions and treat untagged releases as suspect.

actionable.title: Check for fragment-api-py 14.4.2 and flag untagged registry releases
actionable.detail: Run pip show fragment-api-py and grep site-packages for sweep_wallet_to_self, _ensure_swept or the attacker address UQAolfC7fyf__0H-1GzG9y5ZtV2CPC7yDno4W2cSVuYlJ6DU; if 14.4.2 was ever installed, move funds to a new seed. In dependency review, flag new releases that have no matching source tag or whose files match an older release more closely than the previous one, and pin versions with hashes for libraries that handle keys or seeds.

entries.verify_note: Install-time and causal inferences trimmed.
entries.prior_art: Earlier hijacked-token PyPI and npm crypto-drainer releases.
entries.threat: An attacker with publish access uploads a higher-numbered release built from an old version plus a wallet drainer that runs when the client opens and sends TON and USDT to an attacker wallet.
entries.conditions: Users who ran pip install -U or used an unpinned dependency and passed a wallet seed to FragmentClient while 14.4.2 was on PyPI (published 2026-11-08, since deleted).
entries.mitigations: Remove 14.4.2 and pin a known-good version with hashes, move funds from any seed used with it, scan manifests with a malicious-package checker, and for maintainers replace long-lived PyPI tokens with trusted publishing from tagged CI builds.

issues: mild: sentence_words 46 > 45 (SafeDep found that fragment-api-py 14.4.2, a PyPI client for Telegram's Fragment marketplace that holds the user's walle)

entries.title: Datadog's pathrunner automates 80+ AWS IAM privilege-escalation paths for defenders
entries.author: Seth Art
entries.summary: Datadog released pathrunner, a modular Metasploit-style framework that exploits the AWS IAM privilege-escalation paths catalogued in pathfinding.cloud, with identity import/switching, multiple payloads per module, managed 'attacker' infrastructure and a workspace report. The report lists the resources created and the CloudTrail events pathrunner expects to have triggered, turning a red-team run into a detection-engineering checklist. It is incremental over Pacu and Stratus Red Team; its value is the per-payload detection coverage it enables.

lessons.point: In cloud environments lateral movement is mostly identity-to-identity via credentials, so model attack paths as IAM graphs, not network hops.
lessons.excerpt: more often than not, penetration testers and real attacks are hopping from one cloud identity to another by accessing credentials

lessons.point: The tool ships a broad catalogue of exploit modules mapped to required permissions.
lessons.excerpt: As of October 2026, there are over 80 exploit modules in pathrunner.

lessons.point: Write detections per payload, not per single post-exploitation action: a detection for 'create admin user' is blind when the attacker picks another payload.
lessons.excerpt: if you walk through each and every pathrunner payload in your environment and build detections for each of them, you will have a much greater chance of catching malicious activity

lessons.point: The workspace report gives the blue team the CloudTrail events the run is expected to generate (Datadog's expectation, not a verified log) to check detections against.
lessons.excerpt: the report includes a table that lists all of the CloudTrail events that we think pathrunner would have triggered

lessons.point: Demonstrated exploitability is the triage signal for misconfigurations, as a public PoC is for CVEs.
lessons.excerpt: An offensive tool demonstrates the impact of an attack, enabling defenders to prioritize exploitable misconfigurations based on how impactful they are.

entries.takeaway: Run pathrunner in a sandbox (Pathfinding Labs) and use its CloudTrail report to test that every payload, not just one, trips a detection.

actionable.title: Detection coverage drill with pathrunner
actionable.detail: Deploy Pathfinding Labs in a sandbox account, run each pathrunner module with every payload, export `workspace report`, and diff the expected CloudTrail events against what your SIEM alerted on; file a detection gap per miss.

entries.prior_art: Pacu, Rhino Security's AWS escalation methods/CloudGoat, Stratus Red Team (per-technique detection testing), and Datadog's own pathfinding.cloud and Pathfinding Labs.
entries.verify_note: Independent verifier: all excerpts verbatim; novelty 40->35 (incremental over Pacu/Stratus); CloudTrail table is expected, not verified, events.

entries.title: StepSecurity launches scanning for files planted by supply chain campaigns
entries.summary: StepSecurity launched Malicious Files for GitHub (beta). It scans every branch, pull request and tag in an organization's repository history against campaign-specific rules. It also renamed Dev Machine Guard's Suspicious Files to Malicious Files, with a rules management page. The post says 2026 campaigns such as Miasma, ForceMemo, Megalodon, GhostAction and Mini Shai-Hulud trigger execution through planted IDE and AI-agent config files, appended code and injected workflows, rather than install-time scripts. The post is primarily a product announcement, though it publishes an example rule for the Miasma .claude/settings.json and .vscode/tasks.json loader.
entries.takeaway: Scan every ref, not just the default branch, for planted editor, agent and workflow files, because dependency scanners never see them.

lessons.point: Execution triggers have moved from package lifecycle scripts to repo config that runs when a developer or coding agent simply opens the project.
lessons.excerpt: including a .claude/settings.json SessionStart hook and a .vscode/tasks.json task, that run a credential-harvesting payload the moment a developer opens the repository

lessons.point: Planted files evade dependency scanners and code review because they live outside manifests and often off the default branch.
lessons.excerpt: They do not appear in a package manifest or lockfile, so dependency scanners have nothing to flag. They often land on branches other than the default branch, where reviewers rarely look.

lessons.point: Repo and laptop infections feed each other, so cleanup must cover both and include credential rotation for the pushing account.
lessons.excerpt: Malware on a laptop steals a token, and the attacker uses it to push files into more repositories.

actionable.title: Audit all refs for auto-run IDE and agent config files
actionable.detail: Across every branch, PR and tag, search for .claude/settings.json hooks (especially SessionStart), .gemini settings, .vscode/tasks.json with runOn folderOpen, Cursor rules applied to every request, and new .github/workflows files, and flag any that invoke scripts such as node .github/setup.js. Disable workspace auto-run tasks and agent hooks for untrusted repos by default, and when a hit is found, remove it from every ref and rotate credentials of the committing account and affected machines.

entries.prior_art: Core claim: supply chain payloads now persist as planted IDE/agent/workflow files across repo history, outside install-time controls. Nearest entries: ai-security's 'Trojan Horse: Automated Repository Poisoning against Coding Agents' (treat cloned repos as untrusted input to coding agents) and product-security's tensorlake npm worm / Mini Shai-Hulud entry, plus StepSecurity's own earlier Miasma and GhostAction writeups. This post adds a product and a sample detection rule, not new campaign research.
entries.threat: Supply chain worms and account-takeover campaigns planting auto-run editor, AI coding agent and CI workflow files in repositories (often on non-default branches or with backdated commits) that execute credential stealers when a developer opens the repo or a pipeline runs.
entries.conditions: Compromised contributor account or token with push access; developers open repos in Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor or VS Code with workspace hooks or tasks allowed to auto-run; reviews and scanners limited to manifests and the default branch.
entries.mitigations: Scan full repository history across all refs for known campaign files; require review for changes to .claude, .vscode, .cursor and .github/workflows paths; disable auto-run tasks and agent hooks for untrusted workspaces; enforce branch protection and block force-pushes; rotate credentials of pushing accounts and affected machines after a hit.

entries.title: Cisco BroadWorks XML external entity flaw is exploited in the wild
entries.summary: The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-20320, an XML external entity (XXE) flaw in Cisco BroadWorks, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on November 10, 2026, with a November 24 due date. The fetched National Vulnerability Database (NVD) page carries no description or score, only references, one of which is a third-party exploit write-up whose URL names an autonomous AI intrusion campaign.

lessons.point: The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) lists the BroadWorks XML external entity (XXE) flaw as exploited and requires remediation within two weeks.
lessons.excerpt: Cisco BroadWorks Improper Restriction of XML External Entity Reference Vulnerability | November 10, 2026 | November 24, 2026

lessons.point: The National Vulnerability Database (NVD) tags a Malbear Labs post as the exploit reference; its URL suggests the bug was used in an autonomous AI-driven intrusion campaign, but the fetched text does not describe it, so treat this as a lead to verify.
lessons.excerpt: https://malbearlabs.com/posts/operation-snowball-inside-an-autonomous-ai-intrusion-campaign

entries.takeaway: Patch BroadWorks per Cisco advisory cisco-sa-bworks-xxe-uwUd7CEt; CISA lists the flaw as exploited.

actionable.title: Patch the BroadWorks XML external entity flaw
actionable.detail: Apply the fix in Cisco advisory cisco-sa-bworks-xxe-uwUd7CEt before the November 24, 2026 CISA due date, and limit internet exposure of BroadWorks until it is patched.

entries.verify_note: Verifier confirmed both hedged lessons; attack details the NVD page does not contain were removed from the summary, threat and actionable.
entries.prior_art: XXE is a long-known class; Cisco KEV listings already tracked (product-security.json Cisco ASA/FTD KEV entries). The possible link to an autonomous AI intrusion campaign is new but unverified in this source.
entries.threat: An attacker abuses XML external entity processing in Cisco BroadWorks; the fetched source gives no further attack detail.
entries.conditions: Unpatched Cisco BroadWorks reachable by the attacker (details beyond the KEV entry are not in the fetched source).
entries.mitigations: Apply Cisco's fix and limit network exposure of BroadWorks until patched.

entries.title: Authlib accepts a JSON web signature with no signatures as verified
entries.summary: Authlib before 1.9.0 returns the payload of a JSON Web Signature (JWS) object in JSON serialization as verified when its `signatures` array is empty. The validity flag starts as true and only the per-signature loop can clear it, so an empty list skips every check. Any service that calls `JsonWebSignature.deserialize_json()` on outside input accepts a forged payload, even when it passes the correct key; upgrade to 1.9.0.

lessons.point: The bug is a fail-open default: the validity flag starts true and only the loop body can clear it, so zero signatures means zero checks.
lessons.excerpt: `is_valid` is initialised to `True` and only ever set to `False` from inside the loop.

lessons.point: Holding the correct key does not protect the caller, because no signature is ever examined.
lessons.excerpt: and [B] shows that holding the correct key does not

lessons.point: Normal tests still pass, so the flaw hides in a deployment that looks healthy.
lessons.excerpt: [C] proves the verifier works normally on a genuine object, so a deployment looks healthy.

entries.takeaway: Any verifier that loops over signatures must reject an empty list; test your JWS and JWT code for that case.

actionable.title: Add an empty-signatures test to every signature verifier
actionable.detail: Upgrade Authlib to 1.9.0 or move to joserfc. In your own token and multi-signature verifiers, add a negative test that submits a JSON-serialized token with `"signatures": []` and a forged payload, with and without the real key, and require a rejection. Search for validity flags set to true before a loop.

entries.verify_note: Verifier confirmed the core bug; it noted the 1.9.0 fix is inferred from the release reference and rated novelty 30 (known fail-open class).
entries.prior_art: Fail-open signature checks such as JWT alg=none bypasses are a known bug class; this is a new instance in Authlib's JWS JSON path, not a new technique.
entries.threat: An unauthenticated remote attacker forges identity or authorization claims that the relying party accepts as signed.
entries.conditions: A service calls Authlib's JsonWebSignature.deserialize_json() on input it did not produce, with Authlib before 1.9.0.
entries.mitigations: Upgrade to Authlib 1.9.0 or joserfc, and reject JWS objects whose signatures array is empty.

editorial.reason: Critical authentication bypass in a widely used Python library; the fail-open empty-loop pattern is a test every verifier should have.

entries.title: Next.js Image Optimization has unauthenticated RCE via SVG through sharp
entries.summary: A critical GHSA for npm/next reports that a memory-related bug in an upstream library used by Next.js Image Optimization can lead to remote code execution when SVG files are processed on glibc-based Linux; the workaround is to ensure the sharp version Next.js uses is new enough. The fetched advisory page captured only the CVSS boilerplate, so the details here come from the GHSA feed summary alone.

lessons.point: Server-side image optimization turns an image-library memory bug into unauthenticated RCE on the web tier.
lessons.excerpt: A memory-related vulnerability has been discovered in an upstream library used for Image Optimization can lead to possible remote code execution (RCE) when Next.js runs on glibc-based Linux.

lessons.point: The fix is a transitive dependency bump: pin a patched sharp.
lessons.excerpt: Ensure the version of `sharp` used by Next.js is greater

entries.takeaway: Pin a patched sharp under Next.js and consider disabling SVG optimization; image pipelines are unauthenticated RCE surface.

actionable.title: Check the sharp version Next.js resolves
actionable.detail: Run npm ls sharp in each Next.js app, upgrade to the patched sharp, and keep dangerouslyAllowSVG off unless required.

entries.prior_art: Astro's default image optimizer RCE via a libheif bug in sharp (GHSA-26w7-cxv4-gfx2), already in the story ledger: same class, different framework and codec.
entries.verify_note: Advisory body not captured (fetched page holds only CVSS boilerplate); lessons rest on the GHSA feed summary.

entries.title: Wiz: Gheist used stolen GitHub tokens to dump secrets through Actions logs
entries.summary: Wiz Research tracked Gheist, active from September 15 and still running on October 24, which used stolen GitHub tokens to push more than 13,500 branches across more than 850 accounts, each adding a `sync-check` workflow that tries to print the repository's secrets into its own log. The tool downloads the log through the GitHub API and deletes the run seconds later, so no attacker domain is involved. GitHub's July safeguard covers only public repositories; Wiz saw private enterprise repositories hit and, within hours, the same organization's cloud credentials used to list AWS Secrets Manager.

lessons.point: Secrets leave through GitHub's own API, so blocking outbound traffic does not help; detection has to use workflow and audit events.
lessons.excerpt: Because the secrets leave through GitHub's own API, there is no attacker domain or outbound connection to block

lessons.point: GitHub's public-repository safeguard does not apply once an enterprise credential is stolen.
lessons.excerpt: once an enterprise credential is compromised, that control doesn’t apply

lessons.point: Wiz gives concrete hunt indicators: short-lived workflow runs on ci-sync branches.
lessons.excerpt: workflow runs on "ci-sync-*" branches that were deleted within a minute of completion

lessons.point: Cloudsmith's security head notes that a token issued to a person months earlier still carried full write access.
lessons.excerpt: a credential issued to a human months ago still carried full write authority

entries.takeaway: A stolen GitHub token turns your own CI into a secrets-theft channel, so hunt for the sync-check pattern and replace long-lived personal access tokens with short-lived, scoped ones.

actionable.title: Hunt for Gheist workflows and shorten token lifetimes
actionable.detail: Search organization audit logs for branches named ci-sync- plus six characters that only add .github/workflows/sync-check.yml with the commit message "ci: sync config", workflow runs deleted within a minute, and API calls with the user agent "gheist". Rotate every secret those repositories hold, then replace personal access tokens with GitHub Apps or short-lived fine-grained tokens and require reviewers on environments with production secrets.

entries.verify_note: Core claims supported via Dark Reading's write-up of Wiz; the workflow 'tries' to print secrets and the long-lived-token point is a Cloudsmith quote, both now worded so. Novelty lowered to its 40.
entries.prior_art: Secrets-dumping workflows pushed with stolen tokens appeared in earlier campaigns such as GhostAction; Gheist adds log-then-delete theft with no attacker domain and reaches private enterprise repositories past GitHub's public-repository safeguard.
entries.threat: Theft of repository and cloud secrets through malicious GitHub Actions workflows pushed with stolen tokens, followed by cloud enumeration.
entries.conditions: A GitHub token, often from infostealer malware or an earlier supply chain compromise, with write access to repositories that hold secrets.
entries.mitigations: Hunt for the ci-sync and sync-check indicators, rotate exposed secrets, use GitHub Apps or short-lived fine-grained tokens, and require reviewers on production environments.

issues: mild: sentence_words 46 > 45 (Wiz Research tracked Gheist, active from September 15 and still running on October 24, which used stolen GitHub tokens t)

editorial.reason: Active campaign hitting private enterprise repos past GitHub's public-repo safeguard, with concrete hunt indicators and a token-lifetime fix.

entries.title: Google declines to fix zero-click SMS that crashes Android telephony
entries.summary: A malformed WAP (Wireless Application Protocol) Push data SMS makes WapPushOverSms.decodeWapPdu() cast an unchecked header length to a negative int and allocate a negative-size array, killing com.android.phone and dropping active calls, including emergency calls, with no user interaction or visible message. Rapid repeated sends (about 30) corrupt the SQLite SMS store so the phone crashes on every boot, and carrier redelivery re-triggers it even after a factory reset. Google's Android and Devices VRP (Vulnerability Reward Program) closed it as Won't Fix, non-security, with no CVE, and the researcher published a working proof of concept and a one-line bounds-check fix.

lessons.point: The payload arrives as a data SMS that never appears in the inbox, so the victim sees no message and no sender number.
lessons.excerpt: The message is delivered as a data SMS and is never shown to the user

lessons.point: Carrier redelivery of unacknowledged messages turns one crash into repeated outages, and a factory reset alone does not stop it.
lessons.excerpt: because the carrier re-sends the unacknowledged payload and re-triggers the crash

lessons.point: A single message caused intermittent outages for up to a week in the researcher's own testing.
lessons.excerpt: a single message caused intermittent outages for up to a week in testing

lessons.point: The vendor triage outcome was non-security across several tickets, so defenders cannot rely on a patch or CVE and must treat this as an unfixed exposure.
lessons.excerpt: Across three tickets and four engineers, Google classified it as a non-security issue.

entries.takeaway: Any Android device reachable by SMS can be knocked off telephony, emergency calling included, and the vendor treats it as a non-security bug with no fix scheduled.

actionable.title: Track carrier and OEM mitigations for the WAP Push crash
actionable.detail: For managed Android fleets, ask carriers whether they filter malformed WAP Push data SMS on port 2948 and ask OEMs whether they ship the bounds check in WapPushOverSms before the cast. For recovery, the source says moving the physical SIM to a non-Android device stops carrier redelivery, then the SMS records are cleared over ADB (Android Debug Bridge). When auditing parsers, flag any long-to-int cast used as an allocation size without a range check.

entries.verify_note: Verifier upheld all four lessons; outage duration is the researcher's own test claim (novelty 50 vs 70, lower kept; prior art Stagefright and SMS-of-death crashes).
entries.prior_art: No equivalent pool entry. The pool's Android items (GitHub Security Lab's 24 Android vulnerabilities, the Qualcomm zero-day in the March 2026 update) cover other bugs. Earlier SMS-of-death style crashes exist as a bug class, but this one's persistence through database corruption and carrier redelivery, and the vendor's won't-fix outcome, are specific to it.
entries.threat: A remote attacker who knows only the victim's phone number can silently crash Android telephony, drop calls including emergency calls, and with about 20 to 30 messages leave the device persistently without telephony.
entries.conditions: Android devices whose WapPushOverSms casts the WAP Push header length without a range check. The source reports a 100% reproduction rate on a Pixel 9 on April 2026 firmware and several Samsung Galaxy and A-series models. The vendor issued no fix and no CVE.
entries.mitigations: Add a range check on the header length before the cast in WapPushOverSms.java (the source's proposed fix), carrier-side filtering of malformed WAP Push data SMS, and for recovery, move the physical SIM to a non-Android device so redelivery stops, then clear the corrupted SMS records over ADB.
entries.author: MarkBlah

entries.title: New unpatched PHP RCE (CVE-2026-115560) is separate from PHP2Shell
entries.summary: The PHP security team disclosed a third remote code execution bug, CVE-2026-115560, separate from PHP2Shell, and there is no patch yet. It needs an unusual setup: the app sets session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize, then switches it to php with ini_set() before session_start(). The stopgap is session.upload_progress.enabled=0. BleepingComputer also reports that PHP2Shell exploitation attempts began before disclosure, seen by several vendors including Amazon, and Dataminr reported no confirmed compromises as of Thursday.

lessons.point: The new bug needs a specific runtime handler switch. Check exposure by searching code for ini_set calls on session.serialize_handler made before session_start().
lessons.excerpt: An application must set session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start().

lessons.point: Disabling session upload progress is the PHP team's stopgap until a patch ships.
lessons.excerpt: Until a security patch is available, the PHP devs suggested setting session.upload_progress.enabled=0

lessons.point: Pre-disclosure PHP2Shell exploitation attempts came from several actors, judging by different payloads and anonymization infrastructure.
lessons.excerpt: The actual payloads and choices in anonymization infrastructure varied, suggesting these were multiple actors.

lessons.point: For PHP2Shell, the activity seen since disclosure is scanning and non-working exploits, with no known compromises.
lessons.excerpt: observed activity since vulnerability disclosure remains limited to scanning, fingerprinting, and use of non-working exploits, with no known compromises

entries.takeaway: Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 on any PHP host that might switch session serializers at runtime. It is the stopgap for CVE-2026-115560 until a patch ships.

actionable.title: Check for runtime serialize_handler switching and disable upload progress
actionable.detail: Search PHP code for ini_set('session.serialize_handler', ...) calls made before session_start(), and check php.ini for session.serialize_handler set to php_binary or php_serialize. On any host where you cannot rule this out, set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and keep it until the PHP release that fixes CVE-2026-115560.

entries.prior_art: The pool has the Wiz PHP2Shell disclosure and the Talos PHP2Shell newsletter (CVE-2026-109618/109619). CVE-2026-115560 is a distinct new bug, and the multi-actor pre-disclosure exploitation detail is not in the pool yet.
entries.threat: Remote code execution through PHP's session handling in apps that switch the session serializer at runtime.
entries.conditions: session.serialize_handler set to php_binary or php_serialize in config, switched to php with ini_set() before session_start(), and session upload progress enabled.
entries.mitigations: Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until the fixing release ships, avoid switching serialize handlers at runtime, and patch PHP2Shell separately.
entries.verify_note: Two independent verifier passes (draft and final text): all excerpts verbatim and facts supported (not refuted). Lesson 4 now names PHP2Shell as its subject. Novelty: lower of 40 and 72.

editorial.reason: A third, still-unpatched PHP RCE (CVE-2026-115560) during the PHP2Shell week, with a one-line config mitigation every PHP operator can apply today.

entries.title: A Lean 4 string-slice mismatch let native_decide 'prove' Fermat's Last Theorem
entries.summary: Trail of Bits, while experimenting with a code-review skill using GPT-5.6, found that Lean's String.Pos.Raw.extract returns the empty string in its logical definition but the whole original string in compiled native code for an astronomically large position. Combining the two evaluations yields a contradiction, so any theorem, including Fermat's Last Theorem, can be 'proved' using native_decide. The Lean team fixed the memory-safety part within about three hours and the semantic mismatch five days after the report. The authors say it is not a kernel soundness issue.

lessons.point: A disagreement between a prover's logical definition and its compiled implementation is enough to derive a contradiction.
lessons.excerpt: That disagreement is enough to manufacture a contradiction.

lessons.point: native_decide puts the compiler inside the trusted boundary, so check axioms when validating external proofs.
lessons.excerpt: The extra axiom `native_decide` adds the compiler to the trusted boundary, and therefore needs to be used with care.

lessons.point: The bug sits in a low-level string-slicing primitive, not the kernel.
lessons.excerpt: The issue affects `String.Pos.Raw.extract`, Lean’s low-level string-slicing function.

lessons.point: The upstream response was fast.
lessons.excerpt: About 90 minutes after we reported the issue, hargoniX opened a fix for the

entries.takeaway: Machine-checked proofs are only as trustworthy as the evaluators behind them, so audit the axioms (especially native_decide) and prefer independent checkers for high-stakes results.

actionable.title: Audit axioms when accepting external Lean proofs
actionable.detail: Upgrade to Lean v4.34.0-rc1 or later (affected: stable versions up to 4.33.1), run #print axioms on external proofs and treat any dependence on native_decide as adding the compiler to the trusted base; consider independent checkers such as lean4lean for high-stakes proofs.

entries.prior_art: none found in pool. Verifier: none equivalent found (no Lean/proof-assistant entries in the data files)
entries.verify_note: All claims and excerpts verified (3-hour memory-safety fix, 5-day semantic fix, 4.33.1 affected). Genuine, novel logical-vs-native disagreement bug, but narrow audience for appsec engineers.

entries.title: GitHub previews a package firewall that blocks risky npm installs
entries.summary: GitHub put a package firewall into public preview for GitHub Enterprise Cloud. It sits between endpoints (including coding agents and CI/CD hosts) or internal registries and the upstream npm registry, and blocks downloads that fail policy. The policies are known-malware advisories, a vulnerability severity threshold (default Critical only), Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts (SLSA) attestation downgrades, newly added preinstall or postinstall scripts, and a minimum package age (default 1 day, range 1 to 365). Rust's Cargo is adding a similar minimum publish age with a 7-day default.

lessons.point: The firewall is a proxy, so it only protects clients that are pointed at it instead of the public registry.
lessons.excerpt: the firewall is placed between endpoints or internal registries and the upstream package repositories

lessons.point: One policy flags versions that newly add install hooks, which targets the common pattern of a hijacked package gaining a malicious postinstall script.
lessons.excerpt: Block newly-introduced install scripts by checking whether the package recently added scripts that run using preinstall or postinstall hooks

lessons.point: The default cooldown is only 1 day, much shorter than the 7-day default Cargo plans, so teams should raise it deliberately.
lessons.excerpt: The value can range from 1 to 365 days. The default value is 1 day.

lessons.point: Socket notes that cooldowns buy detection time, not safety: a malicious release that nobody detects passes once it is old enough.
lessons.excerpt: A release that escapes detection can simply outlast the cooldown.

entries.takeaway: Install-time gating is moving into the platform, but its value depends on routing agents and CI through it and setting a longer cooldown than the 1-day default.

actionable.title: Route agent and CI npm installs through a policy proxy
actionable.detail: Point coding agents and CI runners at a package firewall or internal registry rather than registry.npmjs.org, and block direct egress to the public registry so they cannot bypass it. Turn on the malware, attestation-downgrade and new-install-script policies, and raise minimum package age above the 1-day default (Cargo plans a 7-day default). Keep a fast exception path for urgent security fixes.

entries.verify_note: Verifier upheld lessons; Dependabot's 3-day figure appears only in a link, so it was removed from the text; the cooldown quote is Socket's.
entries.prior_art: Dependency cooldowns are already in the pool (GitHub's 3-day Dependabot cooldown, Semgrep's one-week org-wide cooldown, Chainguard-style interposed scanning), and commercial registry firewalls exist. New here is a GitHub-hosted install-time gate that combines cooldown with attestation-downgrade and newly-added-install-script checks.
entries.threat: Malicious or hijacked npm versions run code when installed, especially when AI agents and CI runners install dependencies automatically.
entries.conditions: GitHub Enterprise Cloud customers, npm only, public preview. Clients must be configured to use the firewall.
entries.mitigations: Route installs through the firewall, enable malware, severity, attestation-downgrade and install-script policies, set a multi-day cooldown, and still pin lockfiles and monitor runtime egress because import-time payloads are not caught by install-script checks.

entries.title: KeyDrift malware steals Cisco SD-WAN encryption keys from hacked controllers
entries.summary: Cisco Talos says a group it tracks as UAT-11473 exploited CVE-2026-20127, a CVSS 10.0 authentication bypass in Catalyst SD-WAN (software-defined wide area network) control systems, and planted custom malware called KeyDrift. On a compromised Controller, its LittleFilch component hooks the vdaemon process, reads decrypted control messages and copies the AES-256 (Advanced Encryption Standard) key material the Controller passes between routers. The main module, PolyFlame, runs in memory, takes commands inside SD-WAN control traffic and has no hardcoded server address.

lessons.point: The implant targets the key-distribution process itself: on a compromised Controller it reads decrypted control messages, where Talos assesses it collects key material for a preset list of edge routers.
lessons.excerpt: On a compromised Controller, a KeyDrift component called LittleFilch hooks into vdaemon and reads control messages after they are decrypted.

lessons.point: Commands arrive inside SD-WAN control traffic and the analyzed samples carried no hardcoded server address, so there is no fixed command server to block.
lessons.excerpt: It is built to accept commands within SD-WAN control traffic, and the analyzed samples contained no hardcoded server address.

lessons.point: Port restrictions do not remove an implant that is already installed, and Talos does not say whether upgrading does, so compromised devices need a separate investigation.
lessons.excerpt: Blocking the ports does not remove malware already on a device.

lessons.point: Detection has to rely on file paths, auth logs and Snort rules, because Talos published no hash, IP address or domain indicators.
lessons.excerpt: Talos's report does not include a list of file hashes, IP addresses or domains for KeyDrift.

entries.takeaway: Patching an SD-WAN control system that was already compromised is not enough: hunt for KeyDrift's files and treat the inter-site keys as possibly exposed.

actionable.title: Hunt for KeyDrift on Catalyst SD-WAN control components
actionable.detail: Upgrade to the first fixed release for your train. Until then, limit ports 22 and 830 to known controller IP addresses. On every Controller, Manager and Validator, check for a modified etc/sv/sshd/run script, /etc/sv/aaamgr/, conf_sshd, rsshd, libdssl.so, libcommon.so, /tmp/system-vdaemon and /var/tmp/vdaemon.bin. Search /var/log/auth.log for 'Accepted publickey for vmanage-admin' from unknown IP addresses. Turn on Snort 2 rules 67387-67416, which ship disabled. If you find signs of compromise, rebuild from patched images and consider rotating the keys.

entries.verify_note: Verifier: facts hold; two lesson points stated inferences as certain (IP blocking, patching), reworded to the source's hedged wording. Novelty lowered to the verifier's 35.
entries.prior_art: Closest are 'Volt Typhoon hides zero-day attacks behind rotating relays of hacked devices' and 'Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator SQL injection (CVE-2026-114625) is exploited in the wild' in product-security. Neither covers an implant that steals keys from the SD-WAN control plane.
entries.threat: An unauthenticated remote attacker uses CVE-2026-20127 to get admin access on Catalyst SD-WAN control systems. They install an in-memory backdoor that copies the AES-256 keys protecting traffic between sites and hides its commands in SD-WAN control traffic.
entries.conditions: Catalyst SD-WAN Controller, Manager or Validator on an unpatched release, on-premises or Cisco-hosted, regardless of configuration. Implants planted before the upgrade may still be present.
entries.mitigations: Upgrade to the first fixed release, since there is no workaround. Restrict ports 22 and 830 to known controller IP addresses. Follow Cisco's hardening guide. Hunt for the listed KeyDrift files and the vmanage-admin publickey logins. Enable the Talos Snort rules. If compromise is found, rebuild control components from patched images and contact Cisco TAC (Technical Assistance Center).

entries.title: Google Cloud says Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) Turin VMs need guest patches
entries.summary: Google Cloud says VMs on Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) Turin (fifth-generation EPYC) in the C4D, N4D, H4D, Z4D and G4 series need a guest OS patch plus a stop-and-start to mitigate three Transient Scheduler Attack flaws, two previously disclosed for older EPYC (CVE-2024-36350, CVE-2024-36357) and one new (CVE-2026-0004). Google has mitigated cross-VM and VM-to-host attacks; the remaining risk is a local attacker on the same core inferring data from other processes or the kernel inside a VM. Google rates it Medium, nothing is reported exploited, and guest kernel fixes are still landing (Debian has fixed it only in unstable).

lessons.point: The residual risk is intra-VM: the cloud provider fixed cross-tenant paths, but process-to-process and process-to-kernel leakage inside the guest is the customer's to patch.
lessons.excerpt: Inside a VM, the flaws may let an attacker with code on the same processor core infer data from other processes or the kernel.

lessons.point: Guest mitigations depend on the provider updating the reported CPU information; Google says rebooting the guest OS isn't enough and a stop-and-start is needed.
lessons.excerpt: Starting this week, the company will update the CPU information that VMs report, so a patched guest kernel can turn on its mitigations.

lessons.point: Vendor 'not vulnerable' statements for a new CPU generation can be reversed; Zen 5 was earlier declared unaffected by two of these flaws.
lessons.excerpt: AMD had previously said that Zen5 CPUs were not vulnerable to TSA-SQ and TSA-L1.

lessons.point: Distribution kernels lag the upstream fix, so patch availability must be checked per distro.
lessons.excerpt: Debian has fixed CVE-2026-0004 in its Linux kernel only in its unstable branch.

entries.takeaway: Google tells all affected Turin-based Google Cloud Platform (GCP) VMs to install the guest kernel fix and stop-and-start the VM; rebooting the guest OS is not enough.

actionable.title: Patch and stop-start Turin-based Google Cloud Platform (GCP) VMs
actionable.detail: List C4D, N4D, H4D, Z4D and G4 instances (including C4D/Z4D bare metal). Install the OS vendor's kernel fix when available, then stop and start each VM after Google's CPU information update reaches it. On bare metal or your own Turin hardware, apply both platform firmware and OS updates and weigh the performance cost. Prioritize hosts that run untrusted or multi-tenant code inside one VM.

entries.verify_note: Verifier found the store-queue mechanism was not in the source, the takeaway narrowed Google's guidance to multi-tenant only, and lesson 2 used overly causal wording; all three were corrected to match the source.
entries.prior_art: AMD Transient Scheduler Attacks (TSA-SQ CVE-2024-36350, TSA-L1 CVE-2024-36357) disclosed July 8, 2025 for earlier EPYC, with the same Google stop-and-start guidance in bulletin GCP-2025-037. New here is the Zen 5 reversal and the third variant CVE-2026-0004 (TSA-Fill); no TSA entry exists in the tracker. Verifier's closest: 2025 TSA disclosure and GCP-2025-037 (outside the tracker); no TSA entry in the pool.
entries.threat: A low-privileged local attacker running code on the same core inside a VM may infer data from other processes or the kernel, including data in the L1 data cache.
entries.conditions: AMD Turin (Zen 5) processors; attacker can run code on the same core; local, high-complexity attack per AMD; no reported exploitation and not in CISA KEV.
entries.mitigations: Apply guest kernel fixes and stop-and-start VMs after the CPU information update, apply firmware plus OS updates on owned Turin servers, upgrade GKE nodes when updated images ship, and apply Xen XSA-525 patches for Xen hosts.
