editorial.reason: Exploited-in-the-wild Plex chain added to CISA KEV with a due date of today and a public plex2shell write-up; patch now.

entries.title: Google patches its eighth exploited Chrome zero-day of 2026
entries.summary: Google fixed CVE-2026-125350, a high-severity use-after-free in Chrome's XML component that is being exploited in the wild, in Chrome 157.0.8103.50/.51. It is the eighth exploited Chrome zero-day this year, which equals the total for all of 2025. Google has not said who is exploiting it or who is targeted, and is withholding technical details until most users have updated.

lessons.point: 2026 has already matched 2025's full-year total of eight exploited Chrome zero-days with nearly two months left, a faster pace. Browser patch speed needs to be measured in days.
lessons.excerpt: Google has patched its eighth actively exploited Chrome zero-day of 2026, matching its total for the whole of last year

lessons.point: Google confirms exploitation but has withheld technical details, indicators and attribution for now.
lessons.excerpt: Google is aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild

lessons.point: Chrome's staged rollout can leave fleets behind the fix for an exploited bug unless an update is forced.
lessons.excerpt: Google says the latest update will roll out over the coming days and weeks, but users can check manually

entries.takeaway: Force Chrome 157.0.8103.50 or later across your fleet now instead of waiting for the staged rollout.

actionable.title: Force-update Chrome and track version compliance
actionable.detail: Use enterprise policy (relaunch notification and a forced relaunch deadline) to push Chrome 157.0.8103.50 or later, then report the share of endpoints below that version until it is near zero.

entries.verify_note: Pace wording corrected.
entries.prior_art: Routine Chrome in-the-wild zero-day advisories (8 in 2025).
entries.threat: An attacker exploits a use-after-free in Chrome's XML component, likely through crafted web content, to corrupt memory and possibly run code.
entries.conditions: Chrome older than 157.0.8103.50 on Windows, macOS or Linux.
entries.mitigations: Update to Chrome 157.0.8103.50/.51 or later, force relaunch through enterprise policy, and confirm version compliance across the fleet.

entries.title: Wiz markets Green Agent as removing cross-team bottlenecks in cloud remediation
entries.summary: A Wiz marketing post arguing that cloud vulnerability remediation is slowed by coordination across security, engineering and platform teams rather than by detection. It describes Green Agent finding the likely owner from commit history, service catalogs, CMDB and cloud logs, tracing runtime findings back to the exact file and line, and producing code or Terraform fixes as one-click pull requests or via an MCP server for coding agents. Customer quotes claim more than 70% less daily triage time at Fireblocks and 10x remediation velocity at project44, with no methodology given.
entries.takeaway: The useful idea is the pipeline shape (owner attribution, runtime-to-code root cause, fix as a pull request), while the ROI figures are unverified vendor claims.

lessons.point: The core bottleneck described is organizational: the team that finds the risk does not own the code or pipeline that must change.
lessons.excerpt: Security teams discover the risk, but they don't own the code, the infrastructure, or the deployment pipelines.

lessons.point: Owner attribution can be automated by joining several weak signals rather than relying on a stale CMDB alone.
lessons.excerpt: By analyzing repository commit history, Wiz Project assignments, service catalogs, CMDB integrations, and cloud logs

lessons.point: Reported customer gains are large but come only as vendor-selected testimonials with no baseline or method.
lessons.excerpt: cut daily operational triage time by more than 70% and now reaches same-day resolution on critical risks.

actionable.title: Build an owner-attribution step into your remediation pipeline
actionable.detail: Before routing a cloud finding, resolve the owner by joining git blame or commit history on the Dockerfile or infrastructure-as-code (IaC) file, service catalog entries and deploy logs, and fall back to the CMDB last. Attach the runtime-to-code trace (exposed workload, reachable package, originating file) to the ticket and deliver the fix as a pull request to that owner, gated by normal CI checks.

entries.prior_art: Salesforce's claim that AI finds vulnerabilities faster than engineers can fix them (product-security.json) states the same remediation-bottleneck thesis. Code-to-cloud mapping and auto-fix PRs are established features across CNAPP and ASPM vendors; the injected-security-context remediation claim in the ledger covers fix quality, which this post does not measure.

entries.title: Railway says encrypted environment variables may have been accessed
entries.summary: On October 21, 2026 Railway said it detected anomalous activity on systems that store customer environment variables, and an unauthorized party may have accessed them and in some cases decrypted them. Railway believes this is part of a series of attacks on platform companies aiming to compromise AI inference providers, and told those providers to revoke keys. It recommends all users roll every environment variable and registry credential, and paused all deployments.

lessons.point: Env vars may have been decrypted, so rotating them is the safe precaution.
lessons.excerpt: an unauthorized third party may have accessed encrypted environment variables and, for some of them, obtained the decrypted contents.

lessons.point: Railway links the incident to attacks aimed at AI inference providers.
lessons.excerpt: We believe this is part of a series of attacks recently targeting platform companies with the aim of compromising AI inference providers.

lessons.point: Recommended action: rotate everything stored in the platform.
lessons.excerpt: we strongly recommend that you immediately roll all environment variables, including any API keys, stored in Railway

lessons.point: Deployments were paused during the investigation.
lessons.excerpt: All deployments are paused while we investigate.

entries.takeaway: Platform-held env vars are a high-value target; rotate keys, scope them narrowly and keep AI provider keys short-lived and monitored.

actionable.title: Rotate and constrain platform secrets
actionable.detail: Roll Railway env vars and registry credentials, set spend limits and IP restrictions on LLM provider keys, and review provider logs for unexpected usage since October 21.

entries.prior_art: Hosting-platform secret exposures (Heroku/Travis 2022, CircleCI 2023) share the pattern; the AI inference provider targeting is the new element. Verifier: Heroku/Travis CI OAuth token theft 2022, CircleCI 2023 breach (rotate all secrets), Codecov bash uploader
entries.verify_note: Independent verifier found every claim supported by the source.

editorial.reason: Hosting platform secrets exposure tied to attacks on AI inference providers; rotate keys.

entries.title: Wiz scans every new npm version at publish time to catch compromises
entries.summary: Wiz describes a pipeline that analyzes each new npm package version as soon as it is published. It diffs the new version against earlier ones, runs static checks and an AI classifier, then installs, imports and runs suspicious versions in a sandbox while a runtime sensor watches behavior. In the keyv compromise, the malware fetched its command-and-control (C2) domains from an Ethereum smart contract at runtime, so only the dynamic stage could see them.

lessons.point: Diffing a new release against prior versions is the first step for spotting a trusted package gone bad.
lessons.excerpt: When a new package version is released, the pipeline downloads and extracts the current version and previous versions for comparison.

lessons.point: Static analysis missed C2 that was resolved at runtime from a blockchain; dynamic execution caught it.
lessons.excerpt: the malware dynamically retrieved its C2 domains at runtime by querying an Ethereum smart contract.

lessons.point: Wiz reports supply chain attacks rose from about 10% to 25% of significant incidents between H2 2025 and H1 2026.
lessons.excerpt: In H1 2026, that percentage increased to 25%, and now, notable supply chain attacks account for 1 in 4 significant security incidents.

lessons.point: Removing malicious versions within hours is not enough when a package is near-ubiquitous.
lessons.excerpt: Axios was present in approximately 80% of cloud and code environments, and downloaded around 100 million times per week.

entries.takeaway: CVE-based dependency scanning is blind to hijacked trusted packages; you need publish-time behavioral analysis or a cooldown before new versions reach builds.

actionable.title: Gate new dependency versions on behavior, not CVEs
actionable.detail: Do not auto-pull the latest version of popular packages into CI. Add a minimum release age (cooldown) or route new versions through a malicious-package feed or sandbox that installs, imports and runs the package and logs network egress. Alert on unexpected outbound connections from install and import steps, including to blockchain RPC endpoints.

entries.prior_art: Publish-time malicious-package detection is established practice (Socket, Phylum, Aikido feeds); the keyv Ethereum-resolved C2 is already covered in the archive (Chainguard and Snyk keyv write-ups). This adds Wiz's pipeline design and incident share figures. Verifier: Publish-time npm scanning that combines diffing, sandboxing and AI classification is established practice (Socket, Phylum, Aikido Intel, StepSecurity, OpenSSF package-analysis). The keyv Ethereum-resolved C2 is already in archive.json ('keyv/cacheable Mini Shai-Hulud ... Ethereum-resolved C2'), and EtherHiding has been documented since 2023.
entries.verify_note: Independent fresh-context verifier re-read the source and found no unsupported claim.
entries.threat: Compromised maintainer accounts publish malicious versions of trusted packages that auto-update into dev environments and CI before any CVE or advisory exists.
entries.conditions: Build pipelines and developer workflows pull the latest versions of popular packages automatically and rely on vulnerability databases for blocking.
entries.mitigations: Release-age cooldowns, pinned lockfiles, publish-time static plus dynamic package analysis, runtime egress monitoring on install and import.

entries.title: Blockchain analysts tie record Binance hot-wallet theft to North Korea's TraderTraitor
entries.summary: Attackers took about $6.3 billion from Binance hot wallets across ten blockchains on October 29, and most of it left within about 20 minutes. Binance's early findings point to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop that gave access to a service container able to submit withdrawals. TRM Labs judges that the attacker could make Binance's hot-wallet signing system sign any transaction it chose. TRM attributes the theft to the North Korean unit TraderTraitor with high confidence.

lessons.point: Binance's early findings point to one engineer's laptop reaching a service container that could submit withdrawals, and it found no evidence of a private key leak.
lessons.excerpt: may involve a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions

lessons.point: If attackers can drive the signing system, protecting the keys is not enough. Valid signatures across different chains and key types point to abuse of the signer itself.
lessons.excerpt: the most likely explanation is that the attacker gained the ability to make Binance’s hot wallet signing system sign transactions of its choosing across chains

lessons.point: On Ethereum the attackers used EIP-7702 delegation. They pre-signed a batch of permissions so that one would match the wallet's transaction count (nonce) when it ran.
lessons.excerpt: They sent a batch of 50 such permissions, all signed beforehand by a Binance hot wallet, so that one would match the wallet’s transaction count at execution time.

lessons.point: Fast freezes by token issuers held back a large share, but the ETH and BTC the attackers kept have no issuer that can freeze them.
lessons.excerpt: By 00:30 UTC on October 30, TRM tallied around $2.7 billion in frozen assets

entries.takeaway: The signing service, and every container and engineer laptop that can submit requests to it, is the real security boundary for hot wallets. Protecting the keys does not help once an attacker can ask the signer to sign.

actionable.title: Put independent policy checks in front of transaction-signing services
actionable.detail: Make the signer enforce its own limits on withdrawal value, rate and destination before it signs. Require a second approval path that service containers reachable from engineer laptops cannot satisfy. Alert when wallets sign across several chains in a short burst, and when EIP-7702 delegation authorizations are signed from hot wallets.

entries.verify_note: Verifier: mostly supported; 'no private key was stolen' and the native-coin freeze point overreached Binance's hedged early findings, reworded. Novelty lowered to the verifier's 40.
entries.prior_art: The pool has no crypto-exchange heist or TraderTraitor entry. The nearest DPRK items are the archive Axios npm compromise attributed to Sapphire Sleet and a DPRK-linked PHP scanning mention in product-security, both unrelated attack paths. This is a news synthesis of TRM Labs and Binance statements with little technical detail on the signer compromise.
entries.threat: A state-sponsored actor compromises a DevOps engineer's laptop, reaches a service container that can submit withdrawals, and makes the hot-wallet signing system sign attacker transactions across ten chains. On Ethereum it also abuses pre-signed EIP-7702 delegations.
entries.conditions: Hot-wallet signing can be triggered from service containers reachable from engineer endpoints, and the signer has no independent check on value, rate or destination for withdrawals.
entries.mitigations: Isolate signing services from DevOps endpoints. Make the signer enforce withdrawal policy and require out-of-band approval. Monitor for burst signing across chains and for EIP-7702 delegation signatures. Line up rapid-freeze contacts with stablecoin issuers ahead of time.

entries.title: Skimmers hijacked Convertr's self-hosted analytics script to steal checkout card data
entries.summary: A Brazilian card-skimming (Magecart) gang changed the Plausible analytics tracker that Convertr hosts on its own servers. That script loads on the checkout pages of every merchant on the platform. Sansec suspects the way in was CVE-2026-8467, an unauthenticated command-execution flaw in Convertr's outdated Plausible Community Edition, but this is not confirmed. The skimmer stole card numbers, expiry dates, CVVs, cardholder names and CPF tax IDs, and Convertr has since removed it and patched Plausible.

lessons.point: A single shared third-party script served from platform infrastructure exposes every downstream merchant's checkout at once.
lessons.excerpt: which loads on the checkout pages of all merchants using the platform.

lessons.point: An outdated self-hosted analytics server was the suspected entry point, so its patch level directly affects payment security.
lessons.excerpt: an unauthenticated command-execution vulnerability affecting

lessons.point: Attackers tuned the skimmer to the platform's own payment field names after the first wave.
lessons.excerpt: the attackers pushed a more refined version that specifically targeted

lessons.point: Browser caching can keep serving the malicious script after cleanup.
lessons.excerpt: browser caching could keep the malicious script active on impacted sites for up to 24 hours after cleanup

entries.takeaway: Any script loaded on checkout pages, even self-hosted analytics, belongs in the payment attack surface and needs patching and integrity checks.

actionable.title: Treat checkout-page scripts as payment-critical
actionable.detail: List every script that loads on checkout pages, including self-hosted analytics like Plausible. Keep their servers patched, pin or integrity-check script content (for example with Subresource Integrity hashes or change monitoring), and after any cleanup allow for up to 24 hours of cached malicious copies.

entries.prior_art: No Magecart or Plausible entries in the pools. Compromising a shared third-party script to skim cards is a well-known Magecart pattern; the new detail is a self-hosted analytics server as the injection point.
entries.threat: Attackers compromise a shared analytics script served from the platform's infrastructure and inject a skimmer that steals card data and CPF tax IDs from every merchant's checkout.
entries.conditions: An e-commerce platform that serves an outdated, self-hosted Plausible Community Edition tracker on checkout pages (suspected CVE-2026-8467).
entries.mitigations: Patch or upgrade self-hosted analytics, monitor the integrity of checkout-page scripts, notify affected merchants and payment providers, and account for browser caching after cleanup.

editorial.reason: A live Magecart incident in which one self-hosted analytics script skimmed every merchant's checkout. The lesson is concrete: treat every script loaded on checkout pages, analytics included, as payment-critical and check its integrity.

entries.title: Exploited Adobe Commerce and Magento upload flaw can lead to code execution
entries.summary: CISA added CVE-2026-48356 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on 2026-10-27. CISA describes an unrestricted upload of a file with a dangerous type in Adobe Commerce and Magento that could allow arbitrary code execution as the current user and take over the victim's account or session. NVD's configuration list covers Adobe Commerce 2.4.4 through 2.4.9, Commerce B2B releases 1.3.3, 1.3.4, 1.4.2, 1.5.2 and 1.5.3, and Magento Open Source 2.4.6 through 2.4.9, including their patch releases.

lessons.point: NVD lists every Adobe Commerce line from 2.4.4 through base 2.4.9 as affected, including the patch releases in between.
Magento Open Source and the Commerce B2B extension are listed too, so open-source storefronts are in scope, not only paid Commerce.
lessons.excerpt: cpe:2.3:a:adobe:magento:2.4.9:-:*:*:open_source:*:*:*

entries.takeaway: An actively exploited file-upload flaw spans every supported Commerce and Magento line, so storefront operators should patch now rather than wait for a maintenance window.

actionable.title: Patch Adobe Commerce and Magento for CVE-2026-48356
actionable.detail: Inventory Commerce, Commerce B2B and Magento Open Source installs, apply Adobe's security update for CVE-2026-48356, and check upload directories for unexpected executable files dropped before the patch.

entries.verify_note: Lessons upheld from the CPE list; the upload mechanism comes from the CISA KEV record, not the NVD page; B2B releases are discrete, not a continuous range.
entries.prior_art: The pool archive already holds an Adobe Commerce and Magento KEV entry for a different bug (CVE-2026-71362, incorrect authorization). Unrestricted dangerous-type upload is a long-known web bug class. The only new fact is that this specific CVE is exploited.
entries.threat: Per CISA, an attacker uploads a file with a dangerous type, which can lead to arbitrary code execution as the current user and control of the victim's account or session.
entries.conditions: Adobe Commerce, Commerce B2B or Magento Open Source on a release listed in NVD's configuration. The fetched page does not name the fixed release.
entries.mitigations: Apply Adobe's update, restrict upload file types and keep uploaded files out of executable paths, and review upload directories for planted files.

editorial.reason: CISA-listed exploited upload flaw spanning every Commerce and Magento Open Source line from 2.4.4 to 2.4.9; storefronts should patch and check upload directories.

entries.title: Ivanti Connect Secure chain to root is exploited, CISA adds two CVEs
entries.summary: CISA added Ivanti Connect Secure flaw CVE-2026-111357 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 30, 2026, with a November 2 due date, and added the related CVE-2026-118527 the same day. In CVE-2026-111357, the dsinvoked broker trusts DSCache configuration data, which lets a local user escalate to root; NVD says it was exploited in October 2026. NVD lists 22.8R2 through 22.8R2.5 and 25.1.0.0 up to 25.1.1.3 as affected, and cites a Volexity report on chained exploitation of Connect Secure zero-days.
entries.takeaway: Treat any Ivanti Connect Secure appliance on an affected 22.8R2 or 25.1 release as possibly rooted: patch it, then hunt for compromise.

lessons.point: The root escalation comes from a privileged broker that trusts configuration data it should not. The flaw was exploited in October 2026.
lessons.excerpt: Ivanti Connect Secure 22.8R2.4 mishandles the manner in which the dsinvoked broker trusts DSCache configuration data, leading to privilege escalation to root, as exploited in the wild in October 2026.

actionable.title: Patch Ivanti Connect Secure 22.8R2.4 and run a compromise hunt
actionable.detail: Apply Ivanti's fix for CVE-2026-104935 / CVE-2026-111357 / CVE-2026-118527. Then follow CISA's forensics triage requirements and Volexity's indicators. A device rooted before patching stays compromised after it.

entries.verify_note: Verifier: lesson on the root escalation holds; summary trimmed to what the NVD page supports (affected range, Volexity reference); the CVE-2026-118527 facts come from the KEV feed.
entries.prior_art: Repeated exploited Ivanti Connect Secure zero-day chains (2024-2026); this is another chain on the same appliance family.
entries.threat: Chained exploitation of a VPN appliance ending in root.
entries.conditions: Ivanti Connect Secure 22.8R2.4 reachable by an attacker.
entries.mitigations: Apply Ivanti's fixed release, run CISA's forensic triage, and rebuild any appliance showing compromise.

editorial.reason: Exploited-in-the-wild Ivanti Connect Secure root escalation with a three-day CISA deadline; the lesson is to patch and then hunt, since a device rooted before patching stays compromised.

entries.title: VibeRaven checks AI-built Supabase apps for missing row-level security
entries.author: ohad6k
entries.summary: VibeRaven is a local CLI and MCP server that scans Vercel and Supabase apps, a stack many AI app builders generate, for launch gaps. It flags public tables without row-level security (RLS), using (true) policies, the service_role key in browser code, anon-callable security definer functions and unverified Stripe webhooks. It reads migrations and code without connecting to the project, names file and line, and exits 1 on a blocker so it can gate CI.
entries.takeaway: Vibe-coded Supabase apps fail in a handful of predictable ways, and a static check in CI can catch several of them before launch.

lessons.point: The checks target a short list of recurring Supabase mistakes, several with no matching Supabase Security Advisor lint.
lessons.excerpt: A policy with `using (true)` that lets anyone read or write every row

lessons.point: A security definer function left callable by anon runs with its owner's rights, so RLS does not limit it.
lessons.excerpt: is security definer, so it runs with its owner's rights and RLS does not limit what it touches.

lessons.point: It is designed as a CI gate and works offline from the repository alone.
lessons.excerpt: It does not connect to your Supabase project or send requests to your app. It exits `1` when it finds a blocker, so it also works as a CI step.

actionable.title: Gate AI-generated Supabase apps on an RLS and secrets check
actionable.detail: Add `npx -y viberaven@1.6.12 check` (pinned) as a required CI step for Supabase projects. Or replicate its rules: every public table has RLS, no `using (true)` write policy, no service_role key in client bundles, and `revoke execute ... from anon` on security definer functions.

entries.prior_art: Supabase's own Security Advisor lints (rls_disabled_in_public, anon_security_definer_function_executable) and general secret scanners; VibeRaven adds offline, migration-based checks for gaps the Advisor does not cover.
entries.threat: Data exposure in AI-generated apps through missing or permissive row-level security and leaked service keys.
entries.conditions: Supabase-backed apps, especially generated by AI app builders.
entries.mitigations: Enable RLS on every public table, scope policies, keep the service_role key server-side, revoke anon execute on security definer functions, verify webhook signatures.

entries.prior_art: Many prior Pillow decompression-bomb and parser-hang DoS advisories; the inherited-method/overridden-tell() root cause is a routine variation.
entries.title: Pillow DoS: a 5.6 KB MIC file hangs n_frames
entries.summary: A crafted 5.6 KB Microsoft Image Composer file makes Pillow loop forever at 100% CPU when code reads im.n_frames, on installs with the optional olefile package. MicImageFile overrides seek() and tell() but inherits TiffImageFile.n_frames, which relies on tell() advancing, so it re-parses the same directory endlessly. The hang raises no exception and grows no memory; the regression dates to Pillow 7.2.0 (2020).

lessons.point: Exposure depends on an optional dependency: only installs with olefile register the MIC plugin.
lessons.excerpt: This only affects installations that have the optional `olefile` package.

lessons.point: Root cause is a subclass that overrides the primitives an inherited method depends on; audit inherited methods when you change seek/tell semantics.
lessons.excerpt: It does not override the `n_frames` property, so the inherited TIFF implementation runs

lessons.point: Silent CPU hangs evade exception handlers and memory limits; untrusted parsing needs a wall-clock watchdog.
lessons.excerpt: The call never returns, raises no exception, and does not grow memory, so only an external watchdog stops it.

lessons.point: The bug has shipped since Pillow 7.2.0.
lessons.excerpt: first released in 7.2.0

entries.takeaway: Affects installs with olefile, back to Pillow 7.2.0. Parse untrusted images under a timeout and restrict Image.open to the formats you expect.

actionable.title: Bound untrusted image parsing
actionable.detail: Pass an explicit formats= allowlist to Image.open for user uploads, drop olefile if you don't need MIC/FPX, and run frame-count and re-save operations in a worker with a wall-clock timeout.

entries.threat: Denial of service: one crafted upload pins a worker at 100% CPU indefinitely.
entries.conditions: olefile installed; the application opens an untrusted image and reads n_frames (e.g. is-animated checks, save_all re-saves).
entries.mitigations: Upgrade Pillow when patched; restrict formats; remove olefile; enforce worker timeouts.

editorial.reason: Fresh HIGH advisory in Pillow, which nearly every Python upload path uses; the fix pattern (formats allowlist, drop olefile, wall-clock timeouts) applies today.

entries.title: raml-kql runs one KQL query across workspaces without a Defender multi-tenant org
entries.author: Luca Ramseyer
entries.summary: Raml KQL is an open-source VS Code-style desktop app that fans one KQL query out to many Azure Log Analytics/Sentinel workspaces across Entra tenants and accounts (found via Lighthouse delegations and guest access) and merges the results with tenant and workspace on every row. It runs with the analyst's delegated permissions and no stored secrets, aliases customer names on screen and keeps a hash-chained audit log. A convenience tool for MSSPs and consultants without a Defender MTO, not a new capability.

lessons.point: Cross-tenant hunting without a Defender MTO is possible from the analyst's own delegated access.
lessons.excerpt: Run one KQL query against many Azure Log Analytics workspaces at once, across many Entra tenants and many signed-in accounts

lessons.point: The design keeps no credentials of its own: it acts only with the user's delegated permissions.
lessons.excerpt: Raml KQL only ever does what you are allowed to do: it uses your delegated permissions and holds no secrets or service principals.

lessons.point: It records query provenance without storing customer data.
lessons.excerpt: A hash-chained audit log records what ran where, without result values.

lessons.point: Customer names are masked by default for screen sharing.
lessons.excerpt: Tenant and workspace names are aliased on screen by default

entries.takeaway: MSSPs without a Defender MTO can hunt across customer Sentinel workspaces from one query with delegated access only.

actionable.title: Cross-tenant hunt queries
actionable.detail: If you operate across customer tenants via Lighthouse, keep a query pack of hunting KQL in git and run it across all workspaces with raml-kql, grouping by _TenantName.

entries.prior_art: Defender multi-tenant advanced hunting, Sentinel/Lighthouse cross-workspace queries with workspace()/union, Sentinel Workbooks.
entries.verify_note: Independent verifier: all excerpts verbatim; novelty 30 (same); niche v1.0 convenience tool.

entries.title: Plex CVE-2026-96652 SSRF lets the /player/timeline protocol parameter force server POSTs
entries.summary: CVE-2026-96652 is an SSRF in Plex Media Server before 1.43.3.10861. The '/player/timeline' endpoint takes a full URL in its 'protocol' parameter, and the server then sends a POST to whatever destination the attacker chose. Per NVD, the attacker can use any X-Plex-Token value. CISA added it to KEV on October 20, 2026 with a November 3 due date, and NVD links the same plex2shell write-up as the sibling CVEs. Its CVSS 4.0 vector rates confidentiality impact as low only (VC:L, no integrity or availability impact), which fits its role as one link in the chain rather than a standalone shell.
entries.takeaway: Upgrade Plex to 1.43.3.10861 or later: this endpoint turns the server into a POST relay with almost no authentication, and it is exploited in the wild as part of the plex2shell chain.

lessons.point: The SSRF sink is a parameter whose name sounds like it holds a scheme ('protocol') but which takes a full URL. Parameters named for URL parts are worth testing as full-URL injection points.
lessons.excerpt: can include a full URL in the 'protocol' parameter and force the Plex server to POST to the attacker's chosen destination

lessons.point: Authentication is effectively nominal: NVD says any token value works, even though the vector says PR:L. A token that is checked for presence but not validated is a separate weakness to look for.
lessons.excerpt: An attacker using any X-Plex-Token value

lessons.point: The fix boundary is precise, so it is easy to check version inventory against it.
lessons.excerpt: Affected 0 < 1.43.3.10861 Unaffected 1.43.3.10861

lessons.point: Rated on its own, the bug is low-impact (confidentiality only), yet KEV-listed because it is used in a chain. Don't deprioritize low-CVSS SSRFs that sit inside a known chain.
lessons.excerpt: CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:L/UI:N/VC:L/VI:N/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N

actionable.title: Patch Plex and test URL-part parameters for full-URL SSRF
actionable.detail: Upgrade Plex Media Server to 1.43.3.10861 or later before the Nov 3, 2026 KEV deadline. Check egress logs from Plex hosts for unexpected outbound POSTs. In appsec testing, put full attacker URLs into parameters named protocol/scheme/host/callback, and check whether auth headers are actually validated or only required to be present.

entries.verify_note: Verifier supported claims 1-4 from the NVD page; the chain membership comes from the pool's sibling entries, not this page. Verifier novelty 22; kept 22.
entries.prior_art: The pool already has sibling Plex KEV stories for CVE-2026-96654 (encoded-URI-scheme plugin call), CVE-2026-96655 (SSRF via /video/:/transcode/universal) and CVE-2026-96656 (arbitrary file write), all in the same four-CVE plex2shell chain. This entry adds only what is specific to -96652: a second, separate SSRF sink on /player/timeline via the 'protocol' parameter, forced POST (not GET), the any-token-value auth weakness, and the exact fixed build.
entries.threat: Unauthenticated-in-practice SSRF that makes Plex POST to attacker-chosen internal or external destinations, used in the wild as part of the plex2shell chain.
entries.conditions: Plex Media Server older than 1.43.3.10861 that the attacker can reach over the network; the attacker supplies any X-Plex-Token value.
entries.mitigations: Upgrade to 1.43.3.10861 or later; restrict network exposure of Plex; limit egress from Plex hosts to internal services.

entries.title: Cisco ASA and FTD VPN crash bug is exploited, CISA gives three days
entries.summary: CVE-2026-76418 lets an unauthenticated remote attacker reload Cisco Secure Firewall ASA and FTD devices by sending a crafted request to the Remote Access SSL VPN service, but only when secondary authentication is configured on a tunnel group. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 29, 2026 with a November 1 due date. The impact is denial of service (availability only), not code execution.
entries.takeaway: If your ASA or FTD VPN uses secondary authentication on a tunnel group, patch now, because attackers are already using this to knock VPNs offline.

lessons.point: The bug is only reachable when secondary authentication is configured on a tunnel group, so exposure can be scoped from configuration.
lessons.excerpt: This vulnerability is due to logic errors when secondary authentication is configured on a tunnel group.

lessons.point: No credentials are needed. The outcome is a device reload, a denial of service against the VPN edge.
lessons.excerpt: could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to cause the device to reload unexpectedly, resulting in a denial of service (DoS) condition

lessons.point: CISA gave federal agencies three days to remediate. The short deadline signals active use.
lessons.excerpt: October 29, 2026 | November 01, 2026

actionable.title: Find ASA/FTD tunnel groups with secondary authentication and patch them first
actionable.detail: Query ASA and FTD configs for tunnel groups with secondary authentication enabled. Those devices are exposed to CVE-2026-76418. Apply Cisco's fixed release from advisory cisco-sa-asaftd-tunnel-dos-s6mgkb75. Watch for unexpected device reloads as an exploitation signal.

entries.prior_art: Earlier exploited Cisco ASA/FTD WebVPN denial-of-service bugs; this is another instance of the same class.
entries.threat: Unauthenticated remote denial of service against the VPN edge.
entries.conditions: Cisco ASA or FTD running Remote Access SSL VPN with secondary authentication configured on a tunnel group, on an unfixed release.
entries.mitigations: Upgrade to a fixed ASA/FTD release per the Cisco advisory, and alert on unexpected device reloads.

editorial.reason: Actively exploited unauthenticated VPN-edge DoS in CISA KEV with a three-day deadline; exposure is scoped by one config check (secondary authentication on a tunnel group).

entries.title: Exploited VMware ESX flaw lets attacker with admin rights act unlogged
entries.summary: CVE-2026-41709 is an insufficient-logging flaw in VMware ESX: an attacker who already holds administrator rights can perform certain operations without them being logged. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 28, 2026 with a November 11 due date. It needs high privileges, so it is an anti-forensics aid after compromise, not an entry point.
entries.takeaway: ESX audit logs may be silent about what a hijacked admin did, so do not treat clean ESX logs as proof of no tampering.

lessons.point: The flaw helps an attacker who already has admin access hide actions from the hypervisor's logs.
lessons.excerpt: A malicious administrator could exploit this issue to perform certain operations without them being logged.

lessons.point: The vendor's score reflects high privileges required and integrity-only impact.
lessons.excerpt: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N

actionable.title: Patch ESX and add an out-of-band log source for hypervisor admin actions
actionable.detail: Apply Broadcom advisory 38017. Because ESX's own logs can miss these operations, also capture vCenter events and network flow logs for ESX management interfaces, and alert on admin logins from unexpected hosts.

entries.prior_art: Earlier ESXi anti-forensics techniques by intrusion sets such as UNC3886 that disabled or evaded hypervisor logging.
entries.threat: An attacker with ESX admin rights hides operations from logs.
entries.conditions: Unpatched VMware ESX and an attacker who already holds administrator access.
entries.mitigations: Patch per Broadcom advisory 38017 and keep an independent log source for hypervisor management actions.

editorial.reason: Exploited ESX logging gap in KEV; the transferable lesson is that clean hypervisor logs are not proof of no tampering, so keep an out-of-band log source.

entries.title: HPE bulletin HPESBNW05162 lists CVSS 10.0 unauthenticated RCE flaws in ArubaOS
entries.summary: HPE Networking bulletin HPESBNW05162 lists multiple critical flaws in AOS-10 and AOS-8, each scored CVSS 10.0. They include authentication bypass leading to remote code execution, bypass of PAPI protocol controls, unauthenticated command injection and an unauthenticated buffer overflow. HPE says the bugs were generally found by internal research and it knows of no public exploit code, and tells customers to patch quickly and to restrict management interfaces.

lessons.point: The flaws were found internally and no exploit was known at release.
lessons.excerpt: HPE Networking is not aware of any public discussion or exploit code that targets the listed vulnerabilities as of the release date of this advisory.

lessons.point: Workaround: put management on a dedicated segment with firewall controls.
lessons.excerpt: HPE Networking recommends that the CLI and web-based management interfaces be restricted to a dedicated layer 2 segment/VLAN

lessons.point: Unauthenticated memory corruption reaches RCE in AOS-10.
lessons.excerpt: Unauthenticated Buffer Overflow Vulnerabilities leads to Remote Code Execution in AOS-10 (CVE-2026-79847)

lessons.point: Discovery was in-house.
lessons.excerpt: These vulnerabilities were generally discovered by internal security research at HPE Networking.

entries.takeaway: Patch ArubaOS and isolate management interfaces on a dedicated VLAN.

actionable.title: Patch and segment wireless management
actionable.detail: Apply the AOS-10 and AOS-8 fixes, move controllers and conductors' management planes to a dedicated VLAN with firewall rules, and monitor for exploitation once proofs of concept appear.

entries.prior_art: Large vendor advisory batches are routine; no novel technique reported. Verifier: Routine Aruba/HPE multi-CVE bulletins (e.g., ArubaOS PAPI buffer overflow advisories 2022-2025); only the all-10.0 scoring is notable
entries.verify_note: Independent fresh-context verifier re-read the source; discrepancies it found (title/summary overstatements) were corrected before merge.

editorial.reason: Batch of CVSS 10.0 unauthenticated flaws in ArubaOS.

entries.title: Cloudflare pairs Daybreak findings with live traffic to draft WAF rules
entries.summary: Cloudflare's early-access Vulnerability Discovery and Remediation service uses OpenAI models accessed through Daybreak to investigate customer-authorized code. It ranks findings by production context: whether the affected route is live, whether it is getting suspicious traffic, and whether existing controls already cover it. It then drafts both code patches and temporary custom WAF rules, which go through automated checks and Cloudflare staff review before customers see them. It is an OpenAI customer story with no accuracy or false-positive data. The rest is Codex productivity claims.
entries.takeaway: The useful pattern is ranking LLM-found code vulns by runtime reachability and traffic, and pairing each fix with a temporary edge rule. The article gives no evidence that it works well.

lessons.point: Prioritize static or LLM vuln findings using production signals, not severity alone.
lessons.excerpt: Is the affected route active? Is it receiving suspicious traffic? Are existing security controls already protecting it?

lessons.point: Pair each proposed code fix with a temporary edge mitigation, so exposure shrinks while the patch is reviewed.
lessons.excerpt: The service prepares proposed code patches and, where appropriate, custom web application firewall rules to reduce exposure while developers review a fix.

lessons.point: Model-generated fixes go through automated checks and human review before release.
lessons.excerpt: Cloudflare runs automated checks on these proposals, and its team reviews them before sharing them with customers.

actionable.title: Join AI vuln findings to route-level traffic and WAF coverage before triage
actionable.detail: For each AI- or SAST-reported finding, map the vulnerable handler to its HTTP route. Add three fields from edge/APM logs: route hit in the last 30 days, anomalous/attack-signature traffic on it, and an existing WAF rule covering it. Sort on those fields. For live, exposed, unprotected routes, draft a temporary WAF rule alongside the patch PR.

entries.verify_note: Verifier supported all claims; no accuracy or false-positive data in the article. Verifier novelty 35; kept 28.
entries.prior_art: The nearest pool entry is the OpenAI Daybreak/Sophos MDR customer story (product-security.json), which has vendor-only metrics. This one adds a different use, appsec vuln discovery joined to runtime traffic context with WAF virtual patches, but it is still a vendor customer story with no measurements. Reachability-based prioritization and virtual patching are long-established ideas.

entries.title: CISA KEV: Plex Media Server file write CVE-2026-96656 exploited in the wild
entries.summary: CISA's KEV catalog lists CVE-2026-96656, an external control of file name or path flaw in Plex Media Server that lets an admin user write arbitrary files that may be executed on load, as exploited in the wild (added October 20, 2026). It chains with CVE-2026-96652, -96654 and -96655. The fetched NVD page was empty, so nothing here is grounded beyond the KEV catalog text.

lessons.point: An admin-only file write becomes code execution because written files may be executed on load, and the other chained CVEs plausibly supply the admin context.
lessons.excerpt: can allow an admin user to write arbitrary files that may be executed on load

lessons.point: It is one link in a four-CVE chain; patch all of them together.
lessons.excerpt: This vulnerability can be chained with CVE-2026-96652, CVE-2026-96654, and CVE-2026-96655.

entries.takeaway: Treat the four Plex KEV CVEs as one chain and patch together.

actionable.title: Patch Plex Media Server
actionable.detail: Update Plex Media Server to the fixed release covering CVE-2026-96652/-96654/-96655/-96656.

entries.prior_art: Same chain as CVE-2026-96654 in this batch; earlier Plex KEV CVE-2020-5741 was also an admin file write to code execution.
entries.verify_note: Source text not captured (NVD page empty); lessons rest on the KEV catalog text only.

entries.title: Openwave Webtop Media Transcoder file-type restriction bypass is exploited
entries.summary: The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-111793 in Openwave Webtop Media Transcoder to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on November 10, 2026. The transcoder does not enforce administrator-defined file-type restrictions, so an authenticated user who bypasses the Webmail front end can have it convert unintended document types. Versions before 1.1.22.0 are affected, and the CVE Numbering Authority (CNA) vector shows availability impact only.

lessons.point: The transcoder itself does not enforce administrator-defined file-type restrictions, so going around the Webmail front end bypasses them.
lessons.excerpt: Openwave Webtop Media Transcoder does not enforce administrator-defined file type restrictions to restrict the file-types to be converted.

lessons.point: Exploitation requires an authenticated user going around the normal Webmail flow.
lessons.excerpt: This may allow an authenticated user to process and convert unintended document types if bypassing the Webmail experience.

lessons.point: A Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) vector with only low availability impact did not stop this from being exploited, so Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) status should outrank CVSS in patch triage.
lessons.excerpt: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L

entries.takeaway: Operators of Openwave Webtop should upgrade the Media Transcoder to 1.1.22.0 and enforce file-type policy server-side.

actionable.title: Upgrade the transcoder and enforce policy at the backend
actionable.detail: Upgrade Webtop Media Transcoder to 1.1.22.0 or later and ensure file-type allowlists are checked by the transcoder service itself, not only by the Webmail front end.

entries.verify_note: Verifier found the 'low score' label wrong (the vector computes to 4.3, Medium) and the UI-only enforcement mechanism inferred; text corrected, held for a human check.
entries.prior_art: Classic client-side/front-end-only enforcement bypass; routine KEV listing for a niche messaging product. No prior Openwave entry.
entries.threat: An authenticated user calls the media transcoder directly to convert document types administrators meant to block.
entries.conditions: Openwave Webtop Media Transcoder before 1.1.22.0 reachable outside the Webmail front end by an authenticated user.
entries.mitigations: Upgrade to 1.1.22.0 or later per the Openwave advisory and enforce file-type restrictions server-side.

entries.title: CISA says a low-severity VMware ESX logging gap is being exploited
entries.summary: CISA added CVE-2026-41709 to its KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities) catalog on October 28, 2026, with a deadline of November 11. The flaw lets a malicious ESX administrator perform certain operations that are never logged. VMware scores it only 2.7 (low) because it needs high privileges, yet it is exploited in the wild. A gap like this can hide an intruder's actions from forensic review.

lessons.point: The weakness is a missing audit trail, not code execution, so an attacker who already has admin access can act unseen.
lessons.excerpt: A malicious administrator could exploit this issue to perform certain operations without them being logged.

lessons.point: A low CVSS score that requires high privileges did not keep this bug out of real attacks.
lessons.excerpt: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N

lessons.point: Fixed builds are listed per release line, including ESX 8.0 and 9.0.
lessons.excerpt: Affected 9.0.x.x < ESXi-9.0.2.0100-25595025 Affected 8.0 < ESXi80U3j-25429389

entries.takeaway: Do not deprioritize low-CVSS ESX logging bugs: attackers who already hold admin access use them to hide what they do.

actionable.title: Patch ESX and stop relying on host logs alone for admin activity
actionable.detail: Upgrade ESX to ESXi80U3j-25429389, ESXi-9.0.2.0100-25595025 or ESXi-9.1.0.0-25370933 or later. Also patch the bundled VCF, vSphere Foundation and Telco Cloud Platform builds per Broadcom advisory 38017. Until then, treat ESX host logs as incomplete for admin sessions. Watch for admin activity from other places as well, such as vCenter events and network or management-plane telemetry.

entries.verify_note: Verifier: score, dates, fixed builds and advisory confirmed; exploitation rests on the KEV listing alone, with no attack details in the source.
entries.prior_art: Similar to 'Partisan Zmiy hid the Vasilek backdoor in VMware Tools for two years' (hiding on VMware infrastructure) and the routine CISA KEV entries in product-security. An exploited logging-evasion bug with a low CVSS score is a modest variation.
entries.threat: An attacker with ESX admin access uses the logging gap to carry out certain operations without leaving audit records, which weakens detection and forensics.
entries.conditions: VMware ESX 8.0 before ESXi80U3j, 9.0.x before 9.0.2.0100, or 9.1.x before the fixed build, including Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation and Telco Cloud Platform deployments. The attacker must already have admin privileges.
entries.mitigations: Apply Broadcom's fixed ESX builds by CISA's November 11, 2026 deadline. Limit and monitor who holds ESX admin access. Record admin activity from sources other than the ESX host's own logs.

entries.title: Chainguard rebuilds every buildable Linux distribution font from source
entries.summary: Chainguard's audit of prebuilt artifacts in Chainguard OS found that fonts were the largest remaining class of unverified upstream binaries, which most Linux distributions also ship prebuilt. In about three weeks it rebuilt 2,347 font files from source, verified them by comparing glyph tables and rendered pixels rather than bytes, and added a linter that fails any recipe copying a compiled font without a documented exception. The vendor says the direct exploit risk is real but low-probability: no distribution's shipped fonts are known to have been poisoned. The main gains are provenance and fixability, and the rebuilds surfaced stale binaries and broken toolchain output.

lessons.point: Font files contain executable bytecode that renderers run, so a font is code parsed by memory-unsafe C and C++ libraries, not passive data.
lessons.excerpt: Hinting (fpgm, prep, and per-glyph instructions) is bytecode for a stack machine that the rasterizer runs for every glyph at every size.

lessons.point: Font builds are not byte-reproducible across toolchain versions, so verifying a rebuild means comparing tables, metrics and rendered output.
lessons.excerpt: Font binaries are never byte-identical across toolchain versions, so we compared meaning instead of bytes

lessons.point: A linter that fails builds which copy compiled upstream binaries, unless they carry a documented reason, enforces the from-source policy. It found more prebuilt packages than the manual audit did.
lessons.excerpt: The audit counted 19 prebuilt font packages. The linter found 26

lessons.point: Rebuilding exposed packages that shipped older binaries than their declared versions, which shows that unbuilt artifacts' metadata cannot be trusted.
lessons.excerpt: the version on a binary you did not build is a claim, not a fact

entries.takeaway: Container images and distributions ship prebuilt fonts that rendering libraries execute, so treat them as unverified binaries in the supply chain. The concrete payoff of building them from source is provenance, not a known attack.

actionable.title: Lint build recipes for copied prebuilt binaries
actionable.detail: Add a build-recipe lint that fails any step copying a compiled artifact (fonts first: .ttf, .otf) from an upstream download or a cloned repo without a compiler step, unless it carries an allowlisted reason (no sources, license, missing toolchain, broken sources, untagged upstream, conversion in progress) and a tracking issue. Also scan cloned repositories for committed binaries, which Chainguard's manual audit missed.

entries.verify_note: Verifier upheld all four lessons; fonts-as-code and build-from-source are known (novelty 30 vs 50, lower kept).
entries.prior_art: The build-from-source and reproducible-builds movements and distribution font policies (Fedora's guidance that fonts should be built from source) are long-standing, and Project Zero's 2015 font research established fonts as an attack surface. The pool has no entry on fonts as a supply-chain artifact. The nearest is the product-security lesson on treating released binaries as reproducible source.
entries.threat: A tampered upstream font release in a container image could deliver an exploit for a renderer bug, change rendered content without changing the text, or hide a payload in unknown tables. The source finds no case of a distribution's shipped fonts being poisoned.
entries.conditions: Images or distributions that ship prebuilt upstream TrueType or OpenType files and render text with FreeType, HarfBuzz, headless Chrome, LibreOffice, ImageMagick, Java or PDF generators. Exploitation also needs an unpatched renderer bug.
entries.mitigations: Build fonts from source pinned to upstream tags, verify rebuilds against the upstream release by comparing glyph tables and rendered pixels, enforce the policy with a build linter that requires a documented exception, run upgrade tests on package splits, and patch font renderers promptly.

issues: mild: sentence_words 50 > 45 (Add a build-recipe lint that fails any step copying a compiled artifact (fonts first: .ttf, .otf) from an upstream downl)

entries.title: SonicWall says it will not fix two flaws in end-of-life GMS
entries.summary: SonicWall says its legacy Global Management System (GMS) has two flaws it will not patch, because the product reached end of life in October 2025. One is a critical file-read bug that needs no login, and the other is a medium-severity SQL injection. WatchGuard's most severe advisory is CVE-2026-98432 (CVSS 9.8), a Linux kernel use-after-free, and it also fixed three critical authentication bugs in AuthPoint Authentication Gateway. Cisco fixed CVE-2026-76506, a high-severity flaw in UCS (Unified Computing System) Central Software that lets authenticated attackers run code remotely.

lessons.point: End-of-life management platforms keep collecting critical bugs that will never be patched. The only real fix is to retire them or isolate them from the network.
lessons.excerpt: The first, CVE-2026-109593, is a critical-severity file read bug that can be exploited without authentication

lessons.point: A vendor patch can still leave gaps. WatchGuard Dimension runs a vulnerable Ubuntu version with no fix yet.
lessons.excerpt: Dimension runs a vulnerable Ubuntu version, but patches are not available yet, WatchGuard says.

lessons.point: Neither vendor knew of in-the-wild exploitation when the fixes were released.
lessons.excerpt: Both WatchGuard and Cisco say they are not aware of any of these vulnerabilities being exploited in the wild.

entries.takeaway: If SonicWall GMS is still running, take it off the network or replace it, because its pre-auth file-read bug will never be patched.

actionable.title: Retire or isolate SonicWall GMS and patch AuthPoint and UCS Central
actionable.detail: Find any SonicWall GMS instances and remove them from internet and general network reach, then plan migration off the platform. Apply WatchGuard's AuthPoint Authentication Gateway fixes and Cisco's UCS Central fix for CVE-2026-76506. Track WatchGuard Dimension until an Ubuntu kernel patch ships.

entries.verify_note: Independent verifier supported every detail; added the omitted CVSS 9.8 WatchGuard kernel bug (CVE-2026-98432) to the summary.
entries.prior_art: none found (patch roundup; no prior entries for SonicWall GMS, WatchGuard AuthPoint or UCS Central)
entries.threat: Unauthenticated file read and SQL injection in end-of-life SonicWall GMS, critical authentication flaws in WatchGuard AuthPoint Authentication Gateway, and authenticated RCE in Cisco UCS Central.
entries.conditions: Organizations still running SonicWall GMS, or unpatched AuthPoint Authentication Gateway or UCS Central Software.
entries.mitigations: Decommission or network-isolate SonicWall GMS, and apply the WatchGuard and Cisco updates.

entries.title: Russian hackers reportedly use stealthy Exchange malware against government email
entries.summary: CyberInsider reports that Russian hackers used stealthy malware on Microsoft Exchange servers to steal government emails. The captured source holds only the headline and site navigation, not the article body. The URL suggests the malware is called Cereal, but the captured text has no technique, actor attribution, victim list or indicators.

lessons.point: The headline claims a Russian operation used covert Exchange-resident malware to steal government mail. Nothing in the captured text says how it works.
lessons.excerpt: Russian hackers use stealthy Exchange malware to steal government emails

lessons.point: The article URL names the malware 'cereal' and the target 'microsoft-exchange'. That is the only detail beyond the headline, so treat it as unconfirmed until the full report is read.
lessons.excerpt: https://cyberinsider.com/russian-hackers-cereal-malware-microsoft-exchange-attacks/

entries.takeaway: Only a headline is available, so wait for the full CyberInsider or vendor report before acting on it.

actionable.title: Fetch the full report before hunting
actionable.detail: The raw capture has no article body. Re-fetch the CyberInsider article or the original vendor research to get indicators and the persistence method for the 'Cereal' Exchange malware before you scope any Exchange threat hunt.

entries.verify_note: Captured source holds only the headline; lessons are hedged accordingly.
entries.prior_art: Turla LightNeuron; APT28 and APT29 Exchange intrusions.

entries.title: macOS 27 breaks normal access to encrypted HFS+ volumes on CoreStorage
entries.author: colejohnson66
entries.summary: Wade Tregaskis reports that macOS 27 cannot mount, convert to APFS or erase encrypted HFS+ volumes on CoreStorage through Disk Utility or diskutil, while a boot dialog says support ends in macOS 28. A low-level read-only mount with mount_hfs still works, and deleting the logical volumes then rebooting finally lets the disk be erased. The author had to rebuild the volumes from backups.
entries.takeaway: Migrate CoreStorage and encrypted HFS+ volumes to APFS before upgrading to macOS 27, and have backups ready.

lessons.point: The normal tools fail on these volumes in macOS 27, despite the dialog naming macOS 28.
lessons.excerpt: can’t mount them, can’t convert them to APFS, can’t even erase them

lessons.point: A read-only low-level mount still recovers the data.
lessons.excerpt: sudo mount_hfs -o rdonly /dev/disk27 /Volumes/Smash

actionable.title: Inventory CoreStorage volumes before the macOS 27 upgrade
actionable.detail: Run `diskutil cs list` on managed Macs before upgrading to macOS 27. Convert any CoreStorage or encrypted HFS+ volumes to APFS first, and if one is already stranded, copy data off with a read-only `mount_hfs` mount before erasing.

entries.prior_art: Apple's deprecation of CoreStorage and HFS+ conversion problems in macOS 15 Sequoia, which the author describes.
entries.verify_note: Verifier found both lessons supported, from a single-machine anecdote; noted it is a deprecation and data-access issue, not a security flaw. Novelty kept at the lower 30.

entries.title: BeyondTrust Remote Support flaw lets a remote attacker perform file operations
entries.summary: BeyondTrust advisory BT26-05 (CVE-2026-102764, CWE-290) covers a critical flaw in an internal messaging component of Remote Support that did not validate message origin, allowing file operations on the appliance. SaaS customers were patched by October 9, 2026; self-hosted customers on versions 24.3.1 through 26.2.3 must apply the BT26-05-RS patch, and older versions must upgrade first. The advisory does not say whether the flaw is being exploited.

lessons.point: Root cause: messages were accepted without origin validation.
lessons.excerpt: The components did not adequately validate the origin of the messages it received.

lessons.point: SaaS is already fixed; self-hosted needs a manual patch.
lessons.excerpt: As of Oct 9, 2026, a patch that remediates this vulnerability has been applied to all Remote Support SaaS customers.

lessons.point: Old versions must upgrade first.
lessons.excerpt: Customers on a Remote Support version older than 24.3.1 will need to upgrade to a newer version to apply this patch.

entries.takeaway: Patch self-hosted Remote Support now and treat remote-support appliances as top-priority edge assets.

actionable.title: Patch and review remote support appliances
actionable.detail: Apply BT26-05-RS or upgrade, restrict appliance exposure, and review file-system and session activity on the appliance since October 9.

entries.prior_art: BeyondTrust Remote Support has a recurring history of critical pre-auth bugs; this advisory adds nothing technique-wise. Verifier: BeyondTrust Remote Support CVE-2024-12356/12686 and CVE-2025-1094 advisories; generic remote-support appliance flaws (ScreenConnect, Ivanti)
entries.verify_note: Independent fresh-context verifier re-read the source; discrepancies it found (title/summary overstatements) were corrected before merge.

editorial.reason: Critical Remote Support advisory; self-hosted customers must patch manually.

entries.title: Socket finds 319 Chrome extensions that hijacked searches through operator servers
entries.summary: Socket researcher John Tuckner found 319 Chrome extensions with about 13.4 million installs over ten years. They took over the default search setting and sent every query through the operators' servers before passing it on to Yahoo or Bing. Ads for 'PDF converters', 'manual finders' and 'AI search' drove the installs. Most of the extensions were unlisted in Google's official store, so only people with a direct link could find them.

lessons.point: The campaign was large and lasted a long time: 319 extensions and about 13.4 million installs over a decade.
lessons.excerpt: researcher John Tuckner identified 319 extensions with an estimated 13.4 million installs over a decade.

lessons.point: An unlisted extension in the official store still looks trustworthy, but store search never shows it. That keeps it away from casual review while ads send victims straight to the listing.
lessons.excerpt: The extensions were listed in Google’s official store, but most were unlisted.

lessons.point: The search proxy is a privacy breach, not only ad fraud. A unique identifier on each query let the operators build a search history for each user.
lessons.excerpt: Socket says queries were often associated with a unique identifier, which could let the operators link a user’s searches over time.

lessons.point: If Chrome says an extension controls the search setting, review or remove that extension. The absence of that notice does not prove the extensions are safe.
lessons.excerpt: If Chrome says an extension is controlling a setting, review or remove that extension.

entries.takeaway: Treat an official-store listing as no trust signal for browser extensions, because unlisted, ad-promoted extensions can quietly proxy every search a user makes.

actionable.title: Allowlist browser extensions and check for search-setting overrides
actionable.detail: On managed Chrome, use the ExtensionInstallAllowlist/ExtensionInstallBlocklist policies so users cannot install unlisted extensions promoted through ads. Check endpoints for extensions that control the default search engine, and compare installed IDs with Socket's published list at socket.dev/blog/searchjacked.

entries.verify_note: Verifier: claims supported, the 'triage signal' lesson slightly overstated and reworded. Novelty lowered to the verifier's 30.
entries.prior_art: No browser-extension search-hijacking entry exists in the pool. The nearest are the archive entries on Open VSX/Cursor extension identity and the Markdown Preview Enhanced extension RCE, which are IDE extensions with a different claim. This is a Malwarebytes rewrite of Socket's research.
entries.threat: Operators get users to install browser extensions through ads. The extensions take over the default search engine, send all queries through attacker servers that can read and link them per user, and could redirect users to phishing or malware pages, although Socket found no evidence that this happened.
entries.conditions: A user installs an extension advertised as a PDF, manual-finder, safe-search or AI-search tool from an ad link, usually an unlisted Chrome Web Store listing, and lets it change the default search setting.
entries.mitigations: Review chrome://extensions and remove unknown or unused extensions. Check Settings > Search engine for an extension-controlled notice. Compare installed extensions with Socket's list. In enterprises, enforce an extension allowlist through Chrome policy.
entries.author: @Dinosn

entries.title: Joost de Valk's open website specification covers security headers and agent readiness
entries.summary: jdevalk/specification.website (923 stars) is a platform-agnostic specification for websites; the code is MIT-licensed and the content is CC BY 4.0. It gathers rules from the Web Hypertext Application Technology Working Group (WHATWG), the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) and search-engine sources into one sourced reference. Categories include security headers, /.well-known/ Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs) and agent readiness such as llms.txt. Each requirement carries a status (Required, Recommended, Optional, Avoid), and the content is also exposed through a hosted MCP server. The README describes structure only, not the security requirements themselves.

lessons.point: It consolidates web standards from several bodies into one cited reference, useful as a baseline checklist.
lessons.excerpt: This site collects the slices into one platform-agnostic specification — sources cited on every page.

lessons.point: Security and agent readiness are categories alongside search engine optimization (SEO) and accessibility, so it is a general web-hygiene reference rather than a security standard.
lessons.excerpt: **Security** — headers, transport, policies.

lessons.point: The spec is exposed to agents through an MCP server and llms.txt files generated from the source markdown.

entries.title: Attackers exploit a Cisco ASA and FTD VPN bug to crash firewalls
entries.summary: CISA added CVE-2026-76418 to its KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities) catalog on October 29, 2026, with a remediation deadline of November 1. The bug is in the Remote Access SSL VPN service of Cisco Secure Firewall ASA (Adaptive Security Appliance) and FTD (Firewall Threat Defense) software. An unauthenticated attacker can send a crafted request that reloads the device, causing a denial of service, but only when secondary authentication is configured on a tunnel group.

lessons.point: The flaw comes from logic errors in tunnel groups that have secondary authentication configured, so check those configurations first.
lessons.excerpt: This vulnerability is due to logic errors when secondary authentication is configured on a tunnel group.

lessons.point: The attacker needs no credentials, only network access to the SSL VPN endpoint.
lessons.excerpt: An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending a crafted request when connecting to the SSL remote access VPN.

lessons.point: CISA gave a three-day deadline, which signals urgent patching for internet-facing VPN headends.
lessons.excerpt: Cisco Secure FTD Software Unchecked Return Value to NULL Pointer Dereference Vulnerability | October 29, 2026 | November 01, 2026

entries.takeaway: If your ASA or FTD SSL VPN uses secondary authentication, patch now: unauthenticated attackers are already using this bug to reload the device.

actionable.title: Patch ASA/FTD SSL VPN headends that use secondary auth
actionable.detail: List the ASA and FTD devices running Remote Access SSL VPN and find the tunnel groups with secondary authentication configured. The NVD record bounds affected releases below ASA 9.16.4.104, 9.18.4.96, 9.20.4.50, 9.22.3.200, 9.23.1.48 and 9.24.1.27 and FTD 7.0.11, 7.2.13, 7.4.9, 7.7.14 and 10.0.3, and lists FTD 7.6.x through 7.6.7 as affected. Some lines (FTD 7.3, 7.6, 10.1) have no fixed build in that record, so take exact fixed releases from Cisco advisory cisco-sa-asaftd-tunnel-dos-s6mgkb75. Watch for unexpected device reloads.

entries.verify_note: Verifier: claims hold; 'only' secondary-auth tunnel groups was an inference and the version list was NVD upper bounds, not named fixed releases. Both reworded.
entries.prior_art: The pool already has routine CISA KEV appliance entries such as 'CISA KEV: exploited Fortinet CVE-2025-61624 lets read-write admins write or delete files'. This is another exploited edge-appliance bug and adds no new technique.
entries.threat: An unauthenticated remote attacker sends a crafted request to the SSL remote access VPN and triggers a NULL pointer dereference that reloads the firewall, cutting off service.
entries.conditions: Cisco Secure Firewall ASA or FTD software in affected versions with Remote Access SSL VPN enabled and secondary authentication configured on a tunnel group.
entries.mitigations: Apply Cisco's fixed releases from advisory cisco-sa-asaftd-tunnel-dos-s6mgkb75 by CISA's November 1, 2026 deadline, following BOD 26-04 and CISA's forensics triage requirements.

editorial.reason: An exploited, unauthenticated ASA/FTD SSL VPN crash with a three-day CISA deadline; the actionable check is which tunnel groups use secondary authentication.

entries.title: Microsoft Research podcast profiles Cyber Grand Challenge lead Mike Walker
entries.summary: A Microsoft Research podcast interview with Mike Walker, who led DARPA's Cyber Grand Challenge, the first all-machine hacking tournament, and now works on AI and cybersecurity at Microsoft Research. Most of it is career biography: childhood, DEF CON Capture the Flag, and how DARPA asked whether machines could play CTF. The security content is general reflection, such as the view that security controls spend user trust and that autonomous adversarial systems cannot be meaningfully tested before a real fight.
entries.takeaway: A career-profile podcast with little technical content, useful mainly as background on how autonomous hacking competitions began.

lessons.point: Walker frames every security control as a request for user trust, and argues that squandering that trust makes the security regime fail.
lessons.excerpt: every time a security system asks something of users, then you’re asking for their trust. And that trust is a precious commodity.

lessons.point: The Cyber Grand Challenge final ran autonomous systems behind an air gap with no human able to intervene, an early template for fully autonomous offense and defense.
lessons.excerpt: that was run entirely by autonomous systems behind an air gap, so if they failed, there was no person even to turn them off and turn them back on again.

lessons.point: Adversarial autonomous systems are hard to test in advance: teams only had a scripted opponent, so the first real confrontation was the actual competition.
lessons.excerpt: you can’t really preflight an autonomous system whose purpose is to fight.

actionable.title: Test autonomous security agents against live adversaries, not only scripted ones
actionable.detail: If you build autonomous offensive or defensive agents, a scripted opponent prepares the agent only weakly for real adversaries. Plan adversarial exercises against other adaptive systems or red teams before you trust the agent's behavior.

entries.prior_art: DARPA Cyber Grand Challenge history (2016) is widely documented. The nearest entry is Anthropic's red-team note that Claude reached undergraduate-level CTF skill (ai-security.json). This podcast adds no new technical claim.

entries.title: Check Point weekly digest covers cPGuard supply-chain attack and ARTEX campaigns
entries.summary: Check Point Research's weekly digest for November 9, 2026 lists incidents rather than new research. It covers a hijacked cPGuard update channel that ran a backdoor script on about 2,950 customer servers, ransomware at Queens Public Library, and a destructive attack on Russian host Beget. Its AI section repeats Check Point's ARTEX findings (1,608 exposed instances) and a jailbreak bundle for OpenAI Codex that rewrites agent instructions to promote an outside AI gateway. It also lists patches for SonicWall, Barracuda, Android and the OpenSSH flaw that let oversized passwords bypass authentication.
entries.takeaway: A roundup with little new analysis; follow its links to the primary reports for anything actionable.

lessons.point: A compromised security-tool update channel pushed a backdoor to thousands of servers.
lessons.excerpt: Approximately 2,950 customer servers executed the malicious script, which installed a backdoor and collected password hashes

lessons.point: Many ARTEX agentic attack consoles are reachable on the internet.
lessons.excerpt: Researchers identified 1,608 live, publicly accessible instances.

lessons.point: Jailbreak bundles for coding agents can quietly rewrite agent instructions for commercial ends.
lessons.excerpt: a jailbreak bundle targeting OpenAI Codex that weakens safeguards and modifies agent instructions to promote an external AI gateway

actionable.title: Use as a link index only
actionable.detail: Pull the cPGuard, ARTEX and Haiou primary reports linked from the digest if those products are in your estate; the digest itself adds no detail beyond one-line summaries.

entries.verify_note: Independent verifier found every lesson supported by the source.
entries.prior_art: Check Point ARTEX entry already in the pool and earlier weekly roundups (Check Point digest on PHP2Shell, The Hacker News weekly roundup).

entries.title: Apple patches 286 flaws and backports exploited CoreGraphics fix to iOS 18
entries.summary: Apple's October 26 updates fix 263 vulnerabilities in macOS Golden Gate 27.2 and 163 in iOS and iPadOS 27.2, with about 140 shared, for 286 in total. iOS and iPadOS 18.7.11 now carry the fix for CVE-2026-86950, the CoreGraphics zero-day Apple says was exploited in an extremely sophisticated attack and first patched in late September. The macOS release also fixes a Remote Management bug that could let a remote attacker run code.

lessons.point: Devices that stayed on iOS 18 lacked the fix for the exploited CoreGraphics bug until this backport.
lessons.excerpt: iOS and iPadOS 18.7.11 fix three vulnerabilities, including CVE-2026-86950, which had been exploited as a zero-day in what Apple described as an “extremely sophisticated attack.”

lessons.point: macOS 27.2 also closes a remotely reachable code execution bug in Remote Management.
lessons.excerpt: including a Remote Management bug that could allow a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code.

lessons.point: No public details exist about the attacks that used the zero-day.
lessons.excerpt: There does not appear to be any public information detailing the attacks exploiting CVE-2026-86950.

entries.takeaway: Push iOS 18.7.11 to devices that cannot run iOS 27, and patch Macs that expose Remote Management or Screen Sharing.

actionable.title: Patch the iOS 18 fleet and Macs with remote services
actionable.detail: Use mobile device management to push iOS and iPadOS 18.7.11 to devices that cannot move to 27.x, and prioritize macOS 27.2, Tahoe 26.7.2 or Sequoia 15.8.2 on Macs with Remote Management, Screen Sharing or SMB reachable from the network.

entries.verify_note: Numbers and dates check out; the iOS 18 exposure lesson is an inference from the backport.
entries.prior_art: The pool already has the CISA KEV entry for CVE-2026-86950 and its September fix; the new facts are the iOS 18 backport and the size of the 27.2 release.
entries.threat: Exploited CoreGraphics memory corruption on older iPhones, plus remote code execution in macOS Remote Management.
entries.conditions: iPhones and iPads on iOS 18 before 18.7.11, and Macs before the October 26 updates.
entries.mitigations: Install iOS and iPadOS 18.7.11 or 27.2 and the matching macOS updates.
